Key transformation: Sr^2+ pairs with Cl^–, NH4^+ pairs with Br^–. Typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required; water acts as solvent.

Acid‑base hydrolysis (neutralization) of boron trichloride with potassium hydroxide; analogous to the NaOH case, producing boric acid and potassium chloride. Three equivalents of KOH react with BCl3 to give H3BO3 and KCl. Carried out in water at low to moderate temperature (0‑25 °C); no catalyst is needed.

Acid‑salt metathesis (protonation of azide); transforms thallium azide to thallium chloride while liberating hydrazoic acid; TlN3 + HCl → TlCl + HN3; carried out in dilute HCl solution at low temperature (ice bath) in a well‑ventilated hood; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation. Sodium azide exchanges with copper(I) iodide, forming copper(I) azide solid and NaI in solution. Carried out in water or dilute aqueous solvent, kept cold and in the dark; solid filtered and washed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide by hydroxide; converts 8‑bromooctan‑1‑ol to 1,8‑octanediol. Hydroxide attacks the carbon bearing bromine, displacing Br^– and forming the second hydroxyl group. Conducted in aqueous NaOH or aqueous/ethanol mixture, often refluxed to ensure completion; no catalyst needed. Common solvents: water, ethanol, or a water/ethanol blend.

Hydrolysis of an N‑nitrosamine; water attacks the N‑nitroso group, yielding dimethylamine and nitrous acid. This is a nucleophilic addition‑elimination (hydrolytic cleavage) reaction. Usually carried out in aqueous media, sometimes with mild heating; the reaction can be accelerated under acidic conditions (pH ≈ 3–5). No catalyst required; solvent is water.

Methanolysis (transesterification) of an alkyl benzoate. Purpose: exchange the ester alkoxy group, producing methyl benzoate and liberating 2‑(dimethylamino)ethanol. Key transformation: methanol acts as nucleophile attacking the carbonyl of the benzoate ester, displacing the original 2‑(dimethylamino)ethyl alkoxy group. Typical conditions: excess methanol as solvent, catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOMe), reflux (≈65 °C) for several hours; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium toward product formation.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction of amphoteric zinc oxide with sodium hydroxide to form sodium zincate. Zinc oxide reacts with hydroxide ions, generating the tetrahydroxozincate(II) anion (Na2[Zn(OH)4] or related species) and water. Performed in aqueous NaOH solution, often heated to aid dissolution of ZnO. No catalyst; solvent is water.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type) SN2 substitution where fluoride ion from tetra‑n‑butylammonium fluoride replaces chloride on benzyl chloride, producing benzyl fluoride. Reaction proceeds via backside attack of F^– on the benzylic carbon. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF, THF, or acetonitrile under anhydrous conditions; TBAF serves as both fluoride source and phase‑transfer catalyst. No additional catalyst required.

Double displacement/precipitation (neutralization) reaction of indium(III) acetate with ammonium hydroxide, yielding insoluble indium(III) hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium acetate. Indium(III) acetate hydrolyzes in basic medium; OH^– replaces acetate ligands. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; often the precipitate is filtered and washed. No catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Type: double displacement (acid–base) reaction; purpose: generation of anhydrous hydrogen chloride gas from a metal chloride and strong acid; key transformation: proton transfer from sulfuric acid to chloride ions forming HCl and formation of iron(III) sulfate as the solid product; typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄ mixed with solid FeCl₃, heated gently to evolve HCl gas; common setup: dry glass apparatus, often a gas‑washing tube, no solvent or catalyst required.

Type: thermal dehydration (condensation) of a metal hydroxide acid; purpose: preparation of tungsten(VI) oxide from tungstic acid; key transformation: loss of water molecules from H₂WO₄ yielding WO₃; typical conditions: solid tungstic acid heated to about 300–400 °C in a furnace; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Oxidation reaction: hydrogen peroxide oxidizes cuprous oxide to copper(II) oxide, yielding water; purpose is to convert Cu(I) to Cu(II) or for cleaning; key transformation Cu2O + H2O2 → CuO + H2O; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with mild stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (amine acylation) using an acid chloride; purpose: protection or functionalization of phenethylamine as an N‑acetyl amide; key transformation: acetyl chloride transfers the acetyl group to the amine nitrogen, generating N‑acetylphenethylamine and liberating HCl; typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; pyridine acts as a base/scavenger for the generated HCl and as a catalyst.

Type: oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using hydrogen peroxide; purpose: conversion of 4,4,4‑trifluorobutanal into the corresponding acid; key transformation: peroxide oxidizes the aldehyde carbonyl to a carboxyl group, with water as the only by‑product; typical conditions: aqueous or mixed organic solvent (e.g., MeCN/H₂O), catalytic amount of tungsten(VI) oxide (WO₃) at ambient to mild reflux temperature; WO₃ acts as a heterogeneous catalyst.

Type: electrophilic epoxidation of an alkene; purpose: synthesis of styrene oxide from styrene; key transformation: iodosylbenzene transfers an oxygen atom to the C=C bond, forming the three‑membered epoxide and reducing to iodobenzene; typical conditions: aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to room temperature, often under inert atmosphere; iodosylbenzene serves as the oxidant, no additional catalyst required.

Type: Grignard substitution at phosphorus (nucleophilic substitution); purpose: formation of 2‑pyridyldiphenylphosphine by replacing the chlorine on chlorodiphenylphosphine; key transformation: 2‑pyridylmagnesium bromide attacks the phosphorus atom, displacing chloride as MgBrCl and forming the P–C bond; typical conditions: dry ether (THF or diethyl ether), low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) to control reactivity, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); no external catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation; oxalate from ammonium oxalate reacts with cadmium acetate to give cadmium oxalate precipitate and ammonium acetate in solution; performed in water at ambient temperature; the solid is isolated by filtration; no catalyst needed.

Wittig olefination: deprotonation of methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide with n‑butyllithium generates the phosphonium ylide, which reacts with 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde to afford 2‑chlorostyrene and triphenylphosphine oxide. Carried out in dry THF (or ether) at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen or argon.

Halogen displacement/redox reaction. Chlorine gas oxidizes bromide ions in thallium bromide to bromine gas while being reduced to chloride, forming thallium chloride. Typically carried out by passing Cl₂ over solid TlBr at elevated temperature (≈150‑200 °C) in the gas‑phase; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (phosgenation) to synthesize urea. Phosgene reacts with two equivalents of ammonia, giving urea and two equivalents of hydrogen chloride. Conducted in anhydrous inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) at 0‑5 °C, often with an HCl‑scavenging base such as pyridine. No external catalyst; the reaction is driven by the high reactivity of COCl₂.

Negishi cross‑coupling (palladium‑catalyzed carbon‑carbon bond formation); replaces the bromine on 2‑bromo‑3‑methylthiophene with an ethyl group using ethylzinc bromide; typically uses Pd(0) catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(dppf)Cl₂) in THF under inert atmosphere, temperature ranging from 0 °C to reflux; yields 2‑ethyl‑3‑methylthiophene.

Reductive amination (reductive methylation). Formaldehyde condenses with the primary amine of methyl 2‑aminoacetate to form an iminium ion, which is reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to give methyl N‑methylglycinate, releasing water. Performed in methanol/water (1:1) at pH 5‑6 (adjusted with acetic acid) and 20‑40 °C; NaBH₃CN acts as the reducing agent, no metal catalyst needed.

Acid‑carbonate reaction; dysprosium carbonate reacts with aqueous hydrobromic acid to yield dysprosium bromide, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Conducted in aqueous HBr at room temperature or with gentle heating; CO2 evolution drives the reaction forward. No catalyst needed.

Oxidative conversion (redox) of MnO₂ to permanganate. In basic solution (RbOH), potassium persulfate (S₂O₈²⁻) oxidizes manganese dioxide to the permanganate anion, which pairs with rubidium to give rubidium permanganate, while persulfate is reduced to sulfate. Reaction carried out in aqueous medium, heated (≈80‑100 °C) with vigorous stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Partial reduction of an aromatic nitrile to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride; typically performed at –78 °C in dry THF with 1‑1.5 equiv DIBAL‑H, followed by a methanol or aqueous work‑up; converts the –C≡N group to –CHO, giving 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction. Barium chlorate reacts with ammonium carbonate in aqueous solution; insoluble barium carbonate precipitates, while the soluble ammonium chlorate remains in solution. Usually performed at room temperature in water, with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Amide hydrolysis (neutral or acidic). Water hydrolyzes the N‑acetyl group of N‑acetylprocainamide, yielding acetic acid and procainamide. Typically carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base under reflux (80‑100 °C) for several hours. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl; no metal catalyst required.

Metal hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid; purpose is to convert 2‑phenylpropanoic acid to the corresponding primary alcohol. LiAlH₄ transfers hydride to the carbonyl of the acid, forming an alkoxide intermediate that after aqueous work‑up yields 2‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol; inorganic by‑products are aluminum oxide and lithium hydroxide. Carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, usually at reflux (≈70 °C). No additional catalyst is used.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous mixing of soluble barium perchlorate and ammonium carbonate results in insoluble barium carbonate precipitate and soluble ammonium perchlorate; performed in water at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

General type: acid‑metal reaction; purpose: produce soluble zinc sulfate and hydrogen gas; key transformations: Zn⁰ → Zn²⁺ (ZnSO₄) and 2 H⁺ → H₂; typical conditions: dilute sulfuric acid, room temperature to gentle heating, aqueous solution.

Double displacement (ion exchange) reaction; mixing aqueous potassium nitrate with lead(II) bromide swaps anions to give soluble lead(II) nitrate and potassium bromide; carried out in water at room temperature, no catalyst.

Gas‑phase halogen exchange between iodine monofluoride and bromine; produces iodine monobromide and bromine monofluoride; similar bond rearrangement as above; conducted at moderate temperature (≈150‑300 °C) in the gas phase; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Salt metathesis/acid‑base neutralization; aqueous potassium hydroxide reacts with tetramethylammonium bromide to generate tetramethylammonium hydroxide and potassium bromide; conducted in water or methanol, typically at 0 °C to rt, no catalyst.

Direct redox chlorination of platinum dioxide; chlorine gas oxidizes PtO₂ to PtCl₄, releasing O₂; performed in a dry, heated reaction vessel (typically 200–300 °C) under a flow of Cl₂, no solvent needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; cyclohexene reacts with H₂ gas in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) to saturate the C=C bond, yielding cyclohexane; reaction performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at room temperature to 100 °C in an inert solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate.

Halide exchange double displacement; solid or melted ammonium bromide reacts with uranium tetrachloride to replace chloride with bromide, forming ammonium chloride and uranium tetrabromide; usually performed under anhydrous conditions (e.g., in dry acetonitrile or melt) with gentle heating, no catalyst.

N‑methylation (alkylation) of a benzodiazepine; diazomethane acts as a methylating agent, transferring a methyl group to the nitrogen of Nordazepam to afford Diazepam with release of nitrogen gas; carried out in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol; 1‑hydroxy‑1,2‑benziodoxol‑3(1H)-one (IBX) oxidizes cyclohexanol to cyclohexanone while being reduced to 2‑iodobenzoic acid; typically performed in DMSO or acetonitrile at room temperature, no external catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium selenide producing ammonia gas and hydrogen selenide; carried out by heating the solid (NH₄)₂Se (≈100‑200 °C) in a sealed or inert‑gas setup, often without solvent; can be acidified to liberate H₂Se.

Oxidative cleavage of fluoroacetone with potassium permanganate forming fluoroacetic acid, carbon dioxide and water; conducted in alkaline aqueous KMnO₄ solution under reflux (80‑100 °C); MnO₂ precipitates, no additional catalyst.

Generation of a phenyl chloroformate from phenol using triphosgene (a solid phosgene surrogate); the phenol attacks the carbonyl carbon of triphosgene, releasing CO2 and HCl and forming phenyl chloroformate. Typical conditions: phenol (1.0 equiv) and a base such as pyridine or triethylamine (1.1–2.0 equiv) in dry CH2Cl2 at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; the by‑products are carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride, which are scavenged by the base.

Acid-base reaction where aluminum hydroxide reacts with nitric acid to form aluminum nitrate and water. Protonation of hydroxide groups initiates water formation, releasing Al³+ and nitrate ions. Reaction proceeds at room temperature in aqueous solution. No catalyst required.

Oxidation of 2‑chlorobenzonitrile to 2‑chlorobenzoic acid using hydrogen peroxide, commonly catalyzed by a tungstate or phosphotungstic acid in aqueous medium; reaction run at 50‑80 °C, water is the only by‑product.

Halogen displacement/redox where chlorine oxidizes bromide in iron(III) bromide to bromine while forming iron(III) chloride; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with Cl₂ gas bubbled through; no catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of the chloride in N,N‑dimethylaminoethyl chloride hydrochloride by azide ion; introduces an azide functional group useful for click chemistry or subsequent reduction to an amine; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0–50 °C under inert atmosphere; sodium chloride precipitates and is removed, leaving 2‑azido‑N,N‑dimethylethanamine.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (binary metal‑phosphide formation) combining elemental zirconium and phosphorus in a stoichiometric 1:1 ratio; yields zirconium phosphide, a refractory material often used in ceramics or as a catalyst support; performed in an inert glovebox or tube furnace at ≥1000 °C under argon or vacuum; no solvent, the product is obtained after cooling and grinding.

Reductive ozonolysis of 1‑butene using dimethyl sulfide; forms the same aldehydes as in reaction 0 (formaldehyde and propionaldehyde) but the work‑up is reductive instead of oxidative. After ozonide formation at –78 °C in CH2Cl2, dimethyl sulfide is added, reducing the ozonide to the aldehydes without over‑oxidation. Conditions: O3 bubbled through a solution of 1‑butene in dichloromethane at –78 °C, followed by addition of 1–2 equiv DMS, then gradual warming to rt. No metal catalyst required.

Conversion of tert‑butyl alcohol to tert‑butyl iodide using phosphorus triiodide (PI₃); the alcohol is activated by PI₃ and displaced to give the alkyl iodide while forming phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃). Conducted in dry ether or pyridine, typically at 0 °C to reflux, under anhydrous conditions.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange) converting copper(II) acetate to copper(II) trifluorethanesulfonate (Cu(OTf)₂) while generating acetic acid; useful for preparing a non‑coordinating, strong Lewis‑acid catalyst for organic transformations; typically dissolved in anhydrous dichloromethane or acetonitrile, mixed at 0 °C then allowed to warm to room temperature; acetic acid is removed by evaporation or co‑evaporation with toluene, leaving Cu(OTf)₂ as a solid.

Hydrolysis of a selenium halide; aqueous hydrolysis of selenium tetrabromide replaces the Se–Br bonds with an Se=O double bond to give selenium dioxide and hydrogen bromide; purpose is conversion of a bromide to the corresponding oxide and generation of HBr; typically performed by mixing SeBr₄ with water and heating under reflux; solvent is water, no catalyst required.

Selective partial reduction of an ester (2‑methylpropyl benzoate) to the corresponding aldehyde (benzaldehyde) using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H); provides an aldehyde without over‑reduction to alcohol; conducted at low temperature (‑78 °C) in anhydrous toluene or dichloromethane under nitrogen; after addition of DIBAL‑H, the mixture is quenched with dilute acid, affording benzaldehyde and 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol as the liberated alcohol from the alkoxy fragment.

N‑alkylation of aniline by bromoethane under basic conditions (sodium ethoxide) to give N,N‑diethylaniline; proceeds via deprotonation of aniline forming an anilide ion that undergoes two successive SN2 attacks on ethyl bromide; typical protocol uses refluxing ethanol or THF with NaOEt as base, adding bromoethane dropwise; ethanol formed from the base and by‑product NaBr are removed during work‑up, yielding the tertiary aniline.

Free‑radical chlorination of 2,2,3‑trimethylbutane with chlorine gas to give 1‑chloro‑2,2,3‑trimethylbutane and hydrogen chloride. Initiated by UV light or heat, the reaction abstracts a hydrogen atom and substitutes chlorine. Conducted in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, under UV irradiation or at 60–80 °C; chlorine is the reagent, no catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution yielding an anhydride; synthesizes acetic anhydride from acetyl chloride and cesium acetate; cesium acetate attacks acetyl chloride, displacing chloride to afford acetic anhydride and CsCl; conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt; CsCl precipitates and is removed; no additional catalyst.

Hydroformylation (oxo process) of 1‑butene; adds a formyl group and hydrogen across the double bond to give pentanal, extending the carbon chain by one carbon. Catalyzed by homogeneous rhodium or cobalt complexes (e.g., HRh(CO)(PPh3)3) or supported Rh/Co catalysts with phosphine ligands. Typical conditions: 80–120 °C, 20–50 bar syngas (CO/H2, 1:1 or 2:1 ratio) in a solvent such as toluene or dimethyl carbonate. Reaction is regioselective for linear aldehyde.

SN2 substitution of cyclohexylmethyl methanesulfonate (mesylate) by cyanide ion from potassium cyanide to afford cyclohexylacetonitrile; a common route to primary nitriles; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to ambient temperature to avoid elimination; potassium methanesulfonate remains in solution and is removed during aqueous work‑up, giving the nitrile product.

Hydrogenolysis of an aryl iodide (C–I bond reduction). Purpose: remove the iodine substituent to afford the parent aniline derivative. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–I bond with H2, forming N,N‑dimethylaniline and hydrogen iodide. Typical conditions: H2 (1–3 atm), 10 % Pd/C, solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, ambient temperature or mild heating (25–40 °C).

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis); used to liberate free isoquinoline base from its hydrochloride salt for extraction or further synthesis; proton on isoquinoline transferred to hydroxide forming water, sodium chloride formed as by‑product; typically carried out in aqueous NaOH at ambient temperature, often followed by extraction into an organic solvent such as ether or dichloromethane.

Acetal hydrolysis. Cleaves 1,1-diethoxypropane to regenerate propionaldehyde and ethanol. Reaction with water under acidic conditions (e.g., dilute HCl or TsOH) at elevated temperature. Used for deprotection of aldehyde groups in synthesis. Solvent is aqueous acid.

Acid–base salt formation (neutralization). The diamine is protonated by excess HCl to give the bis‑hydrochloride salt, improving water solubility and handling. Typically carried out by adding 1,8‑diaminooctane to aqueous or ethanolic HCl at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: Nucleophilic acyl substitution. Purpose: Ester synthesis. Key transformation: Methoxide attacks carbonyl carbon of benzoyl chloride, forming a tetrahedral intermediate followed by displacement of chloride. Conditions: Aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane), room temperature. No catalyst required.

Metal‑mediated reduction of a quinone to a hydroquinone. Zinc dust reduces menadione (2‑methyl‑1,4‑naphthoquinone) in glacial acetic acid, converting theone to menadiol (the corresponding hydroquinone). The mixture is refluxed under nitrogen for several hours; zinc serves as the reductant and the acid provides a proton source. No external catalyst is needed.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑catalyzed or neutral aqueous hydrolysis) of methyl 4‑hydroxybutanoate to yield 4‑hydroxybutanoic acid and methanol; reaction performed in water (often with added mineral acid such as HCl) and heated (reflux) to drive the equilibrium toward the acid.

Reductive methylation (reductive amination) of an amino acid. Formaldehyde condenses with the primary amine of L‑glutamic acid to give an iminium intermediate, which is then reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to afford N‑methyl‑L‑glutamic acid, releasing water. The reaction is performed in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 6–7) or methanol at room temperature, using NaBH₃CN as a mild, selective reducing agent; no metal catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an allylic iodide with azide ion; analogous to reaction 0 but using KI as the counter‑ion. Performed in DMF or DMSO at 50–80 °C with K N₃, giving 3‑azidoprop‑1‑ene and KI.

Oxidative coupling of thiols to form a disulfide (oxidation). 2‑Nitro‑5‑mercaptobenzoic acid is oxidized by potassium ferricyanide, coupling two thiol units to give 5,5′‑dithiobis(2‑nitrobenzoic acid) (Ellman’s reagent) while the ferricyanide is reduced to ferrocyanide. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at neutral pH, typically at room temperature, with stoichiometric ferricyanide; no additional catalyst is needed.

Oxidative deamination of β‑alanine (3‑aminopropionic acid). In the presence of molecular oxygen and a suitable oxidase (e.g., monoamine oxidase) or a metal catalyst such as Cu²⁺, the amine group is removed, yielding 3‑oxopropanoic acid (malonic semialdehyde), ammonia, and hydrogen peroxide. The transformation is carried out in aqueous buffer under aerobic conditions, often at physiological pH and ambient temperature; the enzyme or metal ion serves as the oxidant.

Elimination (double dehydrohalogenation to form an alkyne); purpose: generate phenylacetylene from a vicinal dibromide; key transformation: two equivalents of HBr are eliminated to give a C≡C triple bond, producing NaBr and NH3; typical conditions: excess sodium amide (NaNH2, 2–3 equiv) in liquid ammonia at –33 °C (dry‑ice/acetone bath), reaction mixture stirred for 1–2 h, then warmed, filtered, and the product isolated after aqueous work‑up.

SN2 cyanation (nucleophilic substitution) of 2‑chloropropane with copper(I) cyanide to give isopropyl cyanide; copper(I) chloride is formed as by‑product. Usually carried out in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at reflux under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic silylation of a Grignard reagent: tert‑butylmagnesium chloride attacks trimethylsilyl chloride, forming tert‑butyltrimethylsilane and magnesium chloride. Performed in anhydrous THF at low temperature (0 °C to rt) under nitrogen or argon.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type nucleophilic acyl substitution); iodide ion from KI displaces bromide on benzoyl bromide to afford benzoyl iodide and KBr; usually run in acetone or ether with reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization of zinc carbonate with trifluoromethanesulfonic (triflic) acid, yielding zinc triflate, carbon dioxide and water. The reaction is typically done neat or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt, with evolution of CO₂ gas.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of methyl butyrate with sodium hydroxide, affording sodium butyrate and methanol. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with a co‑solvent such as ethanol) and heated to reflux until complete ester hydrolysis.

Acid–base neutralization; thorium hydroxide reacts with carbonic acid to form thorium carbonate precipitate and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; dilute acid medium, water as solvent.

Fischer‑type esterification of para‑aminobenzoic acid with 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol to form the anesthetic procaine and water. The reaction is performed in an anhydrous solvent such as toluene or xylene with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid) and azeotropic removal of water (Dean‑Stark apparatus) at reflux.

Redox (dechlorination) reaction; reduction of HOCl by hydrogen peroxide. H2O2 oxidizes to O2 while HOCl is reduced to Cl⁻, the overall products being water, oxygen gas, and hydrochloric acid. Conducted in aqueous solution, often under mild acidic to neutral conditions; used to neutralize residual chlorine in water treatment.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acid chloride with ammonia to give an amide; purpose is the preparation of 4‑hydroxybenzamide; key transformation is attack of ammonia on the carbonyl carbon of 4‑hydroxybenzoyl chloride, displacement of chloride ion, and formation of the amide with concomitant generation of ammonium chloride; typical conditions involve gaseous or aqueous NH₃ in a polar aprotic solvent (THF, Et₂O) at 0 °C to room temperature; a base is not required because the liberated HCl protonates excess ammonia.

Acid‑catalyzed Beckmann rearrangement; converts cyclohexanone oxime into caprolactam, the monomer for nylon‑6, with water as by‑product. The strong acid (methanesulfonic acid) protonates the oxime, promoting migration of the alkyl group and ring expansion to a lactam. Conducted at 120‑180 °C in high‑boiling, aprotic solvents such as toluene, xylene, or chlorobenzene, often under reflux; the acid acts as both catalyst and proton source. No external catalyst beyond the acid is needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of sec‑butyl bromide by nitrite ion to give sec‑butyl nitrite and tetrabutylammonium bromide. The alkyl bromide undergoes backside attack by NO₂⁻, displacing Br⁻. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (acetone, acetonitrile, DMF) at 0‑25 °C; reaction may be performed under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation. Tetrabutylammonium nitrite serves as both nitrite source and phase‑transfer agent; no additional catalyst required.

Fischer esterification; the primary alcohol reacts with acetic acid to give an acetate ester. Key transformation: 3‑bromopropan‑1‑ol + CH₃COOH → 3‑bromopropyl acetate + H₂O. Typical conditions: excess acetic acid, catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), reflux with removal of water (Dean–Stark trap) to drive equilibrium; solvent often the acetic acid itself.

Solid‑gas metathesis (sulfide synthesis); La2O3 reacts with H2S gas at high temperature (≈600‑900 °C) in a flowing H2S or inert atmosphere to replace oxide by sulfide, producing La2S3 and water vapor; no solvent or catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement/acid‑base precipitation reaction: sodium phosphate reacts with amphoteric aluminum hydroxide to form insoluble aluminum phosphate and soluble sodium hydroxide. Net transformation: Al(OH)₃ + Na₃PO₄ → AlPO₄↓ + 3 NaOH. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the formation of the AlPO₄ precipitate drives the reaction. No catalyst needed.

Aqueous metathesis and complexation: zinc sulfate reacts with sodium hydroxide to give sodium sulfate and soluble sodium zincate (typically Na₂[Zn(OH)₄]) in excess base. Overall: ZnSO₄ + 2 NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + Na₂[Zn(OH)₄]. Performed in water at room temperature; excess NaOH ensures dissolution of Zn(OH)₂ as the zincate complex. No catalyst required.

Electrophilic nitration of a primary alcohol using nitronium tetrafluoroborate to produce an alkyl nitrate ester (isopropyl nitrate) and hydrogen tetrafluoroborate. The NO₂⁺ cation attacks the oxygen of isopropanol, forming the nitrate ester while HBF₄ is generated as the acid by‑product. Reaction is carried out at 0‑5 °C in an anhydrous, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or nitromethane to control exotherm and avoid hydrolysis. No additional catalyst; the nitronium salt itself provides the electrophile.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous Na₂CO₃ exchanges its carbonate anion with bromide in BeBr₂, precipitating insoluble beryllium carbonate and forming soluble NaBr; typically carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid BeCO₃ is filtered off and washed.

General type: nitrosation/oxidation; purpose: synthesis of nitramide; key transformation: hydroxylamine is nitrosated by nitrous acid (generated from NaNO₂/H₂SO₄) to give nitramide with water as by‑product and formation of sodium sulfate; typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium, temperature kept low (0‑5 °C) to control reactivity; common solvent: water.

General type: O‑alkylation (methylation) of phenol; purpose: convert the phenolic hydroxyl of 3‑hydroxyamphetamine to a methoxy group; key transformation: phenolate attacks dimethyl sulfate in an SN2 process, displacing a methyl sulfate leaving group to form 3‑methoxyamphetamine; typical conditions: presence of a base (e.g., NaOH, K₂CO₃) in an aprotic solvent, reaction performed at 0 °C to rt or reflux as needed; common solvents/catalysts: acetone, DMF, pyridine.

General type: acid‑base salt formation; purpose: generate ancitabine hydrochloride for improved stability and solubility; key transformation: protonation of the basic nitrogen(s) in ancitabine by hydrochloric acid to afford the hydrochloride salt; typical conditions: dissolve ancitabine in methanol or ethanol, add aqueous HCl or HCl gas, stir at ambient temperature until precipitation; common solvents: methanol, ethanol, water.

Double displacement/acid‑base metathesis in aqueous solution; ammonium hydroxide neutralizes lanthanum acetate, precipitating insoluble lanthanum hydroxide and forming soluble ammonium acetate. Reaction is carried out at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

General type: metal insertion (formation of aryl‑zinc reagent, Negishi‑type); purpose: prepare 2‑methoxyphenylzinc bromide as a nucleophilic partner for cross‑coupling; key transformation: zinc inserts into the C‑Br bond of 2‑bromoanisole producing the organozinc bromide; typical conditions: activated zinc dust in dry THF under inert atmosphere, often initiated with a catalytic amount of iodine or TMSCl, temperature from 0 °C to reflux; common solvent: tetrahydrofuran (THF).

General type: base‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose: synthesize octyl gallate (ester antioxidant) from methyl gallate; key transformation: sodium methoxide attacks the methyl ester, exchanging the methoxy group for an octoxy group, releasing methanol; typical conditions: sodium methoxide in methanol (or another aprotic solvent), reflux under nitrogen; common solvents: methanol, toluene.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation; purpose: reduction of the alkene to the corresponding saturated alkane; key transformation: addition of H₂ across the C=C bond of 2‑methylhex‑1‑ene to give 2‑methylhexane; typical conditions: H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt or Ni, in a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, at room temperature to mild heating.

Acetyl transfer (N‑acetylation) of DL‑aspartic acid using acetyl imidazole; purpose is to protect or modify the amino group. The acetyl group is transferred from acetyl imidazole to the α‑amino nitrogen of aspartic acid, releasing free imidazole. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or aqueous pyridine at room temperature or slight warming; no additional catalyst required, pH is often kept mildly basic to keep the amine nucleophilic.

Salt metathesis/precipitation reaction between mercuric chloride and cesium hydroxide. Mercury(II) hydroxide, an insoluble base, precipitates while soluble cesium chloride remains in solution. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring helps complete the exchange. No special solvent beyond water is needed.

Metal‑acid displacement with halide exchange; aluminum metal reacts with hydrochloric acid, generating hydrogen gas and Al3+ that forms aluminum bromide in the presence of bromide ions; typically carried out in aqueous HCl, often under reflux to ensure complete reaction; water solvent, no catalyst.

Redox fluorination of neodymium metal by nitrogen trifluoride. Neodymium is oxidized to neodymium(III) fluoride while NF₃ is reduced to nitrogen gas. This high‑temperature gas–solid reaction is performed in a sealed tube or furnace under an inert atmosphere (argon) to prevent oxidation by air, typically at 300–500 °C. No solvents are used; the reaction is driven by heat.

Oxidation of diethyl sulfide to diethyl sulfoxide with manganese(IV) oxide; a stoichiometric oxidation where MnO₂ accepts two electrons, producing MnO (MnO is often written as MnO, but the net product is manganese(II) oxide) and water. Conducted in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) at room temperature or gentle reflux; MnO₂ is the oxidant, no additional catalyst.

Ligand‑exchange/complexation in concentrated hydrochloric acid leading to formation of the tetrachloropalladate(II) anion. Palladium(II) nitrate reacts with excess KCl and HCl; the nitrate ions are protonated to nitric acid and the palladium center coordinates four chloride ligands, giving K₂PdCl₄ in solution. Performed in aqueous HCl (6–12 M) at elevated temperature (60–80 °C) with stirring; the reaction is driven by the high chloride concentration. No external catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction; aqueous barium chloride exchanges ions with potassium selenide, forming barium selenide precipitate and soluble potassium chloride; usually performed at ambient temperature with gentle heating to improve solubility; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between sodium sulfide and magnesium bromide to give magnesium sulfide and sodium bromide; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature, the insoluble MgS precipitates and is filtered off; no special catalyst required.

Further oxidation of ethyl sulfoxide to the corresponding sulfone using hydrogen peroxide; the sulfoxide is treated with excess 30 % H₂O₂ in a solvent like methanol or acetonitrile at ambient temperature or slight heating (≤40 °C); acid or a catalytic amount of metal (e.g., Na₂MoO₄, vanadyl acetylacetonate) can be added to accelerate the reaction; water is formed as the sole by‑product.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt‑exchange) reaction; dissolves cobalt(II) phosphate and forms cobalt(II) nitrate. Cobalt(II) phosphate is treated with aqueous nitric acid: Co3(PO4)2 + 6 HNO3 → 3 Co(NO3)2 + 2 H3PO4. Reaction proceeds at room temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein-type) converting an acyl chloride to a more reactive acyl iodide; used to generate benzoyl iodide for subsequent nucleophilic acyl substitutions. Typically performed in anhydrous acetone or dry ether with solid NaI, reflux under nitrogen; the by‑product NaCl precipitates and is filtered off.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis). Sodium hydroxide deprotonates tiletamine·HCl, liberating the free base tileamine and forming water and NaCl. Used to obtain the free amine for extraction or formulation. Typically carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., water/ethanol) ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis). hydroxide converts 2‑imidazoline·HCl into the free imidazoline base, producing water and NaCl. Employed to isolate the free heterocycle. Usually performed in water or dilute aqueous base at room temperature; no special catalyst.

Free‑radical halogenation. Molecular chlorine abstracts a hydrogen from 2,2‑dimethylbutane under UV light or heat, 1‑chloro‑2,2‑dimethylbutane and HCl. Introduces a chlorine substituent at a primary carbon. Conducted in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, with UV irradiation or elevated temperature; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (metal‑halogen exchange). Methyl lithium attacks bromosilane, displacing bromide to give methylsilane (Si‑CH₃) and lithium bromide. Provides a route to organosilanes. Performed in dry aprotic ether solvents (THF, Et₂O) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Iron(II) sulfate reacts with barium nitrate in aqueous solution, precipitating insoluble barium sulfate and leaving ferrous nitrate in solution. Used analytically to detect sulfate or to separate the ions. Carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst.

Acid–base reaction of metal oxide with carboxylic acid. Mercuric oxide reacts with acetic acid to form mercury(II) acetate and water. Serves to prepare the acetate salt of mercury. Typically refluxed in excess glacial acetic acid or in a mixture of acetic acid and a suitable solvent, with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Oxidative decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutaric acid catalyzed by the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex. NAD+ serves as the oxidizing agent, and coenzyme A forms a thioester bond with the decarboxylated succinyl group. Requires Mg2+ and thiamine pyrophosphate cofactors under physiological pH and temperature.

Transfer hydrogenation (hydrosilylation) of 2‑methylquinoline using triethylsilane as the hydride donor, typically catalyzed by a transition‑metal complex (e.g., Rh, Ir, or a Lewis‑acid such as B(C6F5)3). The aromatic quinoline ring is reduced to the saturated 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydro derivative, preserving the nitrogen heterocycle. Common conditions: reflux in an inert solvent (toluene or THF) under nitrogen, with 1–2 equivalents of silane.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between cobalt(II) nitrate and sodium thiocyanate in aqueous solution. The cobalt cation exchanges its anion for thiocyanate, giving cobalt(II) thiocyanate, while sodium ions pair with nitrate to form sodium nitrate. Usually performed at room temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑chloroacetophenone to phenethyl chloride; hydrogen adds across the carbonyl (reducing it to a CH₂ group) while the chloro substituent remains, giving the saturated chloroalkyl product. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni in ethanol or methanol at 25–50 °C.

Nickel‑catalyzed C–P cross‑coupling (phosphination) of 2‑chloropyridine with diphenylphosphine to afford 2‑pyridyldiphenylphosphine. Zinc dust reduces Ni(II) to the active Ni(0) species and generates the organozinc intermediate from the aryl chloride. The reaction is conducted under inert atmosphere in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF, often at 60–80 °C, using 1,2‑bis(diphenylphosphino)ethane (dppe) as ligand.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of phenacemide (an amide/urea derivative) with water to cleave the amide bond, producing phenylacetic acid and urea. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl or NaOH, followed by neutralization and isolation of the acid and urea. Reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon, leading to de‑amidation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) of an alkyl chloride with hydroxide; purpose is conversion of the chloroalkane to the corresponding primary alcohol; key transformation is replacement of Cl by OH to afford 2‑phenyl‑1‑propanol and NaCl; usually performed in aqueous NaOH (≈10–20 % w/w) under reflux (100 °C) or with heating in a sealed vessel.

Complete combustion of 2,2,3,3‑tetramethylbutane with molecular oxygen. Under high‑temperature ignition conditions, the hydrocarbon is fully oxidized to carbon dioxide and water, releasing large amounts of heat. No catalyst required; reaction occurs in the gas phase with excess O₂.

Direct synthesis of a rare‑earth halide: Praseodymium metal reacts with iodine vapor to produce praseodymium triiodide; 2 Pr + 3 I2 → 2 PrI3. Performed by heating the metal with sublimed iodine (≈400–600 °C) under vacuum or inert gas; solid‑state reaction, no solvent needed.

Hydrogenolysis (catalytic reduction) of a tertiary alcohol; converts 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol to 2‑methylbutane by replacing the hydroxyl group with hydrogen. Typically carried out under H₂ pressure (25–50 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C, or Pt at 50–150 °C in a solvent like ethanol, isopropanol, or THF.

Acid‑base deprotonation of phenobarbital; NaH abstracts the acidic imide hydrogen to give the sodium phenobarbital salt and H₂ gas. Conducted in an aprotic, aprotic polar solvent (e.g., dry THF or DM) under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to rt.

Acylation (acetylation) of an aromatic amine; p‑aminobenzoic acid reacts with acetic anhydride to form p‑acetamidobenzoic acid, releasing acetic acid. Usually performed neat or in a low‑boiling solvent (e.g., pyridine) with gentle reflux; the reaction proceeds spontaneously without additional catalyst.

Base‑mediated oxidation of rhenium(VII) oxide; sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes Re2O7 to form sodium perrhenate (NaReO4) and water. The reaction is carried out in water, usually with stirring and gentle heating to promote dissolution of the oxide. No additional catalyst is required.

Transmetallation of a Grignard reagent with HgCl₂; two equivalents of n‑butylmagnesium bromide transfer theyl to mercury, producing dibutylmercury and MgBrCl salts. Carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; the reaction is quenched after completion.

Oxidative N‑dealkylation (metabolic demethylation); cyclizine loses a methyl group from its tertiary amine to give norcyclizine. In vivo mediated by cytochrome P450 enzymes using molecular oxygen and NADPH; in vitro can be mimicked with reagents such as peroxy acids (m‑CPBA) or Oxone in a mixed aqueous‑organic medium at rt.

Reaction type: Fischer esterification (acid-catalyzed ester formation). Purpose: synthesize the methyl ester of 4‑chlorobenzoic acid; provides a protected, more lipophilic derivative. Key transformation: the carboxylic acid protonates, allowing nucleophilic attack by methanol; water is eliminated to give methyl 4‑chlorobenzoate. Typical conditions: excess dry methanol, catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH, or HCl), reflux (≈65 °C) for several hours; removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark trap) drives the equilibrium toward ester formation. Common solvents/catalysts: methanol itself acts as solvent; acid catalyst as noted; sometimes toluene is used as a co‑solvent for azeotropic removal of water.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a bifluoride salt; NaF reacts with HF to give sodium bifluoride (NaHF₂). Performed in aqueous solution or concentrated HF; typically at ambient temperature with stoichiometric amounts, yielding a solid that can be isolated by evaporation.

Neutralization (acid‑base) reaction; lanthanum hydroxide is protonated by hydrobromic acid yielding the lanthanum bromide salt and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Thermal decomposition (dry pyrolysis) of ammonium dithiocarbamate yielding ammonia, carbon disulfide and hydrogen sulfide; employed for gas‑phase generation of these small molecules; key transformation: NH4⁺ [NH2C(=S)S]⁻ → NH3 + CS2 + H2S; conducted by heating the solid salt under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) to 150–200 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Oxidative combustion/oxidation of a metal sulfide; lutetium sulfide reacts with excess oxygen gas to oxidize sulfur to sulfur dioxide and the metal to its oxide, lutetium(III) oxide. Conducted at high temperature (often several hundred °C) in a furnace or tube furnace; gaseous reactants, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonylation; chlorosulfonic acid acts as electrophile introducing a sulfonyl chloride group onto the aromatic ring of toluene, producing p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride with release of HCl. Performed under anhydrous conditions at 0 °C to room temperature, typically in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) to form a nitrile; lithium cyanide displaces bromide from methyl bromide, generating acetonitrile and lithium bromide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) under heating (reflux) to promote substitution; no catalyst is needed.

Mild base neutralization with sodium bicarbonate; palmitic acid reacts with NaHCO₃, generating sodium palmitate, CO₂ gas, and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the evolution of CO₂ drives the reaction to completion.

Condensation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) between aniline and ethyl acetoacetate, producing the β‑keto‑amide acetoacetanilide with elimination of ethanol. Usually performed by refluxing the reactants in ethanol or glacial acetic acid, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., HCl) to accelerate the reaction; solvent serves as reaction medium, no external catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization). HBF₄ protonates silicate ions from sodium silicate, forming silicic acid (H₂SiO₃) and sodium tetrafluoroborate (NaBF₄). Performed in aqueous solution, generally at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation); ethylamine attacks acetic anhydride to form N‑ethylacetamide and one equivalent of acetic acid; typically performed at 0 °C to rt in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or neat, often with a base like pyridine to neutralize the generated acid; no external catalyst is required.

Metallothermic (aluminothermic) reduction; aluminum metal reduces samarium(III) oxide to samarium metal and is itself oxidized to aluminum oxide. Conducted at high temperature (≈1200 °C) in a crucible or furnace; no solvent, often performed under inert gas to prevent oxidation of products.

Electrophilic demethylation of an aryl methyl ether; boron tribromide cleaves the methoxy group of scopoletin to give esculetin (a di‑hydroxy coumarin). Reaction is run under anhydrous conditions in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; BBr₃ itself acts as the reagent and no additional catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); 1,2‑dichloroethanol is treated with PCC in anhydrous dichloromethane, the hydroxyl group is oxidized to form chloroacetaldehyde with water as the only by‑product; reaction proceeds at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, avoiding over‑oxidation to the acid.

Reduction of a primary alkyl bromide to the corresponding alkane using lithium aluminium hydride. Type: hydride reduction of alkyl halide. Purpose: removal of the bromine to give a saturated hydrocarbon. Key transformation: Br‑CH2‑CH2‑CH2‑CH3 + LiAlH4 → CH3‑CH2‑CH2‑CH3 + LiAlH3Br (by‑products). Typical conditions: anhydrous ether solvent (dry THF or diethyl ether), low temperature addition followed by reflux under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of an aldehyde) using palladium on carbon; purpose: convert the aldehyde functional group of indole‑3‑carboxaldehyde to a primary alcohol; key transformation: addition of two hydrogen atoms across the C=O bond to give indole‑3‑methanol; typical conditions: 10 % Pd/C (5‑10 wt % relative to substrate) in ethanol or methanol, hydrogen pressure 1‑3 atm, temperature 25‑50 °C, stirring until the gas uptake ceases; the catalyst is filtered off after completion.

Thermal decomposition of calcium chromate to calcium oxide and chromium(VI) oxide. Type: high‑temperature solid‑state decomposition. Purpose: generation of volatile CrO3 or preparation of CaO residue. Key transformation: CaCrO4 (solid) → CaO (solid) + CrO3 (gas). Typical conditions: strong heating to ≥ 400 °C under a dry atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of allyl ethyl ether to propyl ethyl ether. Type: catalytic hydrogenation/hydrogenolysis of an allylic ether. Purpose: saturation of the C=C bond and removal of the allyl group. Key transformation: CH2=CH‑CH2‑O‑CH2CH3 + H2 → CH3‑CH2‑CH2‑O‑CH2CH3 (propyl ethyl ether). Typical conditions: H2 gas (1–3 atm), Pd/C (5–10 wt % relative to substrate), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–50 °C, stirring under inert atmosphere.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amidation (peptide coupling). Purpose: form N,N‑diethylbenzamide from benzoic acid without using an acid chloride. Key transformation: DCC activates the carboxyl group of benzoic acid to an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is then attacked by diethylamine, yielding the amide and dicyclohexylurea as the insoluble by‑product. Typical conditions: dissolve benzoic acid, diethylamine, and DCC (often with catalytic DMAP) in dry dichloromethane or DMF, stir at 0 °C then warm to rt under nitrogen; the urea precipitate is filtered off.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification between butyric acid and isobutyl acetate. Type: ester exchange (transesterification). Purpose: swap the alkoxy groups to obtain the reverse ester pair. Key transformation: CH3‑CH2‑CH2‑COOH + CH3‑CH(CH3)‑COOCH2CH3 ⇌ CH3‑CH(CH3)‑COOH + CH3‑CH2‑CH2‑COOCH2CH3. Typical conditions: catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H2SO4, 1–5 mol %) or a base catalyst (NaOMe), reflux in a high‑boiling solvent (toluene or xylene) with removal of the more volatile alcohol (ethanol) by azeotropic distillation. Reaction is driven to completion by using an excess of one reactant or by continuous removal of the formed alcohol.

Acid- or base-catalyzed ester hydrolysis; converts furfuryl acetate into furfuryl alcohol and acetic acid; performed in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or aqueous base (NaOH) at reflux, then acid work‑up; common solvent is water or aqueous ethanol.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of 2‑ethylbutyl propanoate with NaOH; yields sodium propionate and 2‑ethyl‑1‑butanol; a route to propionate salts for buffering or polymer precursors; aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) at 60–100 °C, often in methanol/water mixture; after reaction, the mixture is cooled and the organic alcohol layer separated.

Precipitation (metathesis) reaction; aqueous palladium(II) chloride is treated with hydrogen sulfide gas, leading to the formation of insoluble palladium sulfide precipitate and release of hydrochloric acid; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature, often under slight acidic conditions; no special catalyst, water is the solvent.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitro group; SnCl2/HCl reduces 1‑nitroadamantane to 1‑aminoadamantane while oxidizing Sn(II) to Sn(IV); typically carried out in concentrated HCl at 0 °C to reflux temperature; reaction mixture is aqueous, no organic solvent required.

Thermal (or catalytic) cracking of cycloheptane to give smaller hydrocarbons; C–C bond scission produces cyclopentane and ethylene; employed to generate valuable olefin feedstocks; carried out at high temperature (≈500–700 °C) in the gas phase, often over an acidic solid catalyst such as a zeolite or alumina; no solvent; catalyst provides acid sites for bond cleavage.

Esterification with diazomethane (methylation of a carboxylic acid); employed to synthesize methyl acetate. Key transformation: diazomethane transfers a methyl group to acetic acid, releasing N₂ gas and forming CH₃COOCH₃. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous diethyl ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; reaction is exothermic and light‑sensitive. No catalyst required.

Grignard addition to an aldehyde; ethylmagnesium bromide adds to propanal forming the secondary alcohol 2‑pentanol; performed under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar).

Acid‑base neutralization of sodium acetoacetate with HCl. Purpose: protonate the acetoacetate anion to afford acetoacetic acid and form NaCl as a by‑product. Key transformation: proton transfer from HCl to the carboxylate groups. Typical conditions: add aqueous HCl (often 1 M) to an aqueous solution of sodium acetoacetate at 0–5 °C to control exotherm; the mixture is stirred until complete conversion. Solvent: water; product (acetoacetic acid) may be extracted into an organic solvent (e.g., ether) if needed.

Transesterification; converts the acetate ester to phenoxyethanol while forming methyl acetate. Key transformation: exchange of the alkoxy groups between 2‑phenoxyethyl acetate and methanol. Typically acid‑catalyzed (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) or base‑catalyzed (e.g., NaOMe) under reflux in excess methanol; removal of volatile methyl acetate drives the reaction to completion.

Free‑radical chlorination of a cyclic ether; chlorine gas abstracts a hydrogen from tetrahydrofuran giving 2‑chlorotetrahydrofuran and HCl; requires UV or daylight irradiation, often in the gas phase or dilute solution of THF, with no added solvent.

Halogen exchange (Swarts‑type) reaction; HF replaces one chlorine of carbon tetrachloride to give trichlorofluoromethane (CCl₃F) and HCl; carried out at elevated temperature (150–250 °C) with gaseous HF, sometimes catalyzed by a Lewis acid such as SbF₅; no organic solvent needed.

Reductive metal displacement; magnesium reduces PdCl₂ to elemental palladium, forming MgCl₂; typically done in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere at reflux or with gentle heating; serves to generate Pd(0) metal or catalyst precursor.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene sulfite by cyclohexylamine; the amine attacks the electrophilic sulfite carbon, opening the three‑membered ring and forming a β‑amino sulfonic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solvent at mild heating (30‑60 °C); the amine itself acts as nucleophile, no catalyst required. Used to prepare zwitterionic surfactant precursors.

Metathesis/acid‑base reaction; preparation of aluminum sulfate and liberation of hydrochloric acid (often as gas if heated). Aluminum chloride solution is combined with sulfuric acid; sulfate replaces chloride to give Al₂(SO₄)₃ in solution, while HCl is generated. Conditions: aqueous solution, often performed under reflux to drive off HCl gas, temperature 80–120 °C. No catalyst; water is the primary solvent, reflux apparatus used to collect HCl.

Acid-base neutralization; SeO₂ (acidic oxide) reacts with aqueous NaOH to give sodium selenite (Na₂SeO₃) and water. Typically carried out in water at room‑to‑moderate temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Redox reduction (metal displacement); sodium metal reduces Sb³⁺ in SbBr₃ to elemental antimony while forming sodium bromide, key electron transfer from Na to Sb; carried out under anhydrous, oxygen‑free conditions, often in liquid ammonia or THF at low temperature; liquid ammonia is a common solvent, no additional catalyst.

Staudinger reduction of an azide; benzyl azide reacts with stoichiometric triphenylphosphine in an aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or CH₂Cl₂) at room temperature, followed by addition of water. The phosphazide intermediate releases nitrogen gas, hydrolyzes to benzylamine, and generates triphenylphosphine oxide as by‑product. No external catalyst; water is required for the final hydrolysis step.

Oxidation of pentanal to pentanoic acid with potassium permanganate. Aldehyde is converted to the corresponding carboxylic acid under alkaline aqueous conditions, typically using dilute KMnO₄ at room temperature to gentle reflux, followed by acid work‑up to neutralize excess permanganate. A classic strong oxidant oxidation.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between iron(II) sulfate and sodium lactate forming ferrous lactate and sodium sulfate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst needed. Provides the iron(II) chelate ferrous lactate.

Oxime formation (condensation of an aldehyde with hydroxylamine); converts the carbonyl group of 4‑bromobenzaldehyde into an N‑hydroxyimide, releasing water; typically performed in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to reflux, often with a base such as pyridine to neutralize the generated acid.

Hydrolysis of 2,2',2''‑nitrilotrisacetonitrile to nitrilotriacetic acid. The three nitrile groups are converted to carboxylic acids by refluxing in water with either aqueous HCl or NaOH, followed by neutralization to isolate the NTA acid. Typical conditions: 100‑120 °C, several hours, aqueous medium.

Metallothermic reduction of thulium trichloride by sodium metal; solid TmCl₃ is reduced by molten sodium at high temperature (≈600–800 °C) in an inert atmosphere, yielding elemental thulium metal and sodium chloride; reaction conducted in a molten salt bath (e.g., NaCl/KCl eutectic) under argon or nitrogen, no external catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl chloride by formate ion to give benzyl formate and NaCl. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at reflux temperature; excess sodium formate drives the reaction. No additional catalyst required. Used for synthesis of benzyl formate ester.

Metathesis precipitation between ammonium oxalate and silver nitrate forming insoluble silver oxalate and ammonium nitrate. Reaction performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; the silver oxalate precipitates and is filtered. No catalyst needed. Employed to prepare silver oxalate for photographic or analytical applications.

Nucleophilic substitution (double SN2) of a dihalide with aqueous NaOH to give the corresponding diol and NaBr; performed by heating 1,8‑dibromo‑octane in aqueous or alcoholic NaOH (often reflux in ethanol/water); purpose is to convert alkyl bromides to the diol.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction; scandium hydroxide reacts with hydrofluoric acid to give scandium fluoride (ScF3) and water; conducted in aqueous HF solution at low to moderate temperature; no catalyst required.

Type: base‑catalyzed cross‑aldol (Claisen‑Schmidt) condensation. Purpose: synthesize the α,β‑unsaturated ketone (chalcone). Key transformation: piperidine deprotonates acetone to an enolate, which attacks benzaldehyde; subsequent dehydration gives 1‑phenyl‑2‑propen‑1‑one. Conditions: reflux in ethanol or methanol, 0.1–1 equiv piperidine, 2–4 h. No special catalyst beyond the amine.

Nucleophilic addition to an isothiocyanate (thiourea formation); methylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon of phenyl isothiocyanate, yielding N‑methyl‑N‑phenylthiourea; conducted at room temperature in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or ethanol, often without added catalyst.

Mixed anhydride formation (acyl chloride with benzoic acid); acetyl chloride acylates benzoic acid yielding benzoyl acetate (benzoic‑acetyl mixed anhydride) and HCl; carried out in a dry solvent (CH₂Cl₂, THF) with a stoichiometric base (pyridine or triethylamine) at 0 °C to room temperature; HCl is scavenged to prevent hydrolysis.

Radical recombination (termination step); a hydrogen atom reacts with a hydroxyl radical to give water (H· + OH· → H2O); gas‑phase process common in flame and atmospheric chemistry; no special solvents, catalysts, or temperature control needed beyond ambient conditions.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction where antimony(V) oxide reacts with chlorine gas at elevated temperature to produce antimony(V) chloride and molecular oxygen; performed in the gas phase or sealed tube at >200 °C, no solvent required.

Type: dehydration (condensation) polymerization of silanols. Purpose: formation of low‑molecular‑weight silica oligomers (disilicic acid) during early stages of silica gel formation. Key transformation: two orthosilicic acid molecules lose water to give a Si–O–Si bridge (2 Si(OH)4 → H6Si2O7 + H2O). Typical conditions: removal of water by gentle heating or by using a dehydrating agent; reaction can proceed in aqueous solution at pH 2–4, or under neutral/alkaline conditions to promote polymerization. Common solvent/catalyst: water as medium; acid or base catalysis may be used to control of rate.

Type: electrophilic addition of halogen to an alkyne. Purpose: install two chlorine atoms across the triple bond to afford a vicinal dichloroalkene. Key transformation: Cl₂ adds across the C≡C of propyne, yielding trans‑1,2‑dichloroprop‑1‑ene. Conditions: room temperature, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation; aqueous magnesium chloride hexahydrate reacts with sodium hydroxide to precipitate magnesium hydroxide while sodium chloride stays in solution; performed in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring, no catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction of aqueous sodium oxalate with samarium(III) nitrate yielding insoluble samarium(III) oxalate and soluble sodium nitrate; performed by mixing the aqueous solutions at ambient temperature with stirring.
Acid‑base neutralization (proton transfer) between acetic acid and sodium methoxide producing methanol and sodium acetate; typically done in methanol or a mixed solvent at room temperature.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; ammonium nitrate exchanges anion with sodium chlorate to form ammonium chlorate and sodium nitrate; typically carried out by mixing aqueous solutions at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Synthesis (direct combination) reaction; forms xenon hexafluoride by fluorination of xenon. Requires elemental fluorine gas and xenon under high temperature (≈300 °C) in a nickel or quartz vessel, often under inert atmosphere to prevent side reactions. No solvent; reaction proceeds in the gas phase.

Neutralization/precipitation reaction; addition of ammonium hydroxide to lanthanum(III) nitrate yields lanthanum hydroxide as a white gelatinous precipitate and ammonium nitrate in solution. Performed in water by slowly adding NH4OH while maintaining pH ~8–9; temperature usually ambient; no catalyst required.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of triphenyl borate; ethanol attacks the B‑OPh bonds, exchanging phenoxy groups for ethoxy groups, yielding phenol and triethyl borate. Typically carried out by refluxing ethanol with triphenyl borate, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid or base to accelerate exchange. Solvent can be excess ethanol; reaction proceeds under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Type: thermal oxidation (combustion) of a metal. Purpose: produce zinc oxide for use as a pigment or ceramic material. Key transformation: elemental Zn reacts with O₂ to form ZnO. Conditions: heating zinc metal or powder in air at 500–700 °C (furnace). No solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid–base (carbonate) reaction; converts insoluble beryllium carbonate to soluble beryllium nitrate while evolving CO₂ gas and water; performed in aqueous solution using dilute nitric acid at ambient temperature or mild heating; no catalyst required.

Hydrolytic depolymerization of phenol‑formaldehyde resin; water cleaves the methylene bridges, releasing formaldehyde and regenerating phenol. Conducted in aqueous alkaline (NaOH) or acidic (HCl) solution at 80–120 °C with stirring. Excess water serves as solvent; the mixture is later distilled to separate formaldehyde and phenol.

Condensation/amidation via POCl₃ activation; formic acid is converted in situ to the reactive formyl chloride by POCl₃, which then reacts with aniline to give formanilide, generating HCl and phosphoric acid as by‑products. Typically performed at 0 °C to 25 °C under nitrogen, using POCl₃ as reagent and anhydrous conditions. No additional solvent is required, though dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride may be used to dissolve reagents.

This is an acid displacement reaction. Concentrated sulfuric acid displaces nitric acid from ammonium nitrate, producing ammonium bisulfate and nitric acid. Typically occurs under heated conditions; sulfuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent. Solvent may be aqueous or anhydrous. Commonly used to synthesize nitric acid.

This is a calcium‑metal reduction of uranium(III) chloride, yielding uranium metal and calcium chloride. It serves as a method to produce uranium metal, especially when calcium is preferred for its lower melting point. The reaction is conducted at high temperature (≈600–800 °C) in an inert atmosphere, often in a sealed steel or quartz vessel; a molten salt flux (e.g., NaCl–KCl) can be used to facilitate contact, and no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of 2‑chloropyridine with sodium amide; NaNH₂ in liquid NH₃ attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displacing chloride to afford 2‑aminopyridine. Reaction carried out at –33 °C (liquid ammonia temperature) under inert gas, often with excess NaNH₂. After reaction, ammonia is evaporated and product is isolated by extraction.

Palladium‑catalyzed halogen exchange (C–X metathesis). KI supplies iodide which displaces bromide on bromobenzene in the presence of Pd(OAc)₂ and PPh₃, yielding iodobenzene and KBr; typically run in refluxing DMF or MeCN with catalytic Pd(OAc)₂ (≈5 mol %) and stoichiometric KI.

Oxidative homocoupling of 2‑naphthol to give 1,1′‑binaphthol (BINOL). Cu(II) chloride oxidizes the phenol, forming a new C–C bond between the 1‑positions; usually performed in refluxing pyridine or aqueous NaOH with 1–2 equiv CuCl₂, producing BINOL and Cu(I)Cl as by‑product.

Base‑catalysed transesterification between methyl acetate and sodium ethoxide. NaOEt attacks methyl acetate, exchanging the alkoxy groups to afford ethyl acetate and sodium methoxide; conducted in ethanol or methanol solvent, reflux, often with catalytic NaOEt, equilibrium driven by excess ethanol or removal of methanol.

Metathesis/acid–base exchange; sulfuric acid protonates acetate ion of cadmium acetate, forming cadmium sulfate and acetic acid; performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off acetic acid, water as solvent, no catalyst.

N‑alkylation of 3,4‑methylenedioxyamphetamine with ethyl iodide. Potassium carbonate deprotonates the amine, allowing SN2 displacement of iodide to give N‑ethyl‑3,4‑methylenedioxyamphetamine and KI; performed in polar aprotic solvent (DMF or MeCN) at 0 °C to reflux with excess K₂CO₃.

Oxidation; conversion of a primary allylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). Purpose is selective oxidation without over‑oxidation to acid. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Type: strong oxidative degradation (permanganate oxidation). Purpose: fully oxidize chloro‑methane to carbon dioxide and inorganic salts. Key transformation: KMnO₄ oxidizes CH₂Cl₂, breaking C–Cl and C–H bonds, yielding CO₂, H₂O, KCl and a solid MnO₂ precipitate. Conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH), reflux or heated, excess KMnO₄. Solvent: water.

Hydride reduction of a primary alkyl iodide with lithium aluminium hydride to afford the corresponding saturated alkane (2‑methylbutane). LiAlH₄ supplies a hydride that attacks the carbon bearing iodine, displacing I⁻ and forming the C–H bond; work‑up with aqueous acid gives LiI and Al(OH)₃. Typical conditions: dry diethyl ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen). The reaction is performed in a sealed flask or Schlenk line; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralisation forming indium(III) bromide. Three equivalents of hydrobromic acid protonate indium(III) hydroxide, yielding InBr₃ and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, followed by removal of water to isolate the metal bromide.

Acylation (amide formation) – nucleophilic acyl substitution of the an nitrogen by acetic anhydride to give the acetanilide derivative Bucetin and one equivalent of acetic acid; typically carried out at 0 °C to reflux in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or pyridine) with optional base to scavenge the acid.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of triphenyl borate with methanol – each phenyl group is replaced by a methyl group, producing three equivalents of phenol and trimethyl borate; usually performed by refluxing triphenyl borate in excess methanol, often without catalyst or with a catalytic amount of acid/base.

Salt formation (acid–base reaction) – protonation of the basic amine of mianserin by hydrochloric acid in isopropanol to afford mianserin hydrochloride (the pharmaceutically useful salt); the reaction proceeds at ambient temperature with aqueous or gaseous HCl added to a solution of mianserin in isopropanol.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a carboxylic acid – reduction of 2‑ethylhexanoic acid to 2‑ethylhexanol with H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni, Pd/C, or Cu‑Cr‑O₂); requires elevated H₂ pressure (≈30–100 ) and temperatures of 150–200 °C, typically in a high‑boiling solvent such as ethanol or water.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) to form a thioether – deprotonated 4‑chlorothiophenol (thiolate) attacks 4‑chlorobenzyl chloride, displacing chloride to give Chlorbenside and HCl; performed in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO) with a base such as K₂CO₃ or NaH at 0 °C to reflux.

Transesterification – methanol exchanges with the tert‑butyl ester of 2‑phenylacetic acid, yielding methyl 2‑phenylacetate and tert‑butyl alcohol; catalyzed by a small amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base, refluxing methanol is used as both reactant and solvent.

SN2 N‑alkylation of the imidazole nitrogen; the deprotonated nitrogen of ethyl 1H‑imidazole‑5‑carboxylate attacks1‑phenylethyl bromide, displacing bromide to give ethyl 1‑(1‑phenylethyl)‑1H‑imidazole‑5‑carboxylate and HBr; typically run in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, MeCN) at reflux with a base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to neutralize the formed HBr.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation (metathesis); KOH neutralizes holmium nitrate, precipitating insoluble holmium trihydroxide while forming soluble potassium nitrate; carried out in water at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Oxidative halogen exchange between tetraethyllead and iodine; iodine oxidatively cleaves Pb‑C bonds, producing four equivalents of ethyl iodide and precipitating lead(II) iodide; performed in anhydrous non‑polar solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, often at 0 °C to reflux.

Acid‑base neutralization; gallium(III) hydroxide reacts with aqueous sulfuric acid to form soluble gallium(III) sulfate and water. Conducted in water at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst necessary.

SN2 N‑alkylation of morpholine; morpholine nitrogen attacks ethyl iodide, displacing iodide to afford N‑ethylmorpholine and generating HI; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (acetonitrile) with a mild base (NaHCO₃, K₂CO₃) to scavenge HI, at reflux or ambient temperature.

Acid–carbonate reaction; hydroiodic acid protonates beryllium carbonate, releasing carbon dioxide gas and water while forming beryllium iodide; conducted in aqueous HI, often with heating to drive off CO₂; no catalyst.

Aqueous metathesis forming chloric acid; calcium chlorate reacts with nitric acid, exchanging anions to give soluble calcium nitrate and chloric acid (HClO₃) in solution; performed in dilute aqueous acid, generally at low temperature to avoid decomposition, no catalyst needed.

General type: acid‑metal reaction; purpose: generate iron(II) sulfate and hydrogen gas; key transformations: Fe⁰ → Fe²⁺ (FeSO₄) and 2 H⁺ → H₂; typical conditions: dilute sulfuric acid, moderate heating if needed, aqueous medium.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (saponification). Sodium hydroxide aqueous solution hydrolyzes iodoacetamide, cleaving the C–N amide bond to give the carboxylate (iodoacetate) and liberating ammonia. Usually performed in water or water/ethanol at reflux (50‑80 °C). No additional catalyst required.

Silylation of methanol using TMSBr, analogous to the ethanol reaction. Performed in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often with pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize the formed HBr. Methanol is converted to methyl‑O‑SiMe3 (trimethylsilyl methyl ether).

Acid–base metathesis (salt formation). Mixing aqueous acetic acid with silver nitrate leads to exchange of the anions, producing soluble silver acetate and free nitric acid. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; it is driven by the higher acidity of nitric acid. No catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolytic decomposition of a nitrosourea (lomustine). In aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) and gentle heating (40‑70 °C), the nitrosourea core is cleaved, releasing carbon dioxide, cyclohexylamine and 2‑chloroethyl isocyanate. Water acts as the nucleophile; the reaction is typically performed in refluxing aqueous acid without added catalyst.

Formation of a Grignard reagent by reacting bromocyclooctane with magnesium metal; type is metal‑halogen exchange to give cyclooctylmagnesium bromide; carried out under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in anhydrous diethyl ether or THF, usually with gentle heating to initiate the reaction.

Hydride reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine. Lithium triethylborohydride (LiEt₃BH, “Superhydride”) transfers hydride to benzonitrile in anhydrous THF (0 °C to rt), reducing the –C≡N to a –CH₂NH₂ group and generating triethylborane as a by‑product. The reaction is typically done under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Sodium selenide solution reacts with strontium chloride in water, exchanging ions to form insoluble strontium selenide (SrSe) and soluble sodium chloride. The mixture is stirred at room temperature or mild heating (≤60 °C) until precipitation is complete. No catalyst is required.

Type: redox acid‑metal reaction. Purpose: synthesis of indium(III) phosphate while generating hydrogen gas. Key transformation: metallic indium is oxidized by phosphoric acid, producing In³⁺ which combines with PO₄³⁻ to give InPO₄ and releasing H₂. Typical conditions: Indium metal added to dilute H₃PO₄ (1–2 M) at room temperature or gently warmed (30–60 °C) under an inert atmosphere to control gas evolution. Solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Hydrogen reduction of palladium(II) acetate; purpose: generate metallic palladium (0) for catalysis; key transformation: Pd(II) reduced to Pd(0) while acetate is protonated to acetic acid; typical conditions: hydrogen gas at 1‑5 atm, 50‑100 °C in a protic solvent (ethanol, acetic acid) or THF, under inert atmosphere.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; type: metathesis. Aqueous mercury(II) nitrate reacts with aqueous potassium iodide to form insoluble yellow mercury(II) iodide precipitate and soluble potassium nitrate. Conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed. No catalyst required.

Quaternization (ylation) of a sulfoxide. Dimethyl sulfoxide is methylated by methyl iodide to give trimethylsulfoxonium iodide, a sulfonium salt. Purpose: preparation of a methyl‑activated sulfonium species used as a methylating agent or in Swern‑type oxidations. Conditions: stir at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic dry solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane; stoichiometric MeI; reaction completes within 30 min to 2 h. No catalyst required.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitro aromatic ester to the corresponding aniline ester using tin(II) chloride in hydrochloric acid. Purpose is the chemoselective conversion of the nitro group to an amine while leaving the ester intact. Key transformation: SnCl₂/HCl reduces –NO₂ to –NH₂, producing water and oxidizing Sn(II) to Sn(IV) chloride. Typical conditions: refluxing aqueous HCl (≈2–6 M) with stoichiometric SnCl₂ at 60–100 °C for several hours; reaction performed in the same acidic aqueous medium, no additional solvent needed.

Free‑radical halogenation of an alkane. Chlorine abstracts a hydrogen atom from 2‑methylhexane and recombines to give 2‑chloro‑2‑methylhexane (a tertiary chloride). Purpose: synthesis of a tertiary alkyl chloride for further substitution or elimination. Typical conditions: Cl₂ gas dissolved in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., CCl₄ carbon tetrachloride) and the reaction mixture irradiated with UV light or heated to 30–50 °C. Reaction is carried out under inert atmosphere to avoid side oxidation.

Formation of a Grignard reagent from 1,3‑diiodobenzene, followed by formylation with N,N‑dimethylformamide to afford isophthalaldehyde. Purpose is to install aldehyde groups ortho to each other on a benzene ring. Key transformations: Mg insertion into C–I bonds generates 1,3‑phenylene‑di‑MgI species; nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon of DMF gives a magnesium alkoxide intermediate, which upon acidic work‑up yields the aldehyde at each position and MgI₂ as by‑product. Typical conditions: dry THF or diethyl ether, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), low temperature (0 °C to rt) for Grignard formation, then addition of DMF at 0 °C, followed by aqueous ammonium chloride work‑up; no external catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (dehydration); purpose is to obtain uranium trioxide, a common oxide intermediate. Solid dihydroxy(dioxo)uranium (UO2(OH)2) is heated, losing water to give UO3. Typical conditions: heating in air or inert atmosphere at 400–500 °C for several hours; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Acid‑base double displacement between potassium hydroxide and ammonium nitrate, producing potassium nitrate and ammonium hydroxide (which exists in equilibrium with NH₃ and H₂O). Purpose is a simple neutralization/exchange reaction. Key transformation: K⁺ exchanges with NH₄⁺, yielding KNO₃ and NH₄OH. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring until dissolution; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metath) precipitation reaction; aqueous mixing of phosphoric acid with nickel(II) nitrate to swap anions, producing soluble nitric acid and insoluble nickel(II) phosphate precipitate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring, followed by filtration to isolate Ni3(PO4)2; no special catalyst required.

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis) reaction; combines aqueous perchloric acid with potassium nitrate, exchanging anions to generate nitric acid solution and solid potassium perchlorate which precipitates.
