The reaction is typically run in cold aqueous ammonia (1–2 M) or in anhydrous solvent (ether, THF) with excess ammonia, at 0 °C to room temperature. A base (e.g., NaHCO₃) may be added to neutralize HBr.

Acetyl transfer (acetylation); N‑acetylimidazole serves as an activated acetyl donor that acetylates the phenolic OH of eugenol to produce eugenyl acetate, with imidazole released as by‑product; useful for protecting phenols; usually performed at ambient temperature in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or dichloromethane; reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange; hydrogen chloride protonates the cyanide ligand of gold(I) cyanide to generate volatile hydrogen cyanide and replaces it with chloride to form gold monochloride (AuCl); employed to convert AuCN to AuCl or to evolve HCN; carried out in aqueous HCl or gaseous HCl atmosphere, often at low temperature to collect HCN; no catalyst.

Syn dihydroxylation of the C5=C6 double bond of thymine using catalytic OsO4 and stoichiometric N‑methylmorpholine N‑oxide (NMO) as the co‑oxidant; forms the vicinal diol (thymine glycol). Typical conditions: 0.05–5 mol % OsO4, 1–2 equiv NMO, aqueous t‑butanol or acetone/water mixture, ambient temperature, neutral to slightly basic pH; reaction proceeds in 1–4 h.

Direct synthesis of a metal trihalide; elemental gallium is reacted with gaseous hydrogen iodide (HI) at elevated temperature (200‑300 °C) in a sealed vessel, yielding gallium triiodide (GaI₃) and H₂ gas; gas‑phase reaction, no solvent.

Free radical benzylic halogenation; introduces a bromine at the benzylic carbon of ethylbenzene to give 1‑bromo‑1‑phenylethane and HBr. Typically performed with Br₂ under UV light or a peroxide initiator in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at ambient to reflux temperature.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification) of caffeic acid with phenethyl alcohol using DCC and catalytic HOBt. DCC activates the carboxyl group to an O‑acylurea, HOBt suppresses side reactions, and phenethyl alcohol attacks to give caffeic acid phenethyl ester, releasing dicyclohexylurea. Conducted in dry dichloromethane (or DMF) under N₂, 0 °C to rt, 12–24 h.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; converts the tert‑butyl ester of methacrylic acid to the free carboxylic acid and tert‑butanol. Key transformation is cleavage of the C(O)–O‑tert‑butyl bond to give methacrylic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous strong acid (e.g., 1 M HCl or H₂SO₄), reflux 2–4 h, solvent mixture water/THF or dioxane. No special catalyst beyond the mineral acid.

Direct chlorination (high‑temperature halogenation) of zinc arsenide. Six equivalents of Cl₂ gas react with solid Zn₃As₂ to afford zinc chloride and arsenic trichloride. Performed in a sealed quartz or steel tube, temperatures 200–400 °C, under anhydrous, inert atmosphere; gaseous products are distilled away.

Acid‑base/complexation reaction of europium(III) carbonate with oxalic acid. Three equivalents of oxalic acid protonate the carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O, while the oxalate anion coordinates Eu³⁺ to form the soluble complex dieuropium trioxalate (Eu₂(C₂O₄)₃). Carried out in aqueous solution, refluxing gently for 1–2 h, followed by cooling and crystallisation from water or ethanol.

Aerobic oxidative dehydrogenation of 1,2,3,6‑tetrahydropyridine to pyridine. Molecular oxygen serves as the terminal oxidant, often in the presence of a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., CuCl₂, Pd(OAc)₂, or a quinone mediator) to abstract four hydrogen atoms, yielding pyridine and 2 equiv H₂O. Typical setup: dissolved substrate in acetonitrile or toluene, catalyst 5–10 mol %, O₂ balloon pressure, 80–120 °C, 4–8 h.

Catalytic hydrogenation of o‑nitrophenol to o‑aminophenol. H₂ gas (1–5 atm) reduces the nitro group in the presence of 5–10 wt % Pd on carbon. Reaction performed in ethanol or methanol at 25–50 °C for1–3 h; the aromatic ring remains intact, giving 2‑aminophenol as the product.

Type: amide‑forming condensation (acylation of an amino acid). Purpose: synthesis of hippuric acid, a model amide and metabolic marker. Key transformation: the amino group of glycine attacks benzoic anhydride, forming N‑benzoyl‑glycine (hippuric acid) and releasing one equivalent of benzoic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic medium, mild heating (reflux) to keep glycine soluble, pH near neutral to slightly basic. No catalyst required; common solvents are water or water/ethanol mixtures.

Type: redox (oxidation) reaction. Purpose: conversion of thiosulfate ion to sulfate, often used in analytical or waste‑treatment contexts. Key transformation: hydrogen peroxide oxidizes S₂O₃²⁻ to SO₄²⁻ while being reduced to H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature, neutral to mildly acidic pH. No catalyst needed; water serves as the solvent.

Type: Suzuki‑Miyaura palladium‑catalyzed cross‑coupling (C–C bond formation). Purpose: preparation of 2‑methylbiphenyl from an aryl iodide and phenylboronic acid. Key transformation: oxidative addition of Pd(0) to 1‑iodo‑2‑methylbenzene, transmetalation with phenylboronic acid (base‑activated), followed by reductive elimination to give the biphenyl product; KI is generated as a by‑product and Pd(OAc)₂ is reduced to Pd(0). Typical conditions: Pd(OAc)₂ (≈5 mol %), K₂CO₃ (2–3 eq), mixed solvent such as toluene/ethanol/water (or dioxane/water), inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), 80–100 °C for 2–6 h. No additional catalyst beyond Pd(OAc)₂.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation) of lutetium(III) hydroxide with acetic acid; forms lutetium(III) acetate and water. Lu(OH)₃ is added to excess glacial acetic acid and the mixture is heated gently (≈80‑100 °C) to dissolve the solid, producing an aqueous/acetic solution of Lu(OAc)₃. No special catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an ester; Pd/C with H₂ reduces ethyl 2‑methoxyacetate to the corresponding primary alcohol 2‑methoxyethanol and also liberates ethanol from the ethoxy fragment; carried out in a protic solvent such as ethanol or a mixture of ethanol/water, at 1–5 atm H₂, room temperature to 50 °C, with stirring.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); purpose is to replace the benzylic bromide with an amino group to afford pyridin‑4‑ylmethanamine; key transformation is attack of ammonia on the bromomethyl carbon, displacing Br⁻ and forming the primary amine, with ammonium bromide generated as by‑product; conditions typically involve excess aqueous or gaseous NH₃ in ethanol or THF, reflux (50–80 °C) possibly in a sealed tube to maintain pressure, no additional catalyst required.

Type: high‑temperature solid‑state redox / intermetallic synthesis. Purpose: production of iron silicide (Fe‑Si alloy) and silica. Key transformation: elemental silicon reduces Fe₂O₃, yielding SiO₂ and FeₓSiᵧ (commonly FeSi). Typical conditions: intimate dry powder mixing, heating in a furnace to 1300–1500 °C under inert gas (argon) or vacuum for several hours. No solvent or catalyst; atmosphere must be oxygen‑free to avoid oxidation of silicon.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: preparation of calcium stearate, a metallic soap used as a lubricant or surfactant. Key transformation: Ca²⁺ exchanges anions with Na⁺, forming insoluble Ca‑stearate precipitate and soluble Na₂SO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, gentle heating (≈60 °C), vigorous stirring until complete precipitation. Water is the solvent; no catalyst is required.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) using an acid chloride. Purpose: synthesis of pyrilamine (me­pyramine), an antihistamine drug. Key transformation: the amino nitrogen of 2‑aminopyridine attacks the carbonyl carbon of 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoyl chloride, releasing HCl which is scavenged by a base, forming the amide bond of pyrilamine. Typical conditions: aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, base (triethylamine or pyridine) 1.2–2 eq, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, reaction time 1–3 h. No metal catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (de‑acetylation). Water and acidic conditions cleave the acetamido group of 6‑acetamidohexanoic acid, yielding acetic acid and the free primary amine 6‑aminohexanoic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–3 M) or NaOH, reflux 2–6 h, then neutralize. Common solvent: water (or water/ethanol mixture).

Generation of N‑iodosuccinimide (NIS) by oxidative halogenation. Iodine reacts with succinimide in the presence of sodium carbonate, producing N‑iodosuccinimide as a mild electrophilic iodine source, together with NaI, CO₂ and H₂O. Conducted at ambient temperature in a biphasic system (e.g., dichloromethane/water) or wholly in organic solvent; sodium carbonate serves as base to capture HI. No additional catalyst required.

Quaternization (SN2 alkylation) of trimethylamine with benzyl bromide to give the quaternary ammonium salt benzyltrimethylammonium bromide. Reaction proceeds via backside attack of the lone pair on nitrogen on the primary carbon of benzyl bromide. Typical conditions: excess trimethylamine gas or solution, polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile, 0 °C to reflux, 1–4 h. No catalyst needed.

Acidic hydrolysis of 2‑cyanopiperidine to 2‑piperidinecarboxylic acid with formation of ammonium chloride; converts a nitrile group to a carboxylic acid. Conducted in aqueous HCl (4–6 M) under reflux for several hours. The reaction mixture is cooled, and the acidic product is isolated after basification; ammonium chloride remains in solution. No special solvent beyond water is required.

Strong hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Lithium aluminium hydride reduces 2‑phenylbutanoic acid to 2‑phenylbutan‑1‑ol. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, then carefully quenched with water then dilute acid. No additional catalyst; stoichiometric LiAlH₄ (2 eq) is used.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination of anisole using tert‑butyl hypochlorite. The hypochlorite delivers Cl⁺ to the para position of the anisole ring, affording p‑chloroanisole; concomitant cleavage of the O–Cl bond yields tert‑butanol and HCl as by‑products. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or chloroform as solvent, 0–25 °C, often with a Lewis acid promoter such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃ to enhance chlorination. Reaction time 1–3 h.

Metal‑acid reduction (Bechamp reduction) of 1‑nitropropane to 1‑propylamine using zinc dust in hydrochloric acid; nitro group is reduced to amine while zinc is oxidized to ZnCl2, producing water as by‑product; carried out in aqueous HCl under reflux or at 60–80 °C; no additional catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction between sodium sulfide and boron trichloride; forms sodium chloride as a soluble salt and boron sulfide (B₂S₃) as an insoluble product; typically carried out by mixing the solid reagents or their solutions at elevated temperature (often 200‑300 °C) in the absence of moisture; no special catalyst required, inert atmosphere may be used to avoid oxidation.

Aqueous double replacement (metathesis) precipitation; yttrium nitrate reacts with potassium fluoride to give soluble potassium nitrate and sparingly soluble yttrium fluoride (YF₃) which precipitates; performed in water with stirring, often at reflux to ensure complete reaction; no catalyst needed, filtration isolates theF₃ solid.

Formation of an acid chloride from a carboxylic acid using phosphorus oxychloride; a chlorination/dehydrative conversion. Purpose is to obtain 2‑iodobenzoyl chloride for further acylation chemistry. Key transformation: –CO₂H → –COCl, with loss of PO₂Cl⁻ and HCl. Typical conditions: POCl₃ (1.2 eq) added to a solution of 2‑iodobenzoic acid in dry pyridine or dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, 1–2 h; pyridine scavenges HCl.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation) where decanoic (capric) acid is deprotonated by sodium hydride, releasing hydrogen gas and forming sodium caprate; normally conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DMF under inert atmosphere (N₂) at 0 °C to room temperature; NaH acts as both base and hydrogen source; no catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 O‑alkylation); phenol is first deprotonated to phenoxide (often with NaH, K₂CO₃, or NaOH) and then reacts with 1‑bromopentane to afford pentyl phenyl ether and HBr; typical conditions use a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, acetone) at 50‑80 °C; the base both generates the nucleophile and scavenges the liberated HBr.

Hydrolysis of zinc nitride; ZnN₂ reacts with water to produce ammonia gas and zinc hydroxide precipitate; carried out simply by adding the solid nitride to aqueous media at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst needed, the reaction proceeds via protonation of the nitride ions.

Oxidation of dimethyl selenide to dimethyl selenoxide using molecular oxygen; the reaction is an oxidative transformation often requiring a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., CuCl, FeCl₃) or mild heating to activate O₂; performed in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF under an oxygen atmosphere; yields dimethyl selenoxide as the main product.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; aqueous potassium cyanide reacts with nickel(II) acetate tetrahydrate, yielding nickel(II) cyanide precipitate and potassium acetate in solution, together with water. Performed at room temperature in water; excess cyanide should be avoided or controlled because Ni²⁺ can form soluble cyanide complexes; no catalyst needed.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification); used to convert acetic acid into the corresponding 2,2,2‑trifluoroethyl acetate; key transformation is activation of the carboxyl group by DCC to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate which reacts with the alcohol; typically run at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP; dicyclohexylurea precipitates and is removed by filtration.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis/decomposition of hexamethylenetetramine; employed to generate formaldehyde (and ammonium chloride) in situ; the C‑N bonds of the cage‑like hexamethylenetetramine are cleaved by HCl, releasing formaldehyde and forming NH4Cl; usually carried out by refluxing the solid in aqueous hydrochloric acid (conc. HCl) for several hours; no special solvent beyond water/HCl is required.

O‑alkylation (SN2 methylation) of 4‑hydroxypyridine with methyl iodide: the phenolic oxygen attacks MeI, generating 4‑methoxypyridine and HI; usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF or acetone) with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃) at reflux or elevated temperature.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); replaces the chlorine of ethyl chlorooxoacetate with ammonia to give ethyl 2‑amino‑2‑oxoacetate and HCl; typically carried out at 0‑25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to trap the generated HCl.

Thermal decomposition of silver sulfide; used to recover elemental silver and elemental sulfur; upon heating strongly (often >400 °C) under inert atmosphere, Ag2S breaks down into metallic Ag and S8 (or polymeric sulfur); performed in a furnace or tube oven, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Silylation of methanol (formation of methyl trimethylsilyl ether); analogous to the ethanol case, methanol attacks trimethylsilyl chloride, giving MeOTMS and HCl. Performed in anhydrous solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, THF) with a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to capture HCl; reaction proceeds at 0 °C to rt.

Base‑mediated oxime formation using hydroxylamine‑O‑sulfonic acid as the hydroxylamine source; converts acetone to acetone oxime while the sulfonic acid moiety is reduced to sulfite; in aqueous NaOH the reagent generates hydroxylamine which condenses with the ketone; typically conducted at 0 °C to ambient temperature in water, with NaOH in slight excess; sodium sulfite is formed as a by‑product and can be removed by filtration or ion exchange.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 3,5‑dichloroanisole (aryl methyl ether) with hydrochloric acid to cleave the C–O bond, yielding 3,5‑dichlorophenol and methanol; performed in aqueous HCl, often refluxing in a polar solvent such as ethanol or water; no external catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (para‑nitration). N‑methyl‑aniline is treated with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid; the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) attacks the activated aromatic ring, giving N‑methyl‑4‑nitroaniline as the major product. Temperature controlled at 0‑5 °C during addition, then allowed to warm to ≤30 °C to limit over‑nitration. Reaction medium is the mixed acid; after completion, the mixture is poured onto ice, neutralized, and the product extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., EtOAc). No external catalyst is required.

Redox halide metathesis between NbCl5 and CuCl; copper(I) is oxidized to copper(II) chloride while niobium(V) is reduced to niobium(IV) chloride; typically performed in anhydrous, aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or chloroform under an inert atmosphere at low temperature to avoid hydrolysis; the reaction serves to generate NbCl4 for further low‑valent niobium chemistry and CuCl2 as a by‑product.

Copper‑mediated oxidative C–N coupling (Chan–Lam type). Phenylhydrazine is coupled with phenylboronic acid pinacol ester in the presence of Cu(OAc)₂ as catalyst and pyridine as base, generating diphenylhydrazine while the acetate ligand is protonated to acetic acid and the pinacol moiety is released. Typically carried out at room temperature to reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as methanol, ethanol or dichloromethane under air or oxygen atmosphere.

Acid‑base salt formation; ammonia protonates hydrogen cyanide producing ammonium cyanide (NH4⁺ CN⁻); carried out in aqueous solution or gas mixture at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to minimize decomposition; no catalyst needed.

Free‑radical chlorination (photochemical substitution). 1‑Propylbenzene undergoes homolytic C–H abstraction under chlorine gas and UV light, yielding the benzylic chloride (1‑chloropropylbenzene) and HCl as by‑product. Reactions are commonly performed in an inert organic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) under UV irradiation at ambient temperature.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation reaction. Sodium hydroxide neutralizes manganese(II) sulfate, forming soluble sodium sulfate and insoluble manganese(II) hydroxide, which precipitates. Conducted in water at room temperature or with gentle heating; the solid Mn(OH)₂ is isolated by filtration.

Mechanochemical synthesis of sodium aluminum hydride. Ball‑milling aluminum chloride with excess sodium hydride under a hydrogen atmosphere leads to reduction of Al³⁺ and formation of NaAlH₄ together with NaCl as a by‑product. The reaction is carried out in a sealed milling jar, typically at room temperature, under an H₂ pressure of a few bar; no solvent is required.

Jones oxidation of a secondary alcohol. 1‑Phenyl‑1‑propanol is oxidized by the Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄) in acetone to give 1‑phenyl‑1‑propanone, with reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) and generation of water. The reaction is performed at 0 °C to rt, under anhydrous conditions, and the mixture is quenched with isopropanol or methanol after completion.

Chlorination of an alcohol with phosphorus pentachloride. 2‑Chloro‑1‑propanol reacts with PCl₅, converting the hydroxyl group to a chloride and producing 1,2‑dichloropropane, while POCl₃ and HCl are generated as by‑products. Typically carried out in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to reflux, under an inert atmosphere.

Methylation of phenolic hydroxyl; diazomethane acts as a methylating reagent converting the phenol of eugenol to a methyl ether (methyleugenol) with liberation of nitrogen gas. Typically performed in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Disproportionation (redox) of chlorine in hot alkaline solution; chlorine gas reacts with aqueous potassium hydroxide (heated) to give chloride ion and chlorate ion, accompanied by formation of water. Conducted by bubbling Cl₂ through a hot KOH solution (≈80–100 °C); aqueous medium, no additional catalyst.

Halide exchange (metathesis) reaction; converts palladium(II) bromide to palladium(II) fluoride by exchanging bromide for fluoride ions. Typically carried out in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF with excess potassium fluoride, heated under inert atmosphere (e.g., N₂) to promote complete exchange; no additional catalyst required.

Reduction of amide to amine using lithium aluminium hydride; N‑ethylbutanamide is reduced to N‑ethylbutylamine; carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, cooling to 0 °C then allowing reflux; LiAlH4 is quenched with aqueous work‑up producing aluminium hydroxide.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde; Dess‑Martin periodinane oxidizes 1‑pentanol to pentanal. Reaction is carried out in dichloromethane (or other aprotic solvent) at 0 °C to rt, typically under nitrogen; the reagent is used in stoichiometric amount and no metal catalyst is needed.

Amide bond formation (peptide coupling); Dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates the carboxyl group of L‑glutamic acid, allowing nucleophilic attack by ethylamine to form L‑theanine (the ethylamide of glutamic acid) with dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Conducted in dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to rt, often with a base such as N,N‑diisopropylethylethylamine; no metal catalyst required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of a heterocyclic nitrogen; used to introduce a methyl group at the N‑1 position of 7‑methylxanthine to afford paraxanthine; the methyl iodide acts as electrophile and the imide nitrogen as nucleophile, generating hydrogen iodide as by‑product; typically performed with a mild inorganic base (e.g., K2CO3) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at room temperature to gentle reflux under nitrogen atmosphere.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction; converts a divalent sulfate salt and a monovalent acetate salt into the corresponding acetate and sulfate salts; carried out in aqueous solution where the ions freely exchange; usually carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Metal–acid single‑replacement; elemental magnesium dissolves in dilute perchloric acid to yield magnesium perchlorate and hydrogen gas; reaction conducted in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature, with careful control to avoid vigorous gas evolution.

Hydrolysis (decomposition) of sulfuryl fluoride; water attacks the sulfur center, cleaving the S–F bonds to produce hydrogen fluoride and sulfur trioxide; can occur under neutral or slightly basic conditions; typically performed by mixing sulfuryl fluoride gas with excess water at room temperature or mild heating; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst, aqueous medium is sufficient.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive conversion) of a nitrile to a primary amine; phenylacetonitrile is reduced by dihydrogen to phenethylamine, involving sequential addition of hydrogen to the C≡N bond; requires a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Raney nickel, Pd/C, or PtO2, high H2 pressure (30–100 atm), and a protic solvent like ethanol or methanol; reaction temperature is usually 80–120 °C under an inert atmosphere.

N‑alkylation of 2‑methylimidazole via SN2 substitution; benzyl chloride serves as the electrophile, the deprotonated imidazole nitrogen (generated by NaH) attacks to give N‑benzyl‑2‑methylimidazole with NaCl as by‑product; performed in a dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or THF) under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C to room temperature; strong base NaH is required to generate the nucleophilic imide anion.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitro aromatic compound; zinc dust reduces 2‑nitropyridine to 2‑aminopyridine in acetic acid, converting the nitro group to an amine while generating zinc acetate and water; the reaction is conducted by refluxing a suspension of zinc in glacial acetic acid (often 1–2 M) for several hours; no external catalyst is needed, and the solvent serves both as medium and proton source.

Acid‑salt metathesis reaction; concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with cadmium fluoride, exchanging anions to give cadmium sulfate in solution and evolution of hydrogen fluoride gas; performed by heating cadmium fluoride in refluxing H₂SO₄.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; exchanges cations between sodium hydroxide and calcium sulfide to yield sodium sulfide and calcium hydroxide. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required. Calcium hydroxide may precipitate due to limited solubility.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of the tetraazacyclododecane macrocycle by bromoacetic acid to form 1,4,7,10-tetraazacyclododecane-1,4,7,10-tetraacetic acid (DOTA) and release HBr. Conducted in aqueous or mixed water/methanol under mildly basic conditions (e.g., Na2CO3 or NaOH) to deprotonate the amine sites; reflux or gentle heating is common. No metal catalyst required.

Oxidative oxygen evolution (redox) reaction; concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes manganese dioxide and potassium permanganate, producing water, oxygen gas, potassium sulfate and manganese(II) sulfate. Carried out by adding solid KMnO₄ to hot (≈180 °C) 98 % H₂SO₄ containing MnO₂ as a catalyst; the mixture is stirred vigorously, and O₂ evolves as bubbles. No additional reagents are needed beyond the acid and the solid oxidants.

In‑situ peracid oxidation (H₂O₂/AcOH) to N‑oxide; purpose identical to (3) – formation of quinoline N‑oxide. Hydrogen peroxide and acetic acid generate peracetic acid in situ, which oxidizes quinoline nitrogen to the N‑oxide, releasing water. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, excess AcOH as solvent, 1.5–2 eq H₂O₂, reaction time 30–60 min. Solvent/cosolvent: glacial acetic acid (sometimes diluted with CH₂Cl₂).

Acid‑metal displacement; rubidium metal reacts with aqueous perchloric acid to form rubidium perchlorate (RbClO4) and releases hydrogen gas. Typical conditions are ambient temperature in water, with careful control because concentrated perchloric acid is a strong oxidizer; the reaction is performed under an inert atmosphere if needed.

Halogen exchange redox reaction; chlorine oxidizes iodide in tin(IV) iodide to elemental iodine while being reduced to chloride, forming tin(IV) chloride. Typically carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at room temperature or with gentle warming. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose is to convert selenous acid into its water‑soluble salt. The hydroxide ion abstracts a proton from H2SeO3, forming water and the hydrogen selenite anion, which pairs with K⁺ to give potassium hydrogen selenite (KHS​eO₃). Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stoichiometric KOH; no catalyst required.

Double displacement precipitation; barium ions combine with sulfate to precipitate barium sulfate while manganese(II) ions pair with chloride to give manganese(II) chloride in solution; performed in aqueous media under ambient conditions; water as solvent; no catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose is to prepare ytterbium trichloride from the hydroxide; Yb(OH)3(s) + 3 HCl(aq) → YbCl3(aq) + 3 H2O(l); conducted in water at ambient temperature; stoichiometric excess of HCl drives the reaction to completion; no special catalyst required.

Oxidation of osmium(III) chloride to osmium(IV) chloride by chlorine gas; chlorine acts as oxidant, converting OsCl₃ to OsCl₄. Performed by passing dry Cl₂ over solid OsCl₃, often in a sealed tube or flow reactor, at elevated temperature (≈150–250 °C). No additional catalyst necessary.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization). HBF₄ reacts with K₃PO₄ (or other potassium phosphate) to give phosphoric acid and the soluble potassium tetrafluoroborate salt KBF₄. Carried out in aqueous medium, typically at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization of a solid base; magnesium oxide reacts with malic acid to yield magnesium malate and water. Typically performed by suspending MgO in aqueous malic acid solution and heating gently to facilitate dissolution and reaction; no additional solvents or catalysts are required.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of an epoxide; amine attack on ethylene oxide to give N,N‑diethyl‑2‑hydroxyethylamine. Purpose: install a β‑hydroxyethyl substituent on a tertiary amine. Key transformation: lone pair on the nitrogen attacks the less‑substituted carbon of the epoxide, opening the three‑membered ring and forming a new C‑N bond while generating a primary alcohol. Typical conditions: excess ethylene oxide gas or solution added to a solution of N,N‑diethylethanamine in THF or MeCN at 0 °C to 40 °C, sometimes with a catalytic amount of base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to neutralize generated acid. No metal catalyst required.

Halogen displacement redox reaction; chlorine oxidizes iodide to iodine while being reduced to chloride. Purpose: quantitative analysis of halides or generation of iodine. Key transformation: Cl2 + 2 HI → 2 HCl + I2. Typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst required; water or dilute acid serves as solvent.

Aqueous hydrolysis (decomposition) of 2‑cyanoguanidine; purpose: generate urea and cyanamide from the cyanoguanidine scaffold; key transformation: water attacks the C=N bond, cleaving the molecule into urea and cyanamide; typical conditions: aqueous medium, heating to 80–120 °C, optionally acid (HCl) or base (NaOH) to accelerate; reaction can be carried out in a sealed tube or reflux flask; no organic solvent needed.

Dehydrative cyclization using phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) as a dehydrating and activating agent to convert (–)-ecgonine methyl ester into (–)-anhydroecgonine methyl ester (the core skeleton of cocaine). Reaction type: intramolecular dehydration/condensation. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform, usually with pyridine or triethylamine as a base, under an inert atmosphere at 0 °C to 25 °C. POCl₃ facilitates loss of water and formation of the anhydro bridge.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary sulfonate ester by azide ion. Purpose: synthesis of benzyl azide, a versatile intermediate for click chemistry or peptide coupling. Key transformation: NaN₃ + PhCH₂OSO₂CH₃ → PhCH₂N₃ + NaOSO₂CH₃. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 50–80 °C; no catalyst required; reaction proceeds cleanly with stoichiometric sodium azide.

Nucleophilic S‑alkylation (SN2) of L‑cysteine; the thiolate anion attacks allyl bromide displacing bromide to give S‑allyl‑L‑cysteine and HBr; performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑alcoholic medium, pH adjusted to deprotonate the thiol (often with Na₂CO₃), 0–25 °C to limit side reactions; no catalyst needed; purpose: introduce an allyl protecting/group on cysteine sulfur.

Transesterification of succinic anhydride with methanol to give methyl succinate; (CH2CO)2O + CH3OH → CH3OOC‑CH2‑CH2‑COOH; reflux methanol (60–80 °C) with a catalytic acid (p‑TsOH) or base; mono‑ester formation is favored; succinic acid by‑product remains in solution.

Hydrolysis of an acyl chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Purpose: preparation of heptafluorobutyric acid from its chloride. Key transformation: C₃F₇COCl + H₂O → C₃F₇COOH + HCl. Usually performed in a biphasic system (e.g., aqueous buffer with an organic solvent such as dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is rapid and often exothermic; no catalyst needed.

Carbonylative methoxycarbonylation of an aryl chloride; a palladium‑catalyzed carbonylation where CO and MeOH insert into the C–Cl bond of 2‑chloropyridine to give methyl 2‑pyridinecarboxylate (methyl nicotinate) with HCl as by‑product. Typical conditions: 1–10 atm CO, MeOH as solvent, base (e.g., Et₃N), Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(OAc)₂ with phosphine ligand, 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere.

Redox generation of nitric oxide from hydroxyurea by ferrous ion; Fe²⁺ reduces hydroxyurea, producing NO, water and oxidizing to Fe³⁺, which precipitates as ferric hydroxide. Conducted in aqueous solution at near‑neutral pH, ambient temperature, often with slight excess FeSO₄; no special solvent required.

Free‑radical chlorination of cyclopropane producing chlorocyclopropane and HCl; Cl2 undergoes homolytic cleavage under UV light or thermal initiation, abstracting a hydrogen atom from the cyclopropane and forming the mono‑chlorinated product; carried out in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at ambient temperature with light irradiation.

O‑Acetylation (acylation) of a phenolic hydroxyl; synthesis of 3‑acetoxyacetophenone. 3‑Hydroxyacetophenone is treated with acetic anhydride in pyridine, which serves as both solvent and base to neutralize the generated acetic acid. Reaction is typically carried out at 0 °C to rt for 1–2 h. The product is isolated after aqueous work‑up, and pyridine‑derived by‑product is removed by washing.

Oxidation of a secondary phosphine; purpose is to install a P=O functionality, affording diphenylphosphorane; diphenylphosphine is oxidized by m‑chloroperoxybenzoic acid, delivering an oxygen atom to phosphorus and reducing the peroxyacid to m‑chlorobenzoic acid; typically run in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; inert atmosphere is advisable; no additional catalyst.

Transmetalation to form a trialkylindium reagent; three equivalents of methylmagnesium iodide exchange with indium triiodide to give trimethylindium and three equivalents of MgI₂. Performed under dry, inert atmosphere in anhydrous ether or THF, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, using freshly prepared Grignard reagent.

Complex formation (halide complexation) in aqueous solution. Potassium iodide provides excess iodide, converting insoluble bismuth triiodide into soluble potassium tetraiodobismuthate [BiI4]−. Typically carried out by dissolving BiI3 in water containing excess KI at room temperature.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of dimethyl phthalate with 1‑butanol; potassium carbonate promotes exchange of the methyl ester groups for butyl groups, affording dibutyl phthalate and methanol. Reaction run neat or in excess 1‑butanol, heated to reflux (≈120 °C) under nitrogen, with K₂CO₃ as solid base; methanol removed to drive equilibrium.

Electrophilic aromatic alkylation of catechol with isobutylene; under strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, BF₃·OEt₂) the tert‑butyl carbocation adds para to the hydroxyl groups, yielding 4‑tert‑butylbenzene‑1,2‑diol. Conducted at 0–50 °C in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as chloroform or dichloromethane; acid also protonates phenolic oxygens to direct para substitution.

Fluoride‑mediated desilylation of a silyl ether. Purpose: deprotect phenoxytrimethylsilane to give phenol. Key transformation: cleavage of the Si–O bond by nucleophilic attack of F⁻, producing phenol and Me₃Si‑F. Typical conditions: 1.0–1.5 equiv of tetrabutylammonium fluoride (TBAF, 1 M in THF) added to a THF solution of the silyl ether at rt, reaction complete in minutes to an hour. Solvent: THF (or DMF); the tetrabutylammonium cation serves as phase‑transfer carrier.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a carboxylate salt; benzoic acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium benzoate and water. Performed in water at room temperature; simple mixing of equimolar reagents followed by evaporation or crystallization of the sodium benzoate.

Acid‑base neutralization; hydrazoic acid is deprotonated by rubidium hydroxide to give water and the rubidium salt of the azide ion; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, typically in water as solvent, no catalyst required.

Grignard addition to an acyl chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution); benzylmagnesium chloride attacks acetyl chloride, displacing chloride and, after aqueous work‑up, furnishes phenylacetone (a ketone) and magnesium chloride; carried out under anhydrous conditions in ethers such as diethyl ether or THF, usually at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen or argon, no external catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation/neutralization reaction; used to generate soluble sodium hydroxide while removing barium as an insoluble phosphate; aqueous barium hydroxide reacts with sodium phosphate, producing solid barium phosphate and leaving sodium hydroxide in solution; performed in water, often with gentle heating to improve dissolution; no catalyst required.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; the alkoxy group of methyl caffeate is exchanged for an ethoxy group from ethanol, producing ethyl caffeate and methanol; refluxing ethanol with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid or sodium ethoxide is common, ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent, removal of methanol drives the equilibrium.

Free radical bromination (substitution) of tridecane with Br₂ to give 1‑bromotridecane and HBr; purpose is to introduce a bromine leaving group; typically performed under UV light or heat in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) or chloroform, sometimes with a radical initiator.

Acid‑base neutralization to form a metal acetate; acetic acid protonates thorium hydroxide, producing water and thorium(IV) acetate (typically Th(C₂H₃O₂)₄·nH₂O); carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating and stirring, water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Halogen exchange (SN2) using hydroiodic acid; both chlorine atoms of 1,2‑dichloroethane are substituted by iodine atoms from excess HI, giving 1,2‑diiodoethane and hydrochloric acid; refluxing the substrate in concentrated HI (often generated in situ with red phosphorus) drives the reaction, aqueous or glacial HI acts as solvent, no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: derivatization via formation of a 2,4‑dinitrophenylhydrazone. Purpose: create a colored, crystalline hydrazone used for qualitative detection and quantitative analysis of aldehydes. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of 2,4‑dinitrophenylhydrazine on the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde, followed by loss of water to give the C=N‑NH‑Ar (Ar = 2,4‑dinitrophenyl) linkage. Typical conditions: ethanol containing a few drops of glacial acetic acid (or HCl) at room temperature or gentle reflux; reaction proceeds in 10–30 min; product precipitates and is filtered, washed, and dried.

Haloform reaction; base‑catalyzed cleavage of a methyl ketone. Iodine in aqueous NaOH oxidizes the methyl group of methyl ethyl ketone to triiodomethane (iodoform) while the remaining carbonyl fragment is converted to the sodium salt of propionic acid (sodium propionate). Typically performed in water at 0‑25 °C, then warmed; no special solvent beyond aqueous medium is required.

Acid–base double displacement (salt metathesis). Ammonium bisulfate (acidic salt) reacts with sodium bicarbonate (basic carbonate) to exchange cations, producing ammonium bicarbonate and sodium bisulfate. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; simple stirring is sufficient, no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) hydrolysis of a tertiary alkyl chloride; purpose is to convert 2‑chloro‑2‑methylhexane to the corresponding tertiary alcohol; key transformation is ionization to a tert‑butyl carbocation followed by attack of water giving 2‑methylhexan‑2‑ol and HCl; typical conditions are aqueous medium (water or aqueous ethanol) heated under reflux; acid catalyst (e.g., HCl) may be added to promote ionization, but often proceeds without added acid.

Thermal decomposition (denitrosation) of a nitrosamine. Heating N‑nitrosopiperidine induces cleavage of the N–NO bond, yielding the secondary amine piperidine and nitric oxide gas. Usually performed under inert atmosphere, in a non‑reactive solvent (e.g., toluene) or neat, at elevated temperature (≈150‑200 °C); no catalyst is required.

Hofmann degradation of a quaternary ammonium salt. Tetramethylammonium chloride is treated with aqueous NaOH; the resulting tetramethylammonium hydroxide undergoes base‑induced breakdown to give trimethylamine, methanol, and sodium chloride. Conducted in water with excess NaOH, heated (≈80‑100 °C) to promote the elimination; no additional catalyst is needed.

Dehydrative conversion of a thiourea to an isothiocyanate. Alpha‑naphthylthiourea is heated with phosphorus pentoxide, a strong dehydrating agent, which removes water to form alpha‑naphthyl isothiocyanate and phosphoric acid as by‑product. Typical conditions involve heating under anhydrous conditions (often in a dry solvent such as toluene or directly neat) with excess P₂O₅; no catalyst is required.

Acylation (esterification) of a diol using acetic anhydride. Ethylene glycol reacts with two equivalents of acetic anhydride, each hydroxyl group being acetylated to give ethylene glycol diacetate and generating two equivalents of acetic acid as by‑product. The reaction is usually performed or in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with gentle heating (≈50‑80 °C); catalytic DMAP or pyridine can be used to accelerate the acyl transfer but is not essential.

Reaction type: Williamson ether synthesis (alkylation). Purpose: convert ethanol to ethyl methyl ether while generating methyl hydrogen sulfate as byproduct. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of ethanol oxygen on a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, forming ethyl methyl ether and methyl hydrogen sulfate. Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as pyridine or DMF, often with a base to deprotonate ethanol; temperature 0 °C to room temperature; dimethyl sulfate handled with extreme care due to toxicity.

Reaction type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Purpose: exchange anions to form cobalt(II) iodate, which may precipitate from solution. Key transformation: Co²⁺ pairs with IO₃⁻ and K⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻, producing KNO₃ (soluble) and Co(IO₃)₂ (sparingly soluble). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring; occasional gentle heating to improve solubility; no special catalyst required.
double displacement reaction; precipitation of lead(ii) hydroxide; pb^2+ combines with oh- from dissociated nh3/h2o to form pb(oh)2; aqueous ammonia, ambient temperature; no catalyst required

Reaction type: double‑displacement (acid–base) reaction with precipitation. Purpose: generate mercuric chloride and free nitric acid. Key transformation: chloride ions replace nitrate around Hg²⁺, forming HgCl₂ (low solubility) and releasing HNO₃ into solution. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, moderate heating to aid precipitation, filtration to isolate HgCl₂; no catalyst needed.

Reaction type: oxidation of a secondary allylic alcohol to a ketone. Purpose: convert carveol to carvone, an important fragrance/kitchen‑herb compound. Key transformation: Dess‑Martin periodinane oxidizes the –OH group of carveol to a carbonyl, preserving the adjacent double bond and giving carvone Typical conditions: dry dichloromane (CH₂Cl₂) as solvent, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere (N₂), 1.1–1.5 equiv DMP, reaction time 0.5–2 h; work‑up with aqueous NaHCO₃.

Reaction type: redox (halogen‑hydride) reaction. Purpose: reduce chlorine to chloride and evolve hydrogen gas. Key transformation: LiH donates hydride to Cl₂, producing LiCl and H₂. Typical conditions: dry inert solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, under nitrogen or argon, temperature 0 °C to rt; stoichiometric amounts, gas collected over the reaction; no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: acid‑base complexation forming a fluoroaluminate salt. Purpose: produce soluble trisodium hexafluoroaluminate. Key transformation: fluoride from AlF₃ and HF coordinate to Al³⁺ to give the [AlF₆]³⁻ anion, which combines with Na⁺; OH⁻ neutralizes excess HF to water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, excess NaOH to provide three Na⁺ per Al, excess HF to supply six F⁻, temperature 20–60 °C, vigorous stirring until a clear solution forms; no special catalyst required.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; used to isolate dysprosium as an insoluble carbonate. In aqueous solution, dysprosium nitrate is mixed with sodium carbonate, resulting in the formation of a dysprosium carbonate precipitate while sodium nitrate remains dissolved. Typical conditions: room temperature to gentle heating, vigorous stirring; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Metathesis (double displacement) precipitation reaction; acid–base exchange where soluble sulfuric acid swaps anions with strontium perchlorate, precipitating insoluble strontium sulfate and liberating perchloric acid. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (saponification); aqueous NaOH attacks the carbonyl of (E)-but‑2‑enamide, breaking the C–N bond to give the sodium salt of (E)-but‑2‑enoic acid and release ammonia. Conducted in water or water/ethanol at reflux (≈80–100 °C); inert atmosphere not necessary; no added catalyst.

Reductive hydrogenation. Ho2S3 is heated under a flow of H2 gas at 800‑1000 °C. Hydrogen reduces the sulfide to metallic holmium while H2S gas is released. Purpose: recovery of holmium metal from its sulfide. No solvent; high‑temperature gas‑solid conditions.

The reaction is a radical-mediated reduction. It converts an alkyl iodide to an alkane by replacing the iodide with a hydrogen. Tributyltin hydride serves as the hydrogen donor, and radical initiators such as AIBN or heat may be used. The reaction is often conducted in solvents like benzene or toluene under reflux.

Nucleophilic addition of an organolithium reagent to an aldehyde; n‑propyl‑Li adds to the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde, forming a lithium alkoxide that upon aqueous acidic work‑up yields 1‑phenyl‑1‑propanol. Performed under inert atmosphere in anhydrous ether or THF at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C); quenched with dilute acid; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction; magnesium acetate and ammonium chloride swap anions in aqueous solution to give ammonium acetate and magnesium chloride. Usually carried out in water at room temperature; no catalyst; straightforward aqueous work‑up.

Alkaline ester hydrolysis (saponification); NaOH attacks ethyl butyrate, cleaving the ester bond to form ethanol and the sodium salt of butyric acid (sodium butyrate). Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol co‑solvent) under reflux (≈80 °C); afterwards acidification generates free butyric acid if desired; no catalyst.

Condensation/cyclocondensation forming a pyrazine; 2,3‑butanedione reacts with ammonia (generated from ammonium acetate) to give 2,3‑dimethylpyrazine, acetic acid and water; purpose is heterocycle synthesis; usually carried out by heating the mixture (often in ethanol or water) without added catalyst.

High‑temperature solid‑state sulfide formation; iron metal combines with cyclooctasulfur to give iron sulfide (FeS or FeS2). The mixture of iron powder and S8 is heated to 500‑800 °C under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Reaction type: hydrogen reduction of a metal halide. Purpose: recover metallic palladium from palladium(II) chloride and produce hydrogen chloride gas. Key transformation: Pd(II) is reduced to Pd(0) while H₂ is oxidized to H⁺, which pairs with Cl⁻ to give HCl. Typical conditions: solid PdCl₂ exposed to a flow of H₂ at 200–300 °C (often 1–5 atm) in a sealed tube or flow reactor. No solvent; gas‑phase; inert carrier gas may be used; no catalyst beyond the palladium substrate itself.

O‑acylation of phenoxide: sodium 4‑methyl phenolate reacts with acetyl chloride in an aprotic solvent such as acetone or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, yielding 4‑methyl phenyl acetate and NaCl via nucleophilic acyl substitution.

Similar acid‑metal displacement; K metal reacts with aqueous HF at room temperature, yielding K⁺F⁻ in solution and releasing H2 gas. Highly exothermic; carried out in dilute HF aqueous solution, no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization/alkoxide exchange between aluminum trimethoxide and acetic acid; methoxide groups are replaced by acetate, yielding aluminum acetate and methanol; usually refluxed in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or benzene with removal of methanol to drive equilibrium.

Nucleophilic substitution of tert‑butyl bromide with hydrosulfide ion to afford tert‑butyl mercaptan and KBr; essentially an SN1 (or SN2) thiolation; typically refluxed in a polar aprotic solvent such as ethanol, DMF or DMSO, sometimes with a base to generate HS⁻.

Hydrogenation of 2‑methyl‑1‑butene to isopentane; addition of H₂ across the C=C bond using a heterogeneous catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in a liquid solvent (ethanol, methanol, or acetic acid) under moderate pressure (1–5 atm) and temperatures 25–100 °C.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amidation (condensation) of oleic acid with ammonia using N,N′‑dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC). DCC activates the carboxylic acid to an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is attacked by ammonia to give the primary amide (oleamide) and dicyclohexylurea as the by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or DMF, typically at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) – aqueous NaOH hydrolyzes the alkyl chloride to the corresponding alcohol; the chloride is displaced by hydroxide to give 1‑methylcyclopropan‑1‑ol and NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heating under reflux; no special catalyst needed.

Methylation of taurine with dimethyl carbonate (green methylating agent). The primary amine of taurine attacks the carbonyl carbon of dimethyl carbonate, leading to N‑methylation and concomitant release of methanol and carbon dioxide. Requires heating (150‑200 °C) often in a sealed vessel or with a high‑boiling solvent (toluene, xylene) and may be catalyzed by a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃). The overall transformation installs a methyl group on nitrogen while generating CO₂ and MeOH as benign by‑products.

Electrophilic addition of Br₂ across the C=C bond of bicyclo[2.2.1]hept‑2‑ene (norbornene) to give the 2,3‑dibromo adduct; anti‑addition proceeds via a bromonium ion intermediate; carried out in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acylation of the secondary amine in etilefrine with pivaloyl chloride to afford the corresponding amide (etilefrine pivalate). The acid chloride reacts with the amine, forming the amide bond and liberating hydrochloric acid, which is usually scavenged by a base such as triethylamine. Reaction performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to ambient temperature under nitrogen.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic addition (hydration of a conjugated diene). Isoprene undergoes protonation by dilute H₂SO₄, followed by water attack to afford 3‑methyl‑2‑buten‑1‑ol (prenol). Reaction is carried out at 0–25 °C in aqueous sulfuric acid (often 1–5 % w/w) to minimize polymerization; the mixture is then extracted with a non‑polar solvent (e.g., diethyl ether) to isolate the allylic alcohol.

Acid‑base generation of nitrous acid from sodium nit and phosphoric acid. Phosph acid protonates the nitrite ion, producing nitrous acid (HNO₂) and sodium dihydrogen phosphate (NaH₂PO₄). Conducted in aqueous solution, often at 0‑5 °C to minimize decomposition of HNO₂, and used as an in‑situ source of nitrous acid for diazotization or nitrosation reactions.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation between dicyandiamide and 2,6‑dichlorobenzylamine forming a guanidine derivative (Guanoxabenz) with loss of ammonia; serves to build a substituted guanidine framework; generally performed by refluxing in ethanol with a catalytic amount of mineral acid (e.g., HCl).

Redox halogen-selenide exchange; bromine oxidizes Se^2- in cobalt(II) selenide to elemental selenium while being reduced to bromide, yielding cobalt(II) bromide and selenium. Typically performed in refluxing aqueous or alcoholic medium, no catalyst required.

Palladium(II)‑catalyzed intramolecular oxidative cyclization of o‑allylphenol to give benzofuran; involves C‑H activation and O‑aryl coupling; typical conditions use Pd(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %), an oxidant such as Cu(OAc)₂, in DMF or DMSO at 80–120 °C.

Bechamp reduction of a nitro aromatic compound; iron metal reduces the nitro group of 2‑nitronaphthalene to an amine in the presence of concentrated HCl, producing 2‑aminonaphthalene, water, and iron(III) chloride. Typical procedure: reflux 2 M HCl with excess Fe powder (2 eq) for several hours under stirring.

Acid‑catalyzed (or base‑catalyzed) ester hydrolysis of ethyl 2-(4‑chlorophenoxy)-2-methylpropionate to the corresponding carboxylic acid and ethanol. Reaction proceeds in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or aqueous base (NaOH), heated to reflux; after completion the mixture is acidified (if base used) to isolate 2-(4‑chlorophenoxy)-2-methylpropanoic acid and ethanol.

Halogen‑lithium exchange (metal‑halogen exchange) of 2‑chlorothiophene with n‑butyllithium, producing 2‑lithiothiophene and n‑butyl chloride as by‑product. Conducted at low temperature (‑78 °C) in dry THF under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); the organolithium can be used directly in subsequent reactions.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein-type) of allyl chloride with zinc iodide to afford allyl iodide and zinc chloride. Performed in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (acetone or DMF) under reflux; zinc iodide acts as the iodide source, driving equilibrium toward the more soluble zinc chloride and the desired allyl iodide.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous solution of nickel(II) chloride and sodium tungstate reacts to form insoluble nickel tungstate solid and sodium chloride in water; typically performed at room temperature with water as solvent, no catalyst required.

N‑alkylation of a sulfonamide via deprotonation and SN2; sodium hydride generates the sulfonamide anion which attacks ethyl bromide to give N‑ethyl‑4‑methylbenzenesulfonamide; carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or THF, 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Acid dissolution of a mixed‑valent metal oxide; aqueous hydrochloric acid reacts with cobalt(II,III) oxide (Co₃O₄) to produce soluble cobalt(II) chloride and water; usually performed at ambient or mildly elevated temperature, aqueous medium, no catalyst.

Catalytic skeletal isomerization of a branched alkane; 2,7‑dimethyloctane is rearranged to the more stable 2,6‑dimethyloctane over an acid‑functionalized zeolite or Pt/H‑Al₂O₃ catalyst under hydrogen; typical conditions 300–400 °C, hydrogen pressure (10–30 bar), solid catalyst, liquid phase.

Acid‑salt metathesis: nitric acid protonates silver fulminate, exchanging the anion to produce soluble silver nitrate and fulminic acid (HCNO); mainly a laboratory preparation of fulminic acid; performed in aqueous HNO₃ at low temperature because of the explosive nature of the reagents.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous solutions of silver nitrate and praseodymium chloride exchange ions to give insoluble silver chloride precipitate and soluble praseodymium nitrate carried out at room temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolytic cleavage). Isopropyl 2‑chloroacetate is treated with water under acidic conditions (e.g., 6 M HCl, reflux) to regenerate 2‑chloroacetic acid and isopropanol. Reaction proceeds via protonation of the carbonyl, nucleophilic attack by water, and loss of the isopropyl alcohol.

Type: catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation). Purpose: remove the α‑chloro substituent to afford the saturated ester. Key transformation: H₂/Pd‑C reduces the C–Cl bond, giving methyl propionate and HCl (often trapped by a base). Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5–10 % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, room temperature to reflux; a base (e.g., triethylamine) may be added to neutralize HCl.

Double displacement (Metathesis) precipitation; a convenient method to prepare copper(II) carbonate. Aqueous copper(II) nitrate trihydrate is mixed with aqueous sodium carbonate. Key transformation: Cu²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → CuCO₃(s) (light‑green precipitate) while Na⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to give NaNO₃ (soluble). Typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, stirring. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Ester reduction: lithium aluminum hydride reduces methyl 2-chloro-2-methylpropanoate to the primary alcohol 2-chloro-2-methyl-1-propanol; performed in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere, followed by aqueous acidic work‑up.

Fischer esterification; the carboxylic acid group of 4‑methoxybenzoic acid is converted to a methyl ester, releasing water; catalyzed by a strong acid such as sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; reflux in excess methanol (solvent and nucleophile) for several hours; water is removed to drive equilibrium.

Oxidation (high‑temperature roasting) of the intermetallic TaAl (tantalum aluminide) by O₂ to form the refractory oxides Ta₂O₅ and Al₂O₃. Purpose is to convert the alloy into stable insulating oxides for ceramics or protective layers. Conducted in a furnace at 800–1200 °C in a flow of dry oxygen or air; solid‑state reaction, no solvent, inert atmosphere not required.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis/neutralization of nitrosyl chloride (NOCl) with aqueous KOH. Hydroxide attacks NOCl, giving nitrite (NO₂⁻), chloride (Cl⁻) and water. The reaction is a simple acid‑base/redox neutralization used to prepare potassium nitrite. Performed at ambient temperature in aqueous solution; excess KOH ensures complete conversion; no special catalyst needed.

Acid‑base metalation (deprotonation) of 2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine (TMP) with methyllithium. The strong base MeLi abstracts the N‑H proton of TMP, generating lithium tetramethylpiperidide (TMP‑Li) and methane gas. This is a common method for preparing a non‑nucleophilic, hindered lithium amide base. Carried out under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in anhydrous ethereal solvents such as THF or diethyl ether, typically at 0 °C to –78 °C to control exotherm; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of 4‑chloro‑2‑aminopyrimidine by aqueous ammonia. Ammonia attacks the electron‑deficient pyrimidine ring, displacing chloride as Cl⁻ (captured as HCl) and installing an amino group to afford 2,4‑diaminopyrimidine. Used to replace a halogen with an amine on heteroaromatics. Conducted in aqueous NH₃ (often under pressure) with heating (reflux) to accelerate substitution; pH remains basic; no metal catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (Williamson ether/ester synthesis). Purpose: prepare propyl benzoate by alkylating the benzoate anion. Key transformation: benzoate O‑ attacks the primary carbon of 1‑iodopropane, displacing I⁻ and forming a new C‑O bond; NaI is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or DMSO; sodium benzoate is used as the nucleophile, often with a slight excess of the alkyl halide. No additional catalyst required.

Anodic electrosynthesis (oxidative coupling) of anthranilic acid to a diazonium intermediate followed by azo coupling with phenol, yielding 2‑(4‑hydroxyphenylazo)benzoic acid and hydrogen gas at the cathode. The reaction provides a clean, metal‑free route to azo dyes. Performed in an acidic aqueous medium (e.g., 0.1  H₂SO₄), using a platinum or graphite anode, constant current (10–50 mA cm⁻²), temperature 0–25 °C. Hydrogen evolves at the cathode; no additional reagents besides supporting electrolyte.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylacetonitrile to the corresponding carboxylic acid, 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylacetic acid, with formation of ammonium chloride. Nitrile is protonated by HCl, water adds to give an imidic acid that tautomerizes and further hydrolyzes to the acid, releasing NH₄⁺. Conducted by refluxing the nitrile in aqueous HCl (concentrated or 6 M) for several hours; excess HCl ensures complete conversion; aqueous medium; no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: selective nitro reduction; purpose: produce N‑phenylhydroxylamine as an intermediate; key transformation: –NO2 reduced to –NHOH; typical conditions: aqueous solution, sodium dithionite (Na2S2O4) as reductant, pH neutral‑slightly alkaline, 0‑50 °C; common solvent: water (often with a co‑solvent such as MeCN).

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of one iodine atom by cyanide ion, converting 1,1‑diiodoethane to iodoacetonitrile with NaI as by‑product; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0–50 °C.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) ether formation; purpose: synthesize methyl cyclopentyl ether; key transformation: bromide displaced by methoxide forming a C‑O‑CH3 bond; typical conditions: excess NaOCH3, polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO or dry methanol), 0‑50 °C; catalyst: none (base acts as nucleophile).

Reaction type: oxidation of primary alcohol to aldehyde; purpose: convert 2‑methylbenzyl alcohol to 2‑methylbenzaldehyde; key transformation: –CH2OHized to –CHO; typical conditions: Dess‑Martin periodinane (1‑1.5 equiv) in dry CH2Cl2, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; catalyst: none (DMP is stoichiometric oxidant).

Reaction type: alkaline ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose: cleave 2‑hydroxypropyl octadecanoate to give 1,2‑propanediol and sodium octadecanoate; key transformation: ester bond broken producing carboxylate salt and diol; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1‑2 equiv), reflux 1‑3 h, then acidification if free acid desired; solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture.

Reaction type: double displacement (metathesis) ion exchange; purpose: swap anions between ammonium chloride and barium fluoride; key transformation: NH4⁺ pairs with F⁻ to give NH4F, Ba²⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give BaCl₂; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, complete dissolution; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Reaction type: condensation (amide formation) between carboxylic acid and amine; purpose: synthesize N‑propylformamide; key transformation: formic acid reacts with propylamine, water eliminated to form –C(=O)NHPropyl; typical conditions: reflux of formic acid with excess propylamine, removal of water (Dean‑Stark or azeotropic distillation), 80‑120 °C; sometimes a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., HCl) is used to activate the acid.

Fischer esterification of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid with isopropanol catalyzed by p‑toluenesulfonic acid under microwave heating; purpose is to prepare the preservative isopropylparaben. Key transformation: conversion of the carboxylic acid into an isopropyl ester with loss of water. Typical conditions: neat or with a small amount of toluene, PTSA (5–10 mol %), microwave irradiation at 120–150 °C for 5–30 min; excess alcohol drives equilibrium.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1,3‑dichloropropane by isopropylamine (and ammonia) to give N‑(1,1‑dimethylethyl)‑1,3‑propanediamine. The reaction proceeds via double amination of each halide, generating HCl as by‑product. Common practice: use excess isopropylamine as solvent and base, heat under reflux (80–120 °C) for several hours; the liberated HCl is neutralised by the excess amine.

Acid-base reaction. Converts lanthanum aluminate to sulfates. Sulfuric acid protonates the oxide. Key transformations: decomposition to sulfate salts. Heated concentrated sulfuric acid used. Solvent: water.

Direct amidation of 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoic acid (lactic acid) with ammonia to afford 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanamide (lactamide) with loss of water. Usually performed under high‑temperature conditions (150–200 °C) or with activation (e.g., conversion to the acid chloride or use of a carbodiimide coupling agent). Solvent can be a high‑boiling dipolar aprotic solvent such as dimethylformamide; an excess of gaseous or aqueous NH3 is used to drive the equilibrium.

Halogenolysis of a Si–Si bond; hexamethyldisilane reacts with chlorine gas, cleaving the Si–Si bond to give two equivalents of trimethylsilyl chloride. Typically carried out in an inert, non‑reactive solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chlorobenzene at low temperature (0–5 °C) with controlled addition of Cl2; light or mild heating may be used to initiate the reaction. No catalyst is required.

Enzymatic O‑methyltransferase reaction: S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) donates a methyl group to piceatannol, converting one phenolic hydroxyl into a methoxy group and yielding isorhapontigenin together with S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Typically carried out in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C, requiring Mg²⁺ as cofactor and the specific piceatannol O‑methyltransferase enzyme.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of an aryl bromide; purpose is the same as reaction 1 – to obtain 1-benzofuran by replacing the bromine with hydrogen; key transformation C–Br → C–H; conditions: H₂ (1–3 atm) over Pd/C (10 % wt) at ambient temperature to 50 °C; solvent: EtOH, MeOH or EtOAc.

Oxidative deamination of N‑acetylputrescine catalysed by monoamine oxidase (MAO). Molecular oxygen serves as the electron acceptor, producing ammonia, hydrogen peroxide and the aldehyde N‑acetyl‑4‑aminobutanal. Conducted under physiological conditions (pH 7.4, 37 °C) in aqueous buffer; the enzyme contains FAD as a prosthetic group.

Acid‑base/Lewis acid reaction between ammonium fluoride and boron trifluoride forming ammonium tetrafluoroborate. Reaction type: salt formation via BF₃·F⁻ complexation; purpose: prepare BF₄⁻ as a non‑coordinating counter‑ion; key transformation: BF₃ accepts a fluoride ion to give BF₄⁻ paired with NH₄⁺; conditions: anhydrous solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, low to ambient temperature, inert atmosphere.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative methoxy‑carbonylation of 3‑iodophenol using carbon monoxide and methanol to form methyl 3‑hydroxybenzoate. The reaction proceeds via oxidative addition of the aryl iodide to Pd⁰, CO insertion to give an acyl‑Pd intermediate, and methanolysis to release the methyl ester. Typical conditions: CO pressure (5–30 atm), methanol as solvent (excess), Pd(OAc)₂ (2–5 mol %) with a phosphine ligand (e.g., PPh₃), base such as triethylamine, temperature 80–120 °C for 12–24 h.

Direct synthesis (metal halide formation). Elemental lutetium is oxidized while bromine is reduced, yielding lutetium(III) bromide. Typically performed by heating lutetium metal with liquid bromine under an inert atmosphere (nitrogen or argon) at temperatures of 200‑300 °C, often in a sealed tube to contain the corrosive bromine. No solvent or catalyst is required; excess bromine may be used to ensure complete conversion.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; magnesium benzoate reacts with sodium hydroxide to exchange cations, giving soluble sodium benzoate and insoluble magnesium hydroxide precipitate. Usually carried out at ambient temperature in water with vigorous stirring; filtration separates Mg(OH)₂. No catalyst required.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid (Jones oxidation). Chromic acid (CrO₃/H₂SO₄) oxidizes the aldehyde group of 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzaldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid, 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzoic acid. The reaction is usually carried out in acetone as solvent, with aqueous sulfuric acid, at 0 °C to room temperature. Excess oxidant is quenched with methanol or isopropanol. No additional catalyst is needed.

N‑alkylation (quaternization) of imidazole to form an imidazolium salt. 1‑ethylimidazole reacts with methyl iodide, alkylating the remaining nitrogen to give 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium iodide, an ionic liquid. The reaction proceeds typically in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or dimethylformamide, under reflux for several hours. No catalyst is required; the alkyl halide serves as electrophile.

Electrophilic α‑iodination of a nitrile. N‑iodosuccinimide (NIS) transfers an iodine atom to the α‑carbon of acetonitrile, producing iodoacetonitrile and succinimide as the by‑product. The transformation is usually performed in dry dichloromethane (or chloroform) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of a Lewis acid (e.g., TiCl₄) to enhance reactivity, though many protocols proceed without additional catalyst.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed). Water attacks the ester bond of chloroprocaine, cleaving it to give 4‑chlorobenzoic acid and 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol. Typically performed in aqueous HCl (e.g., 1 M) at reflux or with NaOH/MeOH followed by acid work‑up. No special catalyst beyond the acid/base; water is the solvent.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of trimethylsilyl benzoate with ethanol; purpose is to convert the silyl ester into ethyl benzoate while generating trimethylsilanol as by‑product; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ethanol on the carbonyl, displacing the trimethylsilyl group; typically performed by refluxing the substrate in excess ethanol, often with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., pyridine) to accelerate the exchange; ethanol serves as both reagent and solvent.

Hydrolysis of a metal carbide; beryllium carbide reacts with water to yield solid beryllium oxide and methane gas; performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating or reflux; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of diethyl phthalate. A mixture of 1‑butanol and 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol (isobutanol) attacks the ester bonds of diethyl phthalate, exchanging the ethyl groups for butyl and isobutyl groups to afford butyl isobutyl phthalate, while ethanol is liberated as a by‑product. Typical conditions employ a catalytic amount of sodium methoxide or potassium carbonate in excess of the alcohols, heating under reflux (≈120‑130 °C) in a solvent‑free or toluene medium, with continuous removal of ethanol to drive the equilibrium toward product formation.

Reductive amination (second methylation) of N‑methyl dopamine with formaldehyde; purpose is to convert the secondary amine into a dimethylated amine, yielding 4‑(2‑(dimethylamino)ethyl)‑1,2‑benzenediol (N,N‑dimethyl dopamine); key transformations analogous to reaction 3 (imine formation then NaBH₃CN reduction); conditions similar: methanol/water solvent, mild buffered pH, NaBH₃CN added at 0 °C to rt, 1–2 h reaction time.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; forms a biaryl C‑C bond to give 2‑phenylphenol. Typically uses a Pd(0) catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(dppf)Cl₂), a base such as K₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃ or Cs₂CO₃, and a mixed aqueous/organic solvent (toluene‑water, dioxane‑water, or THF‑water). Reaction is carried out under nitrogen or argon at 80–100 °C for several hours.

Silylation reaction; trimethylsilyl iodide reacts with a tertiary alcohol to form a trimethylsilyl ether and liberates hydrogen iodide; carried out in dry, aprotic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2 or THF) at low temperature (0 °C to rt) under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

Intramolecular SN2 cyclisation (ring‑closure) to form tetrahydrofuran. The hydroxyl group of 4‑chloro‑1‑butanol deprotonates, attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and producing THF; the chloride picks up a proton to give HCl. Carried out with a base such as NaOH or K₂CO₃ in ethanol or water, heated to reflux. No added catalyst.

Gabriel synthesis (SN2 alkylation of potassium phthalimide); produces N‑benzylphthalimide, a protected primary amine. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent like DMF, DMSO, or dry acetone, usually at reflux temperature. No catalyst is required; the potassium ion serves to generate the nucleophilic phthalimide anion.

Acid‑base neutralization of citric acid with lithium bicarbonate; yields lithium citrate with evolution of CO₂ and H₂O. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating to accelerate gas release. No special catalysts; the reaction proceeds stoichiometrically.

Ligand substitution and reduction of Pd(IV) to Pd(II) in aqueous ammonia; forms tetraamminepalladium(II) chloride ([Pd(NH₃)₄]Cl₂) together with KCl and NH₄Cl. Conducted in a concentrated NH₃ solution (or NH₄OH) at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature (≈40 °C). The medium supplies both the reducing environment and the coordinating amine ligands.

Redox halogenation: indium metal reduces nitrogen trichloride to nitrogen gas while being oxidized to indium trichloride. Typically carried out in anhydrous inert solvent (dry ether, THF, or acetonitrile) under a nitrogen atmosphere, often with gentle warming (0–50 °C) to promote reaction. No external catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of an epoxide by an organozinc reagent (vinylzinc chloride). The vinyl group adds to the less‑substituted carbon of ethylene oxide, generating a primary homoallylic alcohol (but‑3‑en‑1‑ol). Typically carried out under inert atmosphere in dry THF at 0 °C to –78 °C, then warmed, without added catalyst; the organozinc reagent is prepared in situ or used as a solution.

Acylation (acetylation) of a sulfonamide to afford acetazolamide. Acetic anhydride acetylates the amino group of 5‑amino‑1,3,4‑thiadiazole‑2‑sulfonamide, yielding acetazolamide and one equivalent of acetic acid. Usually run in pyridine or dimethylformamide at 0 °C to room temperature, then warmed to reflux. Pyridine serves as solvent and base; no additional catalyst required.

Esterification of phthalic anhydride with 2‑butoxyethanol to give bis(2‑butoxyethyl) phthalate (a phthalate plasticizer) and water. The anhydride reacts with two equivalents of the alcohol, each opening one carbonyl, forming two ester linkages. The reaction proceeds by heating the mixture of phthalic anhydride and excess 2‑butoxyethanol (which acts as both reactant and solvent) at 150–180 °C, often under reduced pressure to remove water and drive equilibrium toward the di‑ester. No additional catalyst is required, though a catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid can accelerate the process.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of mercury(II) thiocyanate. Sodium thiocyanate in aqueous solution exchanges its anion with perchlorate from mercury(II) perchlorate, precipitating insoluble Hg(SCN)₂ while forming soluble NaClO₄. Performed at ambient temperature in water; the mixture is usually filtered to isolate the white Hg(SCN)₂ solid, which is washed with cold water to remove residual perchlorate.

Oxidative conversion of 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde to its methyl ester (methyl nicotinate) via a Pinnick–type oxidation in methanol. Sodium chlorite (NaClO₂) oxidizes the aldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid; simultaneous esterification with methanol yields the methyl ester, while side products are water and NaCl. The reaction is carried out in a methanol/water mixture at 0–25 °C, often buffered with NaH₂PO₄ to suppress hypochlorous acid formation. After completion, the reaction mixture is extracted, and the ester is purified by distillation or chromatography.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; lead(II) acetate solution reacts with sodium carbonate, precipitating lead(II) carbonate and generating sodium acetate in the aqueous phase; performed in water at ambient temperature.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an aryl ether; diphenyl ether undergoes C–O bond cleavage over Raney nickel under hydrogen pressure to afford phenol and benzene; typical conditions are 50–100 atm H₂, 150–250 °C, in a solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol, with Raney Ni as the heterogeneous catalyst.

Acyl substitution (esterification) of an acid chloride with an alcohol; acetyl chloride reacts with isopropanol to produce isopropyl acetate and HCl; commonly conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent or neat, often with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl; no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkylation) where sodium benzoate attacks the primary carbon bearing iodine in 1‑iodo‑2‑methylpropane, displacing I⁻ to give 2‑methylpropyl benzoate; typically performed in dry polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone) under reflux, with sodium iodide precipitating out.

Full reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; lithium aluminium hydride reduces 3‑methylpentanal to 3‑methylpentan‑1‑ol; carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, followed by careful quench with water then aqueous NaOH to destroy excess LiAlH₄.

This is a metal carbonyl cluster synthesis via a gas‑phase reductive carbonylation. Ruthenium(III) bromide is reduced by a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen under high CO pressure (often 10–50 atm) at elevated temperature (150–200 °C). The process builds the Ru₃(CO)₁₂ cluster and generates hydrogen bromide as a gaseous by‑product. No solvent is typically used; the reaction is carried out in a sealed tube or autoclave.

This is an acid‑base neutralization that converts nicotinic (pyridine‑3‑carboxylic) acid into its aluminum salt. Aluminum isopropoxide acts as a Lewis acid/base reagent, accepting the protons from three molecules of nicotinic acid to form aluminum nicotinate and releasing three equivalents of isopropanol. The reaction is usually performed in refluxing isopropanol or under a dry inert atmosphere, and the resulting aluminum nicotinate precipitates out of solution.

Acid–base neutralization forming aluminum oxalate salt; purpose is to produce a soluble or precipitated aluminum oxalate for analytical or preparative use; key transformation: Al(OH)3 reacts with oxalic acid to give Al2(C2O4)3 (or hydrated Al‑oxalate) and water; typical conditions: aqueous solution, often heated to 50‑80 °C to aid dissolution; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

This reaction is a classic metal‑acid redox where sodium metal reduces propionic acid. Two equivalents of Na donate electrons to the acid, producing sodium propionate and liberating hydrogen gas. It is carried out in anhydrous ether or THF under nitrogen or argon, typically at 0 °C to room temperature to control the vigorous H₂ evolution.

This is an ester hydrolysis (water‑mediated cleavage) of pentyl acetate. In the presence of acid (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) or base (NaOH), water attacks the carbonyl carbon, yielding acetic acid and pentanol. Acidic hydrolysis is performed by refluxing the ester in aqueous acid; basic hydrolysis (saponification) uses aqueous NaOH at moderate temperature followed by acid work‑up to obtain the free acid.

Acid‑base reaction of calcium sulfide with sulfuric acid; purpose is generation of H2S and precipitation of calcium sulfate; key transformation: CaS + H2SO4 → CaSO4 (solid) + H2S (gas); typically performed at room temperature or mild heating in aqueous dilute H2SO4; no catalyst.

Aqueous precipitation/acid‑base neutralization; indium(III) nitrate reacts with hydroxide ions to form insoluble indium(III) hydroxide and soluble sodium nitrate. Key transformation: In(NO3)3 + 3 NaOH → In(OH)3↓ + 3 NaNO3. Performed in water at ambient temperature; stirring ensures complete precipitation. No special catalyst; the product is filtered and washed.

This is a Fischer esterification between ethanol and 2‑chloropropionic acid, forming ethyl 2‑chloropropionate and water.
