Radical chlorination (free‑radical substitution); purpose is to introduce an additional chlorine atom onto chloroethane, yielding 1,2‑dloroethane and HCl; a hydrogen atom on the ethyl chain is replaced by chlorine; carried out under UV irradiation or heat in the gas phase or in an inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) with excess Cl2; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation of neodymium hydroxide from neodymium sulfate and sodium hydroxide; aqueous Nd2(SO4)3 is treated with NaOH, yielding a white Nd(OH)3 precipitate and soluble Na2SO4; conducted at ambient temperature with stirring; water as solvent; excess NaOH may be used to ensure complete precipitation.

Inorganic peroxide synthesis (acid‑base precipitation); converts magnesium hydrox and hydrogen peroxide into solid magnesium peroxide while water is formed; the peroxide anion replaces hydroxide; performed in aqueous solution at low temperature (0–25 °C) with stoichiometric amounts of H2O2, often under stirring; no catalyst, the reaction proceeds spontaneously.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of prop‑2‑enyl formate with water; yields allyl alcohol and formic acid; carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., HCl or H2SO4) under reflux; solvent is water or a water‑alcohol mixture; temperature typically 80–100 °C.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of an aldehyde); reduces octanal to octanol by addition of hydrogen across the carbonyl; key transformation is conversion of –CHO to –CH2OH; typically conducted in a pressure reactor using H2 gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt‑O₂, or Raney Ni in a solvent like ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate at 25–80 °C.

Base‑catalyzed aldol condensation (Claisen‑Schmidt type). The hydroxyl‑acetophenone is deprotonated by NaOH to give an enolate, which adds to benzaldehyde; subsequent dehydration yields the conjugated α,β‑unsaturated ketone 1‑(3‑hydroxyphenyl)‑3‑phenylprop‑2‑en‑1‑one and water. Purpose: synthesis of a chalcone‑type scaffold. Typical conditions: aqueous or ethanolic NaOH (0–25 °C then warming), often performed in water/ethanol mixture; no special solvent beyond the reaction medium.

Iodination/reduction synthesis: GeO2 is reduced and iodinated by excess HI, producing GeI4 and water. Carried out in a sealed quartz tube at 150‑250 °C with gaseous or liquid HI; no additional solvent is required, and excess HI shifts the equilibrium toward product.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ionic exchange; swaps the anions of ammonium chloride and potassium thiocyanate to give potassium chloride and ammonium thiocyanate; occurs in aqueous solution; usually performed at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required and the products remain dissolved unless crystallized.

Acid‑base salt metathesis (fluorination); protonates acetate ions of samarium(III) acetate with HF to form acetic acid while the samarium cation pairs with fluoride to give samarium(III) fluoride precipitate; typical conditions involve aqueous HF (concentrated) at low temperature (0–25 °C) with vigorous stirring; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst, and the insoluble SmF₃ is filtered off.

Halogenation/redox reaction; solid antimony trioxide is chlorinated by chlorine gas to give antimony trichloride and liberate oxygen. Typically performed by passing Cl₂ over heated Sb₂O₃ (200–300 °C) in the gas phase; no solvent required.

Dehydrative cyclocondensation (benzothiazole synthesis); formamide supplies the carbonyl carbon which condenses with 2‑aminophenyl mercaptan to form the thiazole ring of 2‑aminobenzothiazole, releasing water. Conducted at 150–200 °C in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., diphenyl ether) or in polyphosphoric acid; often catalyzed by POCl₃ or P₂O₅.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation; fluorene is oxidized to fluorenone using molecular oxygen in the presence of palladium on carbon. Reaction runs under O₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or toluene at 80–100 °C; Pd/C serves as the catalyst.
Protonolysis of n‑butyllithium with ethanol; yields n‑butane and lithium ethoxide. Same conditions as with methanol: low temperature (0 °C) in ether or THF, ethanol added slowly; no catalyst.

Fluoride‑mediated desilylation of a silyl ether; tetrabutylammonium fluoride (TBAF) attacks the silicon of trimethyl(phenylmethoxy)silane, cleaving the Si–O bond to afford benzyl alcohol and volatile trimethylsilyl fluoride; typically conducted in anhydrous THF at 0 °C to rt, using 1–2 equiv TBAF solutione., 1 M in THF).

Acid–base reaction; carbonate reacts with a strong acid (hydrochloric acid) to give the corresponding metal chloride, carbon dioxide gas, and water; typically performed in aqueous HCl at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent.

Salt metathesis (double displacement) precipitation; silver acetate exchanges its acetate anion with the diethyldithiocarbamate anion of sodium diethyldithiocarbamate, forming insoluble silver diethyldithiocarbamate and sodium acetate in solution. Generally carried out in water or an alcohol at ambient temperature; the silver salt precipitates and is filtered off.

Transesterification (ester exchange); purpose is to replace the ethoxy group with a methoxy group, yielding the methyl ester and ethanol. The carbonyl carbon of ethyl cyclopentanecarboxylate undergoes nucleophilic attack by methanol, followed by elimination of ethanol. Typically performed with an acid catalyst such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, or a base catalyst like NaOCH₃, under reflux. Excess methanol is used as both reactant and solvent; removal of ethanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium toward product.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an imine; N‑methyl‑1‑phenylmethanimine is reduced by H₂ over palladium on carbon to the secondary amine N‑methylbenzylamine. Common conditions are 1–5 atm H₂, room temperature to 50 °C, in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol; Pd/C (5–10 % wt) is the catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of dimethyl sulfate with iodide; iodide displaces a methyl group to give methyl iodide while the remaining methyl group stays bound to sulfate, forming sodium methyl sulfate. Conducted in a polar aprotic medium (e.g., acetone or DMF) with NaI, often at room temperature; Na⁺ pairs with the methyl sulfate anion. Serves as a method to generate CH₃I from the methylating agent.

Electrophilic S‑methylation of thiophenol with methyl triflate – thiophenolate attacks the methyl group of MeOTf, producing methyl phenyl sulfide (thioether) and triflic acid. Conducted in anhydrous CH2Cl2 or CH3CN, 0 °C to rt, with a base (e.g., pyridine) to remove the acid; the reaction proceeds rapidly due to the high nucleophilicity of the thiolate.

Hydrolysis of a metal carbide (acid‑base reaction); lithium carbide reacts with water to generate lithium hydroxide and acetylene gas. Performed by adding Li₂C₂ to aqueous media at room temperature under an inert atmosphere to collect the evolved C₂H₂.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; nitronium tetrafluoroborate provides the NO2⁺ electrophile that installs a third nitro group at the 6‑position of 2,4-dinitroanisole to afford 2,4,6-trinitroanisole, with concomitant formation of HBF₄. Typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C to –20 °C), non‑aqueous solvent such as nitromethane or dichloromethane, inert atmosphere; reaction is quenched with ice‑water to isolate product.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) ortho bromination of phenol; bromine attacks the activated aromatic ring directed by the hydroxyl group, producing mainly 2‑bromophenol and hydrogen bromide; carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, often with a small amount of aqueous NaOH to generate phenoxide and control reaction rate; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of methanol to formic acid using potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid; CH3OH is oxidized by the Cr(VI) species (K2Cr2O7/H2SO4) to HCOOH with reduction of dichromate to Cr(III). Conducted in aqueous acidic medium, typically refluxing the mixture for 1–2 h; the reaction produces formic acid and water as products, along with Cr2(SO4)3 as a by‑product.

Reaction type: halide exchange or metathesis. Purpose: replace chloride with bromide. Key transformation: hydrobromic acid displaces chloride in hafnium tetrachloride. Conditions: heating in solution, likely in a polar solvent like HBr (aq). No specific catalyst mentioned.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl iodide by azide ion, converting the C–I bond into a C–N₃ bond to afford propyl azide; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 50‑80 °C, often with stoichiometric NaN₃; no catalyst required; useful as a route to primary amines after azide reduction.

This is an alcoholysis (halogen exchange) of a boron halide; BCl3 reacts with ethanol to replace the three chlorine atoms with ethoxy groups, forming triethyl borate and releasing HCl gas. It is used to prepare borate esters. Typical conditions involve refluxing excess dry ethanol under an inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) to drive off HCl; the reaction is often performed neat (ethanol as solvent) or in a dry, aprotic solvent such as toluene if a lower concentration is desired.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation). Purpose: synthesize N‑methylformamide. Key transformation: methylamine attacks one carbonyl of formic anhydride, forming the N‑methylamide and liberating formic acid. Typical conditions: 0 – 5 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF under nitrogen; often a base such as pyridine is added to trap the released HCl/formic acid.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; potassium carbonate deprotonates 2‑butoxyethanol, which then attacks the carbonyl of ethyl nicotinate, displacing ethanol and forming 2‑butoxyethyl 3‑pyridinecarboxylate. Commonly carried out under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, MeCN) or under solvent‑free conditions, often 80–120 °C for several hours.

General type: double displacement precipitation (metathesis) in aqueous medium; purpose: isolate barium fluoride and recover manganese(II) chloride; key transformation: MnF2 + BaCl2 → BaF2 (precipitates) + MnCl2 (remains in solution); typical conditions: aqueous solutions of MnF2 and BaCl2 mixed at room temperature, BaF2 precipitates; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Acid‑carbonate reaction (double displacement); lead(II) carbonate is protonated by hydrochloric acid, releasing CO₂ gas and water while precipitating lead(II) chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with dilute HCl; vigorous stirring aids gas evolution. No catalyst needed.

Selective reduction of a ketone; sodium borohydride donates hydride to cyclohexanone to give cyclohexanol, with formation of sodium metaborate as by‑product. Reaction is run at 0 °C to rt in protic solvent (methanol, ethanol) or a mixture of THF/water; work‑up involves aqueous quench and extraction.

Reductive amination of 1‑tetralone with ammonia; sodium cyanoborohydride reduces the imine intermediate formed from the ketone and ammonia to afford 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydro‑1‑naphthylamine. Typical protocol uses MeOH or EtOH as solvent, a slight acidic buffer (pH ≈ 5–6), and ambient temperature for 2–12 h.

N‑methylation via SN2 alkylation; methyl iodide reacts with the secondary amine of 3,4‑methylenedioxyamphetamine in the presence of potassium carbonate, which deprotonates the amine and promotes nucleophilic attack on the methyl halide, yielding 3,4‑methylenedioxymethamphetamine. Conducted in DMF or acetone at rt for several hours, followed by aqueous work‑up and purification.

Decarboxylation (thermal) of isoquinoline‑1‑carboxylic acid; purpose is to remove the carboxyl group and regenerate the parent heterocycle. Key transformation: -CO2 is eliminated, yielding isoquinoline. Typically performed by heating the acid alone or in a high‑boiling polar solvent (e.g., quinoline, DMSO) at 200–250 °C; no catalyst is required, though CuO or ZnCl2 can accelerate the process.

Hydrolysis reaction of rhodium(III) nitrate in aqueous solution, producing rhodium(III) hydroxide precipitate and nitric acid. Typically occurs upon dilution with water or mild heating. Acts as an acid-base decomposition.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1,3‑dichloropropane with sodium cyanide; used to introduce a nitrile function. Cyanide ion attacks one terminal chloride, displacing NaCl and forming 3‑chloropropionitrile. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 50–80 °C under inert atmosphere; excess NaCN is often employed to drive the reaction to completion.

Complete combustion (oxidation) of 3‑ethyl‑4‑methylhexane with molecular oxygen; an exothermic reaction that converts the hydrocarbon to carbon dioxide and water. Occurs upon ignition at temperatures above the flash point, typically in open air or a combustion chamber; no solvent or catalyst required. Reaction is used for energy release or calorimetric analysis.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between calcium carbonate and cobalt(II) chloride in aqueous medium; purpose is to precipitate cobalt(II) carbonate for isolation. Calcium carbonate reacts with CoCl2 to give insoluble CoCO3 (white precipitate) and soluble CaCl2. Performed in water with stirring at ambient temperature; mild heating may improve precipitation. No additional reagents needed.

SN2 alkylation of potassium trifluoroacetate with methyl iodide to produce methyl trifluoroacetate; employed for ester synthesis. The trifluoroacetate anion attacks the electrophilic methyl carbon, displacing I⁻ and forming KI as by‑product. Reaction carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile at 0–25 °C to control side reactions; stoichiometric KI precipitates out and can be filtered.

Redox acid‑metal reaction of thulium metal with sulfuric acid; used to generate thulium(III) sulfate and evolve hydrogen gas. Thulium is oxidized from 0 to +3, while H⁺ is reduced to H₂. Typically performed in dilute (≈2 M) H₂SO₄, with gradual addition of metal and gentle heating (50–80 °C) under a fume hood. No catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds with bubbling of H₂.

This is an activation/derivatization reaction where a silanol is converted to a silyl triflate, a highly reactive silylating agent. It proceeds via nucleophilic attack of trimethylsilanol on trifluoromethanesulfonic anhydride, displacing triflate and forming trimethylsilyl triflate while generating triflic acid. The reaction is typically carried out at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an aprotic, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dry dichloromethane under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst is required; the anhydride itself acts as the activating reagent.

Reaction type: Electrophilic addition of halogen (bromination). Purpose: install two bromine atoms across the double bond to give a vicinal dibromide. Key transformation: formation of a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate followed by nucleophilic attack by Br⁻, yielding 1,2‑dibromohexadecane. Typical conditions: dropwise addition of Br₂ dissolved in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent (carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, under dark or subdued light to avoid radical pathways. Common solvent: CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂.

Type: SN2 substitution of a benzylic chloride with hydroxide (hydrolysis of benzylic halide). Purpose: Convert the chloromethyl side chain into a hydroxymethyl group. Key transformation: OH⁻ attacks the benzylic carbon, displacing Cl⁻ to give 4-(hydroxymethyl)pyridine. Typical conditions: Aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), heating at 50–80 °C for 1–2 h. Common solvents/catalysts: Water or water/ethanol mixture; no additional catalyst required.

Aqueous neutralization of piperidinium acetate with sodium hydroxide; purpose is to convert the salt into the free amine and its corresponding acetate salt. Key transformation: OH⁻ deprotonates the piperidinium cation, producing piperidine, Na⁺ pairs with acetate, and water is formed. Typical conditions: stir the salt in water, add stoichiometric NaOH (1 equiv), ambient temperature, pH adjustment if needed; the piperidine can be extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., ether) after completion.

This is a Hofmann rearrangement (base‑mediated oxidative degradation of an amide) that converts butyramide into the corresponding primary amine, propylamine, with loss of the carbonyl carbon as carbon dioxide. The reaction uses aqueous sodium hydroxide as base and bromine as the oxidant, generating sodium bromide as a by‑product. Typical conditions involve cooling the amide solution in water, adding solid NaOH, then slowly adding a dilute Br2 solution while maintaining the temperature near 0 °C, followed by stirring at ambient temperature. No special solvent beyond water is required; the reaction is performed in the aqueous phase.

This is an acid‑base displacement reaction in which calcium chromate reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce soluble chromic acid (H2CrO4) and calcium chloride. The process is carried out in aqueous solution, often at room temperature, by adding solid CaCrO4 to excess HCl with stirring. The resulting mixture contains chromic acid in solution and precipitated or dissolved CaCl2; no additional catalysts are needed.

Type: acid‑base neutralization (oxidic acid with metal hydroxide). Purpose: form a water‑soluble calcium selenate salt and neutralize selenium trioxide. Key transformation: SeO3 + Ca(OH)2 → CaSeO4 + H2O. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient to modest temperature (often 20‑60 °C) to ensure dissolution and reaction. Common solvent: water; no catalyst required.

This is a hydrolysis of an ester (specifically 2‑phenylethyl 2‑phenylacetate) to give phenylacetic acid and 2‑phenylethanol. The transformation can be effected under either acidic or basic conditions. In acidic hydrolysis, aqueous dilute HCl or sulfuric acid is used as catalyst in a polar protic solvent (e.g., methanol/water), and the mixture is refluxed until the ester is consumed. In basic hydrolysis (saponification), aqueous NaOH or KOH is employed, followed by acidification of the reaction mixture to liberate the free acid and. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of water (or hydroxide) on the carbonyl carbon, leading to cleavage of the C–O bond.

Aqueous metathesis/precipitation: iron(III) chloride and dipotassium hydrogen phosphate exchange ions to yield soluble HCl and KCl and insoluble ferric phosphate that precipitates; conducted in water at room temperature with stirring and filtration to isolate the ferric phosphate.

Solid‑state acid‑base neutralization forming lithium silicate; two equivalents of lithium hydroxide react with silicon dioxide to give lithium metasilicate (Li₂SiO₃) and water; used for synthesis of lithium silicate materials; performed by thoroughly mixing the dry powders and calcining at 600–800 °C in a furnace; no solvent or additional catalyst is required.

Enzymatic O‑methylation (transferase reaction). An O‑methyltransferase uses S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine as a methyl donor to convert the phenolic OH of 2‑naphthol into a methoxy group, yielding 2‑methoxynaphthalene. Typically performed in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 30–37 °C, often with Mg²⁺ as a cofactor. No organic solvent required; the reaction proceeds under mild, biological conditions and produces S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine as a by‑product.

Van Leusen oxazole synthesis (multicomponent cycloaddition). p‑Toluenesulfonylmethyl isocyanide reacts with benzaldehyde in the presence of a mild inorganic base (Na₂CO₃) to generate 2‑phenyl‑1,3‑oxazole. The transformation proceeds via formation of an imidoyl intermediate that cyclizes to the oxazole ring. Typical solvent is DMF or DMSO; the reaction is conducted at room temperature to 50 °C for several hours under anhydrous conditions.

Acid‑base precipitation reaction; forms holmium oxalate by reacting holmium trihydroxide with aqueous oxalic acid; the oxalate product precipitates as a solid while water is generated; reaction is usually performed at room temperature or with mild warming to improve crystal formation; water is the solvent; no catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of N,N'-diacetylhydrazine; cleavage of the two amide bonds to regenerate free hydrazine and produce two acetate ions; performed with aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) and heating (reflux, 60–100 °C), often in water or water/ethanol, followed by acidification to isolate hydrazine.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification (ester exchange). Ethanol attacks the ester bond of 2‑ethylhexyl 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoate, displacing the 2‑ethylhexyl group and forming ethyl 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoate together with 2‑ethylhexanol as the by‑product. The process is usually catalyzed by a base such as NaOMe or K₂CO₃ (or by an acid catalyst like p‑TsOH) in a high‑boiling solvent (toluene, xylene) with reflux and azeotropic removal of ethanol to drive the equilibrium toward products.

Redox oxidation; copper(I) bromide is oxidized by elemental bromine to copper(II) bromide while bromine is reduced to bromide ion. Usually performed in an inert or mildly acidic aqueous or organic medium at room temperature; no additional catalyst needed.

Precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction; iron(III) acetate dissolved in water is added to aqueous sodium hydroxide, causing neutralization of the acetate and formation of insoluble iron(III) hydroxide; sodium acetate remains in solution.

Acid‑base neutralization; purpose is to convert nickel(II) oxide to a soluble chloride salt. Key transformation: NiO + 2 HCl → NiCl2·6H2O (in solution) + H2O. Conducted in aqueous HCl at room temperature or with mild heating; water serves as solvent, no catalyst required.

SN1 solvolysis in ethanol to form a tert‑alkyl ether; purpose is synthesis of 2‑ethoxy‑2‑methylbutane. The carbocation formed from 2‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane is captured by ethanol, producing the ether and HBr. Conditions: excess ethanol as both reagent and solvent, gentle heating (reflux); no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative cleavage of a benzylic carbonyl (KMnO₄ oxidation). Potassium permanganate in alkaline aqueous medium oxidizes the carbonyl‑bearing side chain of acetophenone, cleaving the C–C bond adjacent to the carbonyl and yielding benzoic acid. The reaction is performed with excess KMnO₄ at reflux (100 °C) for several hours; the mixture is then acidified to precipitate the benzoic acid. No special catalyst beyond KMnO is required; the reaction tolerates polar protic solvents (water).

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive conversion of aldehyde to primary alcohol). Molecular hydrogen (H₂) reduces pentadecanal to 1‑pentadecanol in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt‑O₂, or Raney Ni. The reaction is carried out in an inert solvent (e.g., ethanol, THF) at 1–5 atm H₂ pressure and temperatures ranging from 25 °C to 80 °C. The catalyst facilitates selective reduction of the aldehyde carbonyl without over‑hydrogenation of the alkyl chain.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation) of magnesium peroxide; upon heating, MgO2 breaks down to give magnesium oxide and molecular oxygen. Typical conditions: dry solid heated to 300‑400°C in a furnace; no solvent required; inert atmosphere often used to avoid side reactions.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose is to convert insoluble manganese(II) oxide into a soluble manganese(II) chloride salt; oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to give chloride and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent.

Selective reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H); the ethoxy group of ethyl 2‑methoxyacetate is displaced as ethanol while the carbonyl carbon is reduced to 2‑methoxyacetaldehyde. Common conditions: 0 °C to –78 °C, inert solvent such as toluene, THF or hexanes, 1 equiv DIBAL‑H under nitrogen; reaction quenched with methanol or aqueous acid.

Conversion of picolinic acid to pyridine‑2‑carbonyl chloride using thionyl chloride; formation of an acid chloride from a carboxylic acid. Reaction is run neat or in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, with excess SOCl₂, and refluxed (or gently heated) under nitrogen. Gaseous by‑products (SO₂ and HCl) are vented; the resulting acyl chloride is typically distilled or used directly.

Oxidative insertion / organometallic preparation: zinc metal inserts into the carbon‑bromine bond of ethyl bromide to give ethylzinc bromide, an organozinc reagent used in Negishi couplings. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF, with activated Zn dust, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere, often at reflux.

Nitrosation of semicarbazide; nitrous acid generated in situ (NaNO₂ + HCl) reacts with the primary amine of semicarbazide to give N‑nitroso‑semicarbazide and water. Usually performed in aqueous acidic medium at 0–5 °C to minimize side‑product formation; the reaction is stopped by cooling and adjusting pH.

Partial catalytic hydrogenation of chloroacetylene to vinyl chloride; hydrogen adds across the triple bond of Cl‑C≡C‑H to afford the corresponding alkene (Cl‑CH=CH₂). Typical conditions: low‑pressure H₂ (1–5 atm), Lindlar catalyst or poisoned Pd/C to avoid over‑reduction, solvent such as ethanol or THF, temperature 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere.

Base‑mediated deacetylation (saponification) of an acetate ester; converts oxolan‑3‑yl acetate to tetrahydrofuran‑3‑ol while forming sodium acetate. Usually performed by treating the acetate with aqueous NaOH (1 equiv) in a methanol/water mixture at room temperature to reflux (20–80 °C); the alkoxide is protonated on work‑up to give the free alcohol.

Disproportionation (redox) of sodium chlorite in aqueous solution; upon heating, ClO₂⁻ ions convert to chloride (Cl⁻) and chlorate (ClO₃⁻) ions in a 1:2 ratio. Conducted by warming an aqueous NaClO₂ solution (often 70–100 °C); no added catalyst required, though acidic or basic conditions can influence rate.

Precipitation/condensation reaction forming a heteropoly acid salt (ammonium phosphomolybdate). Key transformation: condensation of MoO₄²⁻ units with PO₄³⁻ in the presence of NH₄⁺ to produce the polyoxometalate [NH₄]₃[PMo₁₂O₄₀]·nH₂O and water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of phosphoric acid and molybdic acid (as H₃PO₄ and H₂MoO₄), adjust pH to ~1–2 with NH₄OH, stir at room temperature; the precipitate forms spontaneously. No additional catalyst; common solvent: water.

Nucleophilic substitution/organometallic metathesis forming tetraphenylgermane; four phenyl‑lithium reagents attack germanium tetrachloride, replacing each Cl with a Ph group and precipitating LiCl. Reaction carried out at –78 °C to 0 °C in dry ether or THF under nitrogen; stoichiometric 4 equiv PhLi, followed by work‑up to isolate GePh₄.

reaction type: Esterification. purpose: Synthesis of methyl esters from carboxylic acids. key transformations: Butyric acid undergoes methylation at the carboxylic acid oxygen, forming a methyl ester group. diazomethane acts as a methylating agent and source of nitrogen gas. reaction conditions: Typically performed in inert solvents (e.g., diethyl ether, dichloromethane) at low to moderate temperatures. solvents: Commonly used solvents include dichloromethane or ether. catalysts: None required.

Aminolysis (amidation) of a methyl ester with ammonia to afford 4‑chlorobenzamide; key transformation is nucleophilic substitution of the methoxy group by NH3, releasing methanol; typically performed by heating methyl 4‑chlorobenzoate with excess gaseous or aqueous NH3 at 100–150 °C, often in a sealed tube or high‑pressure reactor; solvent may be absent or a low‑boiling solvent like ethanol can be used.

Decarboxylation; loss of CO₂ from a β‑hydroxy‑α‑keto acid to give the α‑hydroxy‑ketone (acetoin). Typical in metabolic pathways or performed chemically with heating (80‑120°C) in aqueous buffer or with enzymatic decarboxylase (e.g., thiamine diphosphate‑dependent) under neutral pH.

reaction type: Solid-state metathesis reaction. purpose: Formation of magnesium zirconate ceramic material. key transformations: Magnesium carbonate and zirconium dioxide undergo thermal decomposition and recombination to form magnesium zirconate with carbon dioxide evolution. reaction conditions: High-temperature calcination (typically above 800°C). solvents: None. catalysts: None.

Acid-base reaction (neutralization); converts gadolinium oxide to a soluble nitrate salt; gadolinium oxide reacts with nitric acid to form gadolinium nitrate and water via protonation of oxide ions; typical conditions involve heating in aqueous nitric acid solution.

reaction type: Redox reaction. purpose: Simultaneous reduction and oxidation of nitrogen dioxide. key transformations: Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) undergoes disproportionation in aqueous solution to form nitrate (NO3^-) and nitrite (NO2^-) ions, while sodium bicarbonate decomposes to release carbon dioxide and water. reaction conditions: Aqueous solution at moderate temperatures. solvents: Water. catalysts: None.

Oxidation of primary allylic alcohol to aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). Pent‑4‑en‑1‑ol is oxidized to pent‑4‑en‑al without over‑oxidation to the acid. Conducted in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under anhydrous conditions, typically under nitrogen; PCC acts as the oxidant.

reaction type: Oxidation (N-oxidation). purpose: Conversion of pyridine to pyridine N-oxide. key transformations: Peroxybenzoic acid oxidizes the pyridine nitrogen, forming a coordinate bond to the peroxidic oxygen, which then rearranges to yield the N-oxide. benzoic acid is a byproduct from the reduction of the peroxy group. reaction conditions: Typically carried out in organic solvents (e.g., chloroform, acetic acid). solvents: Chloroform, acetic acid. catalysts: None.

Halogenation of hydrogen cyanide: bromine adds to HCN to generate hydrogen bromide and cyanogen bromide (BrCN); typically performed at 0–5 °C in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂ with controlled addition of Br₂ gas; no catalyst required.
Acid‑base neutralization; converts insoluble SnO to soluble SnSO4; SnO + H2SO4 → SnSO4 + H2O; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating; water is the solvent.

reaction type: Hydrolysis. purpose: Conversion of acyl chlorides to carboxylic acids. key transformations: 3-Methylbenzoyl chloride reacts with water to form 3-methylbenzoic acid, releasing hydrogen chloride gas. reaction conditions: Rapid and exothermic; occurs in aqueous conditions. solvents: Water or aqueous mixtures. catalysts: None required.

Type: nucleophilic alkylation (SN2) of a biguanide nitrogen; purpose: laboratory synthesis of the antidiabetic drug metformin; key transformation: two methyl groups from methyl iodide are transferred to the biguanide, generating metformin and releasing hydrogen iodide; typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, often with an added base (e.g., Na2CO3 or NaHCO3) to neutralize HI; common solvents/catalysts: DMF, acetonitrile, optional inorganic base, inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralisation forming an ammonium salt; trimethylamine accepts a proton from HCl to give trimethylammonium chloride; typically performed in anhydrous ether or dilute aqueous HCl at 0–25 °C; purpose is to prepare the stable ionic salt; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation: aqueous barium chloride reacts with sodium selenate to give soluble NaCl and sparingly soluble barium selenate, which precipitates; performed at room temperature with stirring, followed by filtration; no catalyst needed.

Type: thermal decomposition (calcination) of a metal oxalate; purpose: conversion of gadolinium oxalate to gadolinium oxide for materials or ceramic applications; key transformation: heating breaks C–C and C–O bonds, releasing CO2 and CO gases while the metal center oxidizes to Gd2O3; typical conditions: gradual heating to 300–500 °C in a furnace, often in air or under nitrogen to control oxidation; common solvents/catalysts: none, solid‑state reaction.

Type: halide exchange (double displacement) reaction; purpose: synthesis of nickel(II) fluoride and removal of bromide as soluble potassium bromide; key transformation: bromide ions are replaced by fluoride ions, yielding NiF2 and KBr; typical conditions: aqueous solution, may be heated gently to enhance solubility; common solvents/catalysts: water, no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) amination of a primary alkyl bromide with ammonia; purpose is to generate a primary alkyl amine. Key transformation: NH₃ attacks the carbon bearing Br, replacing Br⁻ with NH₂⁻ to afford 3‑chloropropylamine and HBr (neutralized by excess NH₃). Typical conditions: excess gaseous or liquid NH₃ serving as solvent, ambient to mildly elevated temperature (0‑50 °C); often performed in a sealed pressure vessel to retain ammonia.

Hydration/solvation; dissolution of anhydrous lanthanum(III) chloride in water followed by crystallization yields the hexahydrate LaCl3·6H2O; the process is carried out at ambient temperature, typically by evaporating the aqueous solution, no catalyst.

Type: base‑induced E2 elimination; purpose: preparation of trans‑β‑methylstyrene (an alkene) from a benzylic bromide; key transformation: NaNH2 abstracts a proton β to the bromine, causing simultaneous loss of bromide and formation of the C=C double bond (trans geometry); typical conditions: dry liquid ammonia or THF at low temperature (–33 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; common solvents/catalysts: sodium amide as base, liquid NH3 or THF as solvent.

Reaction type: conversion of an alcohol to an alkyl chloride using thionyl chloride (nucleophilic substitution). Purpose: to replace the hydroxyl group with chlorine, generating an alkyl chloride useful for further substitution or coupling reactions. Key transformation: the OH of 2-(4‑chlorophenoxy)ethanol is replaced by Cl, producing 2-(4‑chlorophenoxy)ethyl chloride while releasing SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: anhydrous environment, reflux in a non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a base like pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl; reaction proceeds at 0 °C to reflux temperature under nitrogen. No additional catalysts are required.

Type: transesterification (ester exchange); purpose: synthesis of octyl acetate (a flavor/fragrance ester) and regeneration of methanol; key transformation: the alkoxy group of methyl acetate is exchanged with the hydroxyl group of 1‑octanol, forming octyl acetate and methanol; typical conditions: reflux of the two components with catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (e.g., NaOMe) in excess methyl acetate or a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene; common solvents/catal: acidic or basic catalyst, toluene or excess acetate, removal of methanol by azeotropic distillation.

Amide formation (condensation) – reaction of a carboxylic acid with ammonia to give the corresponding amide and water; purpose is to synthesize 3,3‑dimethylbutanamide; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of NH₃ on the carbonyl carbon with loss of water; typically performed by heating the acid neat or in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., toluene) with removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap) or by first converting the acid to its acid chloride; no metal catalyst required, acid catalysts (e.g., HCl gas) may be used to promote the reaction.

Combustion (oxidation) – complete oxidation of 2,3‑dimethylpentane in excess O₂ to CO₂ and H₂O; purpose is energy release or analytical determination of fuel content; key transformation is radical chain oxidation of all C–H bonds to carbonyl groups; performed by igniting the hydrocarbon in air or pure O₂ at atmospheric pressure; no solvent; temperature of flame typically 1500–2000 °C.

Fischer esterification – conversion of 2‑octanol into 2‑octyl acetate with acetic acid, producing water; purpose is synthesis of a fruity‑smelling ester; key step is proton‑catalyzed nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the carbonyl of acetic acid followed by loss of water; usually carried out with excess acetic acid, catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, reflux in toluene or cyclohexane, and removal of water via azeotropic distillation or Dean‑Stark trap.

Oxidative decomposition of a metal carbonyl – hydrogen peroxide oxidizes tungsten hexacarbonyl to tungsten trioxide, liberating CO₂ and H₂O; purpose is to convert volatile carbonyl to an insoluble oxide for waste treatment or material preparation; key transformation is oxidation of CO ligands to CO₂ and oxidation of W(0) to W(VI); typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) with excess H₂O₂; no additional catalyst required.

DCC‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification) – coupling of benzoic acid and benzyl alcohol using dicyclohexylcarbodiimide to afford benzyl benzoate and dicyclohexylurea; purpose is mild, water‑free synthesis of esters; key steps are activation of the carboxyl group by DCC to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate, followed by nucleophilic attack by the alcohol; normally run in dry dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; by‑product dicyclohexylurea precipitates and is removed by filtration.

Oxidative combustion of zinc phosphide – reaction of Zn₃P₂ with O₂ to give ZnO and P₂O₅; purpose is disposal or conversion to oxides; key transformation is oxidation of Zn²⁻ to Zn²⁺ (ZnO) and P³⁻ to P⁵⁺ (P₂O₅); typically carried out by heating Zn₃P₂ in a flow of dry air or oxygen at 500–800 °C; no solvent; reaction may be performed in a quartz tube furnace under controlled O₂ flow.

Single‑electron redox (metal displacement) reaction; lithium metal reduces uranium(III) bromide to metallic uranium while being oxidized to lithium bromide; performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at elevated temperature, often in a molten salt or sealed tube; no catalyst, but careful exclusion of moisture and oxygen is essential.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1 hydrolysis) of benzhydryl bromide with water; the tertiary benzylic bromide forms a benzhydryl carbocation that is captured by water to give diphenylmethanol, releasing HBr; usually carried out in aqueous medium, often warm (reflux) or with a small amount of acid/base to neutralize HBr; no special catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis (salt exchange) used to prepare zinc triflate, a Lewis‑acid catalyst. The strong Brønsted acid (trifluoro­methanesulfonic acid) protonates the acetate ligands of Zn(OAc)2, releasing acetic acid and forming Zn(OTf)2. Typically performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at ambient temperature; the volatile acetic acid is removed by evaporation or gentle reflux.

E2 elimination (base‑induced dehydrohalogenation); potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from (E)-1‑bromobut‑1‑ene producing conjugated 1,3‑butadiene, while the tert‑butoxide is protonated to tert‑butanol and KBr is formed as the salt. Typically carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or DME) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization of an acidic oxide: chromium(VI) oxide (CrO₃) reacts with aqueous potassium hydroxide, neutralizing the acidic oxide to give potassium chromate (K₂CrO₄) and water; performed in water, often with gentle heating to ensure dissolution.

Synthesis/oxidation; chlorine oxidizes phosphorus trichloride (P(III)) to pentavalent phosphorus pentachloride (P(V)); essentially a gas‑phase chlorination; typically carried out by passing dry Cl₂ gas over PCl₃ at ambient to mildly elevated temperature (0–50 °C) in a sealed reactor; no solvent or catalyst required.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone. Dimethyl sulfide is oxidized by potassium permanganate in acidic medium (provided by sulfuric acid) to the corresponding sulfone (dimethyl sulfone). Manganese is reduced from Mn(VII) to Mn(IV) oxide (MnO2) and potassium sulfate forms as the spectator salt. Reaction is conducted in aqueous solution, often with cooling (0–25 °C) to control the exotherm; the solid MnO2 is filtered off after completion.

Hydrolysis of an amide to a carboxylic acid. Water reacts with 2,2‑dibromoacetamide, cleaving the C– to afford 2,2‑dibromoacetic acid and releasing ammonia. Usually performed under heating (reflux) in aqueous medium; optionally a small amount of acid or base can be added to accelerate the hydrolysis.

Oxidative cleavage of a benzylic acetate; aqueous alkaline KMnO₄ oxidizes the CH₂OAc side chain of 2‑hydroxybenzyl acetate to a carboxyl group, yielding salicylic acid (2‑hydroxybenzoic acid) and liberating acetic acid. Conducted in warm aqueous solution (often pH ≈ 8–10) with excess KMnO₄; the reaction is usually performed under reflux.

Metal‑halide reduction (low‑valent halide preparation); titanium metal reduces titanium(IV) iodide to titanium(II) iodide. Conducted in sealed, evacuated quartz tubes or in a dry inert‑gas atmosphere at elevated temperatures (300–500 °C); solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst other than the metallic titanium.

Acid‑base dissolution of silica; solid SiO₂ reacts with aqueous sodium carbonate at elevated temperature to give soluble sodium silicate (Na₂SiO₃) and evolve CO₂ gas. The process is carried out in water with heat (often > 100 °C) and vigorous stirring; no organic solvent is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl halide by nitrite ion. Purpose: replace the chlorine atom with a nitro group to give a nitro‑propionic acid. Key transformation: Cl‑CH2CH2CO2H + NaNO2 → O2N‑CH2CH2CO2H + NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic medium (e.g., water/ethanol) at 0 °C to reflux; stoichiometric sodium nitrite; no special catalyst required.

Ligand exchange of phenylmercuric acetate with hydroiodic acid. Purpose: convert the acetate ligand to iodide, producing phenylmercuric iodide and acetic acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic substitution of the acetate by I⁻. Typical conditions: aqueous HI (excess), temperature from 0 °C to reflux as needed; reaction carried out in water or dilute acid media; no catalyst.

Redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction between elemental phosphorus and concentrated nitric acid. Purpose: oxidize phosphorus to phosphoric acid while reducing nitric acid to nitrogen dioxide gas. Key P4 + 20 HNO3 → 4 H3PO4 + 20 NO2 + 4 H2O. Conditions: excess conc. HNO3, vigorous stirring, heating (often 80–120 °C); reaction carried out in a glass apparatus resistant to corrosion; nitrogen dioxide evolved is collected or vented.

Alcohol addition to isocyanic acid producing a carbamate ester; methanol adds across the N=C=O moiety of HNCO, forming methyl carbamate and a proton on nitrogen; a common route to alkyl carbamates used as protecting groups or intermediates; reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature using excess methanol as both reactant and solvent; may be catalyzed by a weak base (triethylamine) to neutralize the generated acid, but often proceeds without added catalyst.

Hydrogenation (high‑temperature gas‑phase synthesis) reaction: Germanium is reduced by hydrogen to produce germane, germanium hydride (Ge + 2 H₂ → GeH₄). Conducted at 800–1000 °C under a stream of H₂ gas, typically in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent, inert carrier gas may be used.

Selective reduction of an ester to an aldehyde (Luche‑type reduction). Purpose: convert methyl salicylate into salicylaldehyde while liberating methanol. Key transformation: MeO‑C(=O)‑C6H4OH + TiCl4 + NaBH4 → CH3OH + O=CH‑C6H4‑OH. Typical conditions: anhydrous solvent (dry THF or diethyl ether), TiCl4 (1–1.5 eq) added at 0 °C under inert atmosphere, then NaBH4 (1.5–2 eq) added slowly; reaction kept below 0–5 °C to avoid over‑reduction; work‑up with aqueous acid.

Ester hydrolysis (acidic or basic); 2‑ethylhexyl fluoroacetate is cleaved by water to produce fluoroacetic acid and 2‑ethylhexyl alcohol. Usually carried out by refluxing the ester in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (NaOH) for several hours; the reaction mixture is then acidified to isolate the acid.

Carboxylation of an organolithium reagent with carbon dioxide followed by acidic work‑up. Purpose: elongate the carbon chain by one carbon to afford a carboxylic acid. Key transformation: cyclopropyl‑Li + CO2 → cyclopropyl‑CO2Li, then protonation → cyclopropanecarboxylic acid. Conditions: dry ether or THF, temperature –78 °C to 0 °C during addition of CO2 (dry ice or CO2 gas), then quench dilute aqueous HCl; inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) throughout.

Base‑catalyzed saponification; benzyl acrylate reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium acrylate (the sodium salt of acrylic acid) and benzyl alcohol. Conducted at reflux or ambient temperature in aqueous/ethanol solvent; after completion, the mixture is acidified to isolate acrylic acid if desired.

α‑Halogenation of aldehydes using aqueous sodium hypochlorite; purpose is to introduce a chloro substituent at the α‑position of acetaldehyde, giving chloroacetaldehyde. Reaction proceeds via enolate formation under mildly basic conditions (pH 9–10) at 0–25 °C in water; the organic product is usually extracted with an ether. No external catalyst is required.

Rosenmund‑type catalytic hydrogenation of an acyl chloride to an aldehyde. Purpose: obtain isobutyraldehyde from isobutyryl chloride while generating HCl as by‑product. Key transformation: (CH3)2CH‑C(O)Cl + H2 (CH3)2CH‑CHO + HCl. Typical conditions: Pd on BaSO4 catalyst (often poisoned with quinoline), low pressure H2 (1–5 atm), solvent such as dry benzene or toluene, temperature 0–25 °C; reaction monitored to prevent over‑reduction to the alcohol.

Oxidation of an α‑hydroxy ketone (benzoin) to a 1,2‑diketo compound (benzil) using a peracid. Purpose: convert benzoin intoil; peracetic acid serves as the oxidant, producing acetic acid and water as benign by‑products. Key transformation: PhCH(OH)C(O)Ph + CH3CO3H → PhC(O)C(O)Ph + CH3CO2H + H2O. Conditions: dilute peracetic acid (generated in situ or commercial) in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetone, temperature 0–25 °C, reaction time 1–3 h; work‑up with aqueous sodium bicarbonate to neutralize acetic acid.

Hydrolytic cleavage of a carbamate (promecarb) – aqueous hydrolysis. Purpose: detoxification/degradation of the pesticide by breaking the N‑methylcarbamate linkage. Key transformation: the carbamate C–O bond is cleaved by water giving N‑methylcarbamic acid and the phenolic fragment 3‑methyl‑5‑(1‑methylethyl)phenol. Typical conditions: excess water, pH neutral to mildly acidic or basic, temperature 25–80 °C, reaction time 1–24 h. Common solvent: water or aqueous buffer; no additional catalyst required, though mild base (NaHCO₃) or acid (HCl) can accelerate the reaction.

Amide hydrolysis (neutral or acid/base‑catalyzed); converts N‑yl‑‑hydxyphenethyl‑amide to the free 4‑(2‑aminoethyl)phenol and acetic acid; typically reflux in aqueous solvent (water or water/acetone) with a catalytic amount of HCl, NaOH or enzyme; purpose is de‑protection of the acetamide group.

Formation of an acid chloride from acetic acid using oxalyl chloride – acyl‑chloride synthesis (Vilsmeier‑type reagent). Purpose: generate acetyl chloride for further acylation chemistry. Key transformation: acetic acid reacts with oxalyl chloride, releasing CO₂ and CO, while the chloride is transferred to the acyl moiety producing acetyl chloride; pyridine scavenges the released HCl forming pyridinium chloride. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to room temperature, addition of oxalyl chloride dropwise, pyridine added in stoichiometric amount. Reaction time 30 min to 2 h. Common solvents/catalysts: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂, pyridine (base).

Acid‑catalyzed cleavage of a dialkyl ether – hydrolysis of diethylene glycol dibutyl ether. Purpose: deprotect or convert the ether to a mono‑butyl glycol and liberate butanol. Key transformation: protonation of the ether oxygen by HCl followed by nucleophilic attack of water, breaking the C–O bond to give 1‑butanol and diethylene glycol monobutyl ether. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl (conc. 6 M) for 2–6 h, temperature ~100 °C. Solvent: water or water/acetone mixture to improve miscibility. No additional catalyst needed beyond the acid.

Hydrolytic depolymerization of a cyclic siloxane – ring‑opening of octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane (D4). Purpose: reduce siloxane molecular size or generate silanol functional groups. Key transformation: water attacks a Si–O bond of D4, cleaving the four‑membered ring to give hexamethylcyclotrisiloxane (D3) and a molecule of dimethylsilanol (SiMe₂OH). Typical conditions: aqueous medium at 50–120 °C, often under acidic (p‑TsOH) or basic (NaOH) catalysis to accelerate Si–O bond cleavage. Solvent: water or water/organic co‑solvent (e.g., THF). Reaction time varies from minutes (catalyzed) to several hours (uncatalyzed).

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of ethyl 3‑sulfanylpropanoate; typically reflux in aqueous ethanol with NaOH (or 1 M HCl) followed by acid work‑up; yields 3‑sulfanylpropanoic acid and ethanol, reversing the esterification to regenerate the free acid.

Metathesis/precipitation (acid–base salt exchange); thulium(III) acetate reacts with oxalic acid in aqueous solution to form insoluble thulium(III) oxalate and liberate acetic acid; carried out by dissolving the acetate and oxalic acid in water, heating gently to ensure complete reaction, then allowing the thulium oxalate to precipitate; the solid is filtered, washed, and dried; no organic solvent or catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation; forms cobalt(II) sulfide, a black insoluble solid, from cobalt(II) acetate and sodium sulfide, with concomitant formation of sodium acetate; the sulfide ion replaces acetate on cobalt; typically carried out in aqueous solution under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of sulfide, often at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic dichlorination of an alkene using trichloroisocyanuric acid (TCCA) – halogenation. Purpose: convert cyclohexene to the vicinal 1,2‑dichlorocyclohexane. Key transformation: TCCA releases Cl₂ (or equivalent Cl⁺) which adds across the C=C double bond, forming 1,2‑dichlorocyclohexane; the TCCA core is reduced to cyanuric acid and three equivalents of HCl are produced. Typical conditions: room temperature to 40 °C, organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a slight excess of TCCA (≈1 equiv per alkene). Reaction time 0.5–2 h under stirring. No additional catalyst; the reaction proceeds via in‑situ generated Cl₂.

Acid‑base neutralization of a metal carbonate; purpose is to prepare soluble gadolinium(III) acetate; Gd2(CO3)3 reacts with excess acetic acid, liberating CO2 and H2O and forming Gd(CH3COO)3; usually performed in aqueous or aqueous‑acetic acid solution at ambient to gentle heating (20‑60 °C); no additional catalyst required.

Mitsunobu esterification; benzyl alcohol reacts with cinnamic acid in the presence of triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate (DEAD) to form benzyl cinnamate with inversion of configuration (not stereochemically relevant here). The reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions in dry THF (or sometimes diethyl ether) at 0 °C to room temperature, typically under nitrogen.

Reaction type: oxidation of a primary allylic alcohol to a carboxylic acid (chromic acid oxidation). Sodium dichromate (Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O) with concentrated H₂SO₄ oxidizes cinnamyl alcohol to cinnamic acid. Reaction is run in aqueous medium, often with a co‑solvent such as acetone, at reflux (80–100 °C) until the alcohol is consumed; chromium(VI) is reduced to Cr³⁺.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis and decarboxylation of a carbamate; Meprobamate treated with aqueous HCl (reflux) undergoes cleavage of one carbamate linkage, releasing isopropylamine, carbon dioxide (from decarboxylation of the carbamate moiety) and forming carisoprodol as the remaining carbamate. Conditions: aqueous HCl, reflux for several hours; water is the solvent.

Base‑promoted transesterification (alkaline ester exchange); sodium 3‑hydroxybutanoate reacts with ethanol to give ethyl 3‑hydroxybutyrate and sodium ethoxide; typically reflux ethanol (or ethanol/THF) for several hours; no additional catalyst required beyond the sodium salt.

Ketene acetylation of phenol (Friedel‑Crafts‑type acylation); purpose is to prepare the acetate ester p‑cresyl acetate; the phenolic O attacks the electrophilic carbonyl of ketene forming an O‑acyl bond; usually carried out at 0–25 °C in an inert aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a mild base like pyridine to neutralize the generated acid; no metal catalyst required.

Solid‑state oxidation of cadmium arsenide; employed to convert the intermetallic Cd₃As₂ into the corresponding oxides for materials‑processing or waste treatment; oxygen oxidizes cadmium to CdO and arsenic to As₂O₃; performed by heating the powdered solid in a flow of dry air or pure O₂ at 500–800 °C; no solvent; the reaction proceeds via gas‑solid diffusion.

Hydrolysis of a cyclic carbonate; employed to convert butylene carbonate into the diol monomer 1,4‑butanediol while releasing CO2. Usually performed with aqueous acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) at elevated temperature (150‑200 °C) in a sealed reactor. Water acts as both solvent and reactant; the reaction proceeds via ring opening and decarboxylation to afford 1,4‑butanediol and carbon dioxide.

Aqueous precipitation (double‑displacement) of samarium(III) hydroxide; used to isolate Sm(OH)₃ from its oxalate salt and to regenerate ammonium oxalate; ammonium hydroxide provides OH⁻ which replaces the oxalate ligands, producing insoluble Sm(OH)₃ precipitate and soluble (NH₄)₂C₂O₄; carried out at ambient temperature in dilute NH₄OH (≈1 M) with stirring; water is the reaction medium.

Hydrolysis of erbium oxide; Er₂O₃ reacts with liquid water at ambient or mildly heated conditions to form Er(OH)₃; simple aqueous reaction with no catalyst, employed to prepare the hydroxide precursor.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acyl chloride to ester). Cyclohexanecarbonyl chloride reacts with methanol to give methyl cyclohexanecarboxylate and HCl. Conducted in an inert solvent (CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, or THF) at 0 °C → rt, employing pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃ as an HCl scavenger; the reaction is usually fast and proceeds to completion within an hour.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration with nitronium tetrafluoroborate; aimed at installing a nitro group para to the trifluoromethyl substituent on the phenol ring; the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) attacks the activated aromatic ring, giving 4‑nitro‑3‑trifluoromethylphenol and generating HBF₄ as a by‑product; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or nitromethane under nitrogen; no additional acid catalyst is needed because BF₄⁻ serves as the counter‑ion.

Acid chloride formation; thionyl chloride converts 2,5-dimethoxybenzoic acid to its benzoyl chloride, releasing SO2 and HCl; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane or chloroform under reflux or 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; pyridine may be added as base.

Dess‑Martin periodinane oxidation of a primary alcohol; converts 1‑octanol to the corresponding aldehyde octanal while the periodinane is reduced to iodobenzene and acetic acid; the reaction proceeds via formation of an alkoxy‑iodine intermediate followed by elimination; usually conducted at 20–25 °C in dry dichloromethane (0.1–0.2 M), employing 1.0–1.2 equivalents of Dess‑Martin periodinane; no external catalyst is required, and the by‑products are removed by aqueous work‑up.

Redox gas‑absorption reaction; sodium peroxide reacts with carbon dioxide to produce sodium carbonate and release O2 gas; used in CO2 scrubbers and oxygen generation; key transformation is peroxide oxidizing CO2 to carbonate while being reduced to O2; typically performed at ambient temperature in dry conditions, often in sealed reactors; no solvent, catalyst generally not required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Lithium hydroxide in aqueous or alcoholic solution attacks the carbonyl of ethyl acetate, generating lithium acetate and liberating ethanol. Typically performed at room temperature to 80 °C in water or a water/ethanol mixture; no additional catalyst required.

SN2 thiolation; sulfide (HS⁻ from Na₂S) displaces iodide on methyl iodide to afford methanethiol (CH₃SH) and NaI. Usually performed in aqueous ethanol or THF/water mixture, heated under reflux; reaction proceeds without external catalyst.

Metathesis precipitation of silver chloride; silver selenocyanate (often prepared as a suspension) is treated with aqueous potassium chloride, resulting in exchange of the selenocyanate ion for chloride and precipitating AgCl, while potassium selenocyanate remains in solution. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the AgCl precipitate is filtered off.

Redox (metal‑mediated halogen exchange) reaction. Aluminum metal reduces molybdenum(V) chloride (MoCl5) to molybdenum(IV) chloride (MoCl4) while being oxidized to aluminum trichloride (AlCl3). The process is conducted under anhydrous conditions, often in a non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, and requires heating (≈150–200 °C) to drive the reaction to completion.
Acid‑base neutralization; ammonia reacts with hydrofluoric acid to produce ammonium fluoride (NH₄F). Carried out in aqueous medium, often at low temperature for safety; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic carboxylation of an organolithium. 4‑Lithiopyridine reacts with carbon dioxide gas to give the corresponding pyridine‑4‑carboxylate, which on aqueous work‑up furnishes isonicotinic (pyridine‑4‑carboxylic) acid. The reaction is carried out at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in THF under an atmosphere of CO2, followed by protonation with dilute acid.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ketone. 3‑Octen‑2‑one is reduced by molecular hydrogen in the presence of palladium on carbon, selectively saturating the C=C double bond while leaving the carbonyl group intact, yielding 3‑octanone. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, Pd/C (5–10 wt %), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, ambient to 50 °C.

Acid‑base condensation/addition reaction; peroxynitrous acid (ONOOH) adds carbon dioxide to form nitrosoperoxycarbonate (ONOOCO₂⁻). Occurs rapidly in aqueous solution, especially at physiological pH, and is relevant to atmospheric and biological chemistry. No external catalyst; the reaction proceeds spontaneously under ambient conditions.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of cellulose to 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF). Concentrated sulfuric acid protonates the hydroxyl groups of cellulose, promoting intramolecular dehydration and ring closure to give HMF and water. Conducted at 140–200 °C, often in a biphasic system (water plus an organic co‑solvent such as DMSO, γ‑valerolactone, or an ionic liquid) to extract HMF and suppress further polymerization.

Controlled oxidation (combustion) of white phosphorus. Phosphorus reacts with three equivalents of oxygen to form tetraphosphorus hexoxide (P4O6), the lower‑oxide of phosphorus. The reaction is performed at moderate temperature (≈200 °C) with a limited O2 flow to avoid over‑oxidation to P4O10; no catalyst is required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of bicarbonate; yields solid calcium carbonate, carbon dioxide gas and water; Ca(HCO3)2 → CaCO3(s) + CO2(g) + H2O; induced by heating to ≈100 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Fischer esterification; n‑butanol reacts with hexanoic acid in the presence of a catalytic strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) under reflux. Water formed is removed (Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic distillation) to drive equilibrium, yielding n‑butyl hexanoate and water. Common solvent is toluene or the excess alcohol; temperature 60–100 °C.

General type: Double displacement reaction. Purpose: Ion exchange to prepare specific silver salts. Key transformations: Exchange of hexafluorophosphate and chloride ions between pyridinium and silver. Typical reaction conditions: Room temperature in aqueous or organic solvents like water or acetonitrile.

Acid-catalyzed ether cleavage; purpose is to split methyl pentyl ether into its constituent alcohols. Key transformation: protonation of the ether oxygen followed by nucleophilic attack of water, breaking the C–O bond to give methanol and 1‑pentanol. Usually carried out by refluxing the ether in aqueous sulfuric acid (≈80–100 °C). The reaction medium is water with excess H₂SO₄, which acts as both acid catalyst and dehydrating agent.

Acid‑induced decomposition of sodium percarbonate (acid‑base reaction). Dilute hydrochloric acid protonates the percarbonate ion, releasing hydrogen peroxide, carbon dioxide, and forming sodium chloride. Reaction occurs at ambient temperature in aqueous solution; excess water serves as solvent. No additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) neutralization; purpose is to exchange cations and generate a soluble sodium propionate while precipitating calcium hydroxide. Key transformation: OH⁻ from NaOH replaces the propionate anion on Ca²⁺, forming Ca(OH)₂ (sparingly soluble) and Na⁺ pairs with propionate. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with vigorous stirring; no special solvent beyond water is required.

Precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction; purpose is to isolate insoluble cobalt(II) oxalate. Key transformation: oxalate anion from potassium oxalate pairs with Co²⁺ from cobalt(II) chloride, producing cobaltous oxalate precipitate, while K⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to remain in solution as potassium chloride. Performed in water at ambient temperature; the solid cobalt oxalate is filtered off after mixing the two aqueous solutions.

Fischer esterification; metronidazole (bearing a secondary alcohol) reacts with benzoic acid in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid under reflux to give metronidazole benzoate and water. Typically conducted in excess benzoic acid or a suitable organic solvent (e.g., toluene) with removal of water (Dean–Stark trap) at reflux temperature.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); purpose is to introduce a bromine substituent para to the hydroxyl group of phenol. Key transformation: Br₂ electrophilically attacks the activated aromatic ring, yielding para‑bromophenol and HBr as by‑product. Conducted in dilute aqueous bromine (often with a small amount of acetic acid) at 0–5 °C to limit polysubstitution; the reaction mixture is usually aqueous or aqueous‑acetone.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis). Urea nitrate, an acidic salt, is treated with aqueous NaOH. The base protonates the nitrate, yielding water, free urea and sodium nitrate. Typically carried out in water at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑metal single‑displacement (redox) reaction; gadolinium metal reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to produce gadolinium(III) chloride (GdCl3) and hydrogen gas; typically performed at room temperature or with gentle heating in dilute HCl solution; water is the reaction medium, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of secondary alcohol; phosphoric acid protonates propan‑2‑ol, leading to loss of water and formation of propene. Carried out by heating the alcohol with excess H3PO4 (≈10 % w/w) at 140‑170 °C, often using a distillation apparatus to collect the alkene; no additional solvent or catalyst is required.

Acid‑base double displacement; protonation of sulfite by strong sulfuric acid yields sulfurous acid while the sulfate anion pairs with silver to form silver sulfate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalysts required.

Redox disproportionation of hypofluorous acid; water acts as an oxygen acceptor, being oxidized to hydrogen peroxide while HOF is reduced, releasing hydrofluoric acid. Conducted in dilute aqueous medium, often at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation (redox) of calcium sulfite to calcium sulfate; O2 from air oxidizes the sulfite ion (SO3^2‑) to sulfate (SO4^2‑), yielding gypsum (CaSO4); commonly employed in flue‑gas desulfurization where a slurry of CaSO3 is exposed to humid air or oxygen at ambient to moderate temperature (20‑60 °C), often with trace iron or manganese salts as catalysts; aqueous slurry is the typical reaction medium.

Metal displacement/reduction; metallic sodium reduces aluminum phosphide, forming sodium phosphide and liberating elemental aluminum. Requires dry, inert atmosphere and gentle heating to initiate the exothermic reaction; performed in anhydrous solvents such as THF or directly as a solid‑state mixture.

Acid–base (salt metathesis) reaction; hydrogen bromide protonates the sulfide anion of BeS, liberating gaseous H2S and forming soluble BeBr₂; typically performed by passing HBr gas over solid BeS or stirring a suspension of BeS in aqueous HBr, often with gentle heating.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction. In aqueous solution potassium iodide exchanges anions with cadmium bromide to give cadmium iodide and potassium bromide. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Solid‑state high‑temperature synthesis of potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP), a nonlinear optical crystal. Phosphoric acid, dipotassium hydrogen phosphate and titanium dioxide powders are intimately mixed and heated to 500‑700 °C in a furnace, allowing condensation with release of water. No solvent; the reaction proceeds by solid‑state diffusion.

Type: thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of a metal carbonyl. Purpose: recover elemental nickel and release carbon monoxide. Key transformation: Ni(CO)4 breaks down to solid nickel metal and CO gas. Typical conditions: 180‑250 °C, often under reduced pressure or flowing inert gas, in a furnace or heated tube. Common solvents/catalysts: none required.

Reductive dehalogenation (Wurtz‑type of 1‑bromo‑1‑chloroethane with zinc dust; zinc reduces the carbon–halogen bonds, yielding ethene gas and zinc halides (ZnCl₂, ZnBr₂). Conducted under reflux in dry ether or THF, often with gentle heating and an inert atmosphere; zinc serves as both reagent and reductant.

Acid–base metathesis (salt exchange). Used to prepare fluorosilicic acid, an industrial source of fluoride. The hexafluorosilicate anion (SiF6²⁻) is protonated by H₂SO₄, generating H₂SiF₆ (fluorosilicic acid) while potassium ions combine with sulfate to give K₂SO₄. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of a secondary amine. Dimethylamine attacks the primary carbon bearing bromine in 1‑bromo‑3‑methoxypropane, displacing Br⁻ to form 3‑methoxy‑N,N‑dimethylpropan‑1‑amine and HBr. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, mild reflux; often a base (e.g., NaHCO₃ or K₂CO₃) is added to trap the liberated HBr.

Acid‑base salt metathesis generating volatile gases. Ammonium ion protonates cyanide ion to give hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and ammonia (NH₃), while K⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to form KCl. Performed in aqueous solution, usually at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to control HCN evolution; no catalyst needed. The reaction is employed for in‑situ HCN generation.

Acetylation (esterification) of a primary alcohol using acetic anhydride. 1‑Butanol attacks one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, yielding n‑butyl acetate and acetic acid as the by‑product. Can be run neat or in a non‑reactive solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with gentle heating (40‑60 °C). Catalysts such as pyridine or DMAP are optional to accelerate the reaction.

Williamson ether synthesis (O‑alkylation). The phenolic OH of 5‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)‑1,2‑dithiole‑3‑thione is deprotonated by potassium carbonate, forming the phenoxide, which then attacks methyl iodide in an SN2 step to give the methoxy ether product. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, reflux for several hours; potassium carbonate acts as the base, no additional catalyst required.

Esterification via acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose is to form pentan-3-yl acetate; the hydroxyl of pentan-3-ol attacks the carbonyl of acetyl chloride, releasing HCl; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane with an added base (pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann amination (nucleophilic aromatic substitution); ammonia replaces the bromine of methyl 4‑hydroxy‑3‑bromobenzoate to give methyl 3‑amino‑4‑hydroxybenzoate, releasing HBr. Typical conditions: CuI (5–10 mol %), excess NH₃ (gas or aqueous), polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMSO or NMP), reflux 80–120 °C, often with a base such as K₂CO₃ to neutralize HBr.

Radical bromination reaction. Introduces bromine at benzylic position. Purpose: prepare bromomethyl intermediate for further functionalization. Key transformation: methyl (-CH3) to bromomethyl (-CH2Br). Conditions: N-bromosuccinimide with radical initiator (e.g., peroxides), elevated temperature. Solvent: carbon tetrachloride or similar inert solvent.

Eschweiler‑Clarke reductive methylation of ethylenediamine; formaldehyde and formic acid methylate both nitrogen atoms, producing N,N,N′,N′‑tetramethylethylenediamine (TMEDA) with CO₂ and H₂O as by‑products. Conducted in methanol or water, heated to 80–120 °C, no external reducing metal required; the reaction is self‑contained and proceeds under mildly acidic conditions.

Chlorination of indium(III) oxide with phosgene; phosgene (COCl₂) acts as a chlorinating/oxidizing agent, converting In₂O₃ to soluble indium(III) chloride (InCl₃) while liberating carbon dioxide. Usually performed in the gas phase or in dry inert solvent (e.g., toluene) at 200–300 °C under anhydrous conditions; no catalyst is needed.

Acid–base double‑replacement precipitation; concentrated sulfuric acid protonates strontium phosphate, forming soluble phosphoric acid and insoluble strontium sulfate precipitate (SrSO₄). Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; stirring until complete precipitation, followed by filtration and washing of the SrSO₄ solid.

Reaction type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (acyl chloride amidation). Purpose: synthesize N‑ethyl‑2‑hydroxybenzamide. Key transformation: 2‑hydroxybenzoyl chloride reacts with ethylamine to form an amide bond, releasing hydrogen chloride. Typical conditions: carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, THF, or ether at 0 °C to room temperature; a tertiary amine (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) is added to neutralize the HCl. No metal catalyst required.

Wöhler synthesis of urea (cyanate‑ammonium condensation). Sodium cyanate reacts with ammonium chloride to form urea and sodium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution, often heated to 150–200 °C (or refluxed) to promote rearrangement of the cyanate to the carbamyl intermediate that cyclises to urea. No catalyst needed.

Acid–base metathesis (double‑replacement) between sodium bisulfate (acidic salt) and potassium hydroxide (strong base); produces potassium bisulfate (new acidic salt) and sodium hydroxide (strong base). Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with mild heating; no special solvent beyond water is required, and the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon mixing.

Acid‑metal phosphide reaction; used to liberate phosphine gas; zinc phosphide is protonated by aqueous sulfuric acid to give zinc sulfate and phosphine; typically carried out in dilute H2SO4 solution at room temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an organophosphate fluoridate; aqueous HCl protonates the O‑isopropyl methylphosphonofluoridate, leading to cleavage of the isopropyl ester (producing isopropanol) and substitution of the fluorine by proton to give methylphosphonic acid, with HF released. Typical conditions: dilute HCl (1–3 M), water as solvent, temperature 0–50 °C; reaction proceeds rapidly and is often used for detoxification of nerve‑agent analogues.

Carbamate (urethane) formation via chloroformate activation; isopropyl chloroformate reacts with 2‑methyl‑2‑propyl‑1,3‑propanediol to give the mono‑carbamate product carisoprodol, liberating HCl. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the generated HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

copper(I) chloride + thioacetamide -> acetamide + hydrogen chloride + copper(I) sulfide: This is a precipitation reaction where thioacetamide provides sulfide ions upon acidic hydrolysis. Key transformation involves sulfide binding to copper(I) to form insoluble Cu₂S. Reaction typically occurs in aqueous solution under heating. No specific catalyst mentioned; HCl is a byproduct from thioacetamide decomposition.

Amine salt neutralization: Releases free amine from its hydrochloride salt using strong base. Hydroxide abstracts proton from protonated amine site, reforming amine and creating salt byproducts including water. Typically aqueous reaction conditions allowing ion separation and free amine precipitation.

Transesterification with 1‑propanol; methyl hexanoate and propanol are refluxed with a catalytic amount of acid (H₂SO₄) or base (NaOEt) to afford propyl hexanoate and methanol. Excess propanol drives the reaction; removal of methanol by azeotropic distillation or nitrogen sweep helps reach completion.

Type: [2+1] cyclopropenation via carbene addition; Purpose: synthesis of cyclopropene, a strained carbocycle used in polymer chemistry; Key transformation: a singlet methylene (:CH2) adds across the C≡C triple bond of acetylene to give cyclopropene; Typical conditions: generated carbene from CH2I2/Zn‑Cu or from photolysis of diazomethane in the presence of acetylene; Solvent: diethyl ether or dichloromethane at low temperature (‑78 to 0 °C); No additional catalyst beyond the metal‑mediated carbene source.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide with methanol to form 2‑methoxyethanol (ethylene glycol monomethyl ether). Methanol attacks the less hindered carbon of the strained epoxide, yielding the primary alcohol ether. Reaction is usually carried out in excess methanol solvent at 50 °C–80 °C, catalyzed by a base (e.g., NaOH, K₂CO₃) or an acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) to accelerate the ring opening. Provides an industrial route to a common solvent and intermediate.

1 Ammonia gas + 1 Indium trichloride -> 3 Hydrogen chloride + 1 Indium nitride: Metathesis reaction yielding indium nitride. Purpose is synthesis of semiconducting InN. High-temperature conditions required, likely under a nitrogenous atmosphere. HCl is byproduct; no catalyst specified.

1 benzoyl chloride + 1 (-)-Ecgonine methyl ester -> 1 hydrogen chloride + 1 (-)-Cocaine: Acyl substitution reaction forming cocaine via benzoylation of a hydroxyl group in ecgonine ester. Key transformation is ester bond formation. Conducted in organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane), often with base to scavenge HCl. No specific catalyst mentioned in reaction stoichiometry.

1 Hydrogen (Pd/C) + 1 2-(Iminomethyl)phenol -> 1 2-(Aminomethyl)phenol: Hydrogenation reaction reducing imine (C=N) to amine (C-NH₂). Utilizes palladium on carbon as catalyst. Conducted under H₂ atmosphere in protic solvents (e.g., ethanol). Mild to moderate temperatures typical.

Aminolysis (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of ethyl methacrylate with dimethylamine; purpose is preparation of N,N‑dimethylmethacrylamide. Key transformation: substitution of the ethoxy group by dimethylamine, producing the amide and ethanol as by‑product. Typical conditions: reaction of ethyl methacrylate with excess dimethylamine (often as a gas or aqueous solution) at 0 °C to room temperature, in an inert solvent such as THF or dichloromethane; the ethanol formed is removed or distilled off.

1 phosphoric acid + 1 magnesium carbonate -> 1 carbon dioxide + 1 water + 1 magnesium hydrogen phosphate: Acid-carbonate neutralization producing magnesium hydrogen phosphate. CO₂ released during carbonate decomposition. Reaction occurs in aqueous media, often with heating to drive off gas.

Alkaline saponification of methyl gallate; converts the methyl ester into the sodium salt of gallic acid while releasing methanol. Key transformation: MeOOC‑Ar(OH)₃ + NaOH → NaOOC‑Ar(OH)₃ + MeOH. Performed in aqueous sodium hydroxide (0.5–2 M) often with methanol or ethanol as co‑solvent, heated at reflux (≈80 °C) until disappearance of the ester; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑chloride hydrolysis; but‑2‑ynoyl chloride is treated with aqueous water (often at 0 °C to rt) to convert the acyl chloride to but‑2‑ynoic acid, releasing HCl; the reaction can be performed in a biphasic system such as DCM/water and neutralized with base after completion.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of benzene with valeryl chloride using AlCl3 as Lewis acid, yielding 1‑phenyl‑1‑pentanone (phenyl valerone) and HCl. Conducted in anhydrous non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2, CS2) at 0 °C then reflux under nitrogen.

5 sulfuric acid + 2 arsenic -> 2 arsenic acid + 2 water + 5 sulfur dioxide: Redox reaction oxidizing elemental arsenic to arsenic acid (H₃AsO₄) using concentrated sulfuric acid as oxidizing agent. Sulfur dioxide is reduced byproduct. Requires heating; no catalyst needed.

Reductive carbonylation; preparation of a metal carbonyl. Chromium(III) chloride is reduced by magnesium under a carbon monoxide atmosphere, converting Cr³⁺ to Cr⁰ and forming Cr(CO)₆ while chloride is transferred to MgCl₂. Typical conditions: CO pressure 50–100 atm, 150–200 °C, inert atmosphere, often performed without solvent or in a sealed tube.

N‑formylation via silyl ester transfer; triethylsilyl formate acts as a mild formyl donor to the nucleophilic amine. The amine attacks the carbonyl of the silyl formate, displacing triethylsilanol and giving N‑formyl aniline. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; often a mild base such as pyridine is added to absorb the generated acid.

Oxidative conversion of iodide to higher oxidation‑state oxy‑iodine species. In alkaline aqueous solution, ozone oxidizes I⁻ (from KI) to iodate (IO₃⁻) and periodate (IO₄⁻), with water formed. Typically carried out at 0–25 °C with ozone gas bubbled through a NaOH/KI solution; no catalyst is needed.
High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of titanium phosphide. TiP reacts with excess O₂ to give TiO₂ and P₂O₅. Carried out in a furnace or flow of air at >500 °C; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification of a carboxylate salt (Fischer‑type); methanol and catalytic H2SO4 convert sodium furan‑2‑carboxylate to methyl furan‑2‑carboxylate, generating sodium hydrogen sulfate. Reaction is refluxed in methanol (≈65 °C) with a few drops of concentrated H2SO4.

Jones oxidation; primary alcohol to carboxylic acid. n‑Hexanol is oxidized by chromic acid (CrO₃/H₂SO₄, Jones reagent) to hexanoic acid, water is formed and Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III). Conditions: aqueous acetone, 0 °C to rt, 1–2 h reaction time.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an oxime; acetone oxime is reduced by molecular hydrogen over a nickel catalyst to produce isopropylamine and water. Reaction is performed at 80–120 °C under 1–5 atm H₂ in a protic solvent such as ethanol or water; nickel (Raney or supported) serves as the catalyst.
