Typical conditions: mildly acidic (pH ≈ 5‑6) methanol or ethanol solution, 0‑25 °C to reflux, NaCNBH₃ added portionwise. No strong acid catalyst required; ammonium acetate serves as both ammonia source and buffer.

Acid‑base neutralization/salt formation – reaction of glycine with sodium methoxide in methanol. Purpose is to generate the sodium salt of glycine (sodium glycinate). Key transformations: Na⁺ exchanges with the proton of the carboxylic acid, forming Na⁺ OOC‑CH₂‑NH₂⁻; the transferred proton protonates methoxide giving methanol. Typical conditions: stoichiometric NaOMe dissolved in dry methanol at 0‑25 °C, often performed under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture. Solvent: methanol (also the source of the methanol product).

Fischer esterification – condensation of 2‑methylbutanoic acid with methanol to give methyl 2‑methylbutanoate. Purpose is to form an ester from a carboxylic acid. Key transformations: protonation of the carbonyl, nucleophilic attack of methanol, loss of water, regeneration of the acid catalyst. Typical conditions: excess methanol as solvent, catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TSA), reflux 60‑80 °C; removal of water (Dean–Stark trap or azeotropic distillation) drives reaction to completion. Common solvent/catalyst: methanol with 1‑5 % H₂SO₄.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) – solid‑state or aqueous ion exchange between potassium carbonate and sodium formate. Purpose is to swap the cations, yielding sodium carbonate and potassium formate. Key transformations: CO₃²⁻ pairs with Na⁺, HCOO⁻ pairs with K⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature or gentle heating (≤80 °C) to ensure dissolution and complete exchange; products may crystallize on cooling. No special catalyst required; water is the reaction medium.

Nitrosation of a primary amine; used to generate N‑nitrosomethylamine for analytical or synthetic purposes. In aqueous acidic medium, methylamine hydrochloride is treated with sodium nitrite and nitrous acid (generated in situ). The key transformation is conversion of the –NH2 group to an –N(NO)‑ moiety, yielding N‑nitrosomethylamine, NaCl and H2O. Typically carried out at 0–5 °C to limit side reactions; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Oxidation of dimethyl sulfide to dimethyl sulfoxide using tetrabutylammonium tribromide; the tribromide serves as a mild bromine source that transfers an electrophilic bromine to the sulfide, which is then hydrolyzed to the sulfoxide while the tetrabutylammonium cation captures the liberated HBr, yielding tetrabutylammonium bromide; performed at 0 °C to ambient temperature in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile; no additional catalyst is needed.

Free‑radical halogenation. Chlorine atom substitutes a hydrogen of bromochloromethane via a radical chain (initiation by UV or heat). Purpose: install an additional chloro substituent to give bromodichloromethane while releasing HCl. Typical conditions: dilute Cl₂ in an inert solvent such as CCl₄ or CHCl₃, UV light or elevated temperature (≈80 °C). No catalyst needed beyond the radical initiator.

Selective reduction of a nitroso group. Sodium borohydride reduces nitrosobenzene to N‑phenylhydroxylamine without affecting the aromatic ring. Purpose: prepare hydroxylamine intermediates for further transformations (e.g., azo coupling). Conditions: NaBH₄ (1–2 eq) in methanol, ethanol or a MeOH/THF mixture, 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen. Reaction is typically complete within 1–2 h.

Thermal decarboxylation of a β‑nitrocarboxylic acid. Heating 3‑nitropropionic acid causes loss of CO2 and yields nitroethane. The reaction proceeds via a carboxylate‑derived radical or anionic decarboxylation intermediate. Typical conditions: reflux (150–200 °C) in the presence of a metal oxide (CuO, Cu₂O) or under basic conditions (NaOH) to facilitate decarboxylation; the reaction may be carried out in a high‑boiling solvent such as xylene or without solvent (distillation). This transformation shortens the carbon chain by one carbon atom.

Radical oxidative coupling of phenol. Phenol undergoes radical‑mediated self‑coupling in the presence of cumene hydroperoxide (used as a radical initiator/oxidant) to give diphenyl ether; the hydroperoxide is reduced to 2‑methyl‑1‑phenyl‑1‑propanol. Purpose: synthesize diaryl ethers via C–O bond formation. Conditions: phenol (excess) with 0.5 eq cumene hydroperoxide, heated to 80–120 °C in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or chlorobenzene, often with a small amount of a metal catalyst (e.g., CuCl) to promote radical generation.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of 4‑chloronitrobenzene with sodium dimethyl dithiophosphate to produce methyl parathion; purpose is preparation of the organophosphate insecticide; key transformation: the electron‑deficient aromatic chloride is displaced by the dimethyl dithiophosphate anion, yielding O,O‑dimethyl O‑(4‑nitrophenyl) phosphorothioate and NaCl; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required, the anion functions as nucleophile.

NaBH₄ reduction of a cyclic ketone. Sodium borohydride reduces 2‑methylcyclopentan‑1‑one to the corresponding secondary alcohol, 2‑methylcyclopentan‑1‑ol. Purpose: convert carbonyl to alcohol for further functionalisation. Conditions: NaBH₄ (1.5 eq) in methanol, ethanol or 1,4‑dioxane at 0 °C to rt, reaction proceeds within 30 min to 2 h. Quench with water, then work‑up to isolate the alcohol.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (ester exchange). Diethyl malonate (diethyl propanedioate) reacts with methanol in the presence of catalytic HCl (and water) to give dimethyl malonate and ethanol (ethyl alcohol) as the by‑product. Purpose: prepare the dimethyl ester from the diethyl analogue. Typical conditions: reflux of diethyl malonate with excess methanol and a few drops of conc. HCl (≈0.1 M),60–80 °C for several hours. Removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium toward the dimethyl product.

Base‑catalyzed crossed‑aldol (Knoevenagel) condensation; purpose is to form an α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde (4dimethylamino‑cinnamaldehyde); key transformation is C‑C bond formation between acetaldehyde and 4‑(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde with loss of water; typically performed in aqueous NaOH or NaOH/ethanol solution at 0 °C to room temperature, then warmed; no special catalyst beyond the base, ethanol often serves as solvent.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to convert pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid (nicotinic acid) into its methyl ester (methyl nicotinate); key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methanol on the protonated carboxyl carbon followed by water loss; carried out in excess methanol with catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid under reflux (≈65 °C) for several hours; removal of generated water (e.g., Dean–Stark) drives the equilibrium; no additional reagents needed.

Aqueous salt metathesis/complexation forming potassium ferrocyanide; purpose is to generate the stable Fe(II) cyanide complex K₄[Fe(CN)₆]; key transformation is coordination of six cyanide ligands to Fe²⁺ and precipitation of KCl; performed in water with excess KCN to keep Fe²⁺ in solution, typically at ambient temperature; the reaction is exothermic and may be carried out under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation to ferricyanide.

Carbodiimide‑mediated coupling to synthesize a hydrazide (isonid); purpose is to activate isonicotinic acid for nucleophilic attack by hydrazine; key steps are formation of an acyl‑imidazole intermediate from the acid and CDI, followed by substitution with hydrazine to give the hydrazide; usually conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; CDI is the reagent that acts as a dehydrating/coupling agent, with imidazole generated as by‑product.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; purpose is to reduce the vinyl side chain of 4‑vinylguaiacol to an ethyl group (4‑ethylguaiacol); key transformation is addition of H₂ across the C=C bond; carried out with 5 %–10 % Pd/C in a protic solvent (e.g., ethanol or ethyl acetate) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–50 °C until gas uptake ceases; reaction is typically filtered to remove the catalyst and the product isolated by distillation or chromatography.

Acid‑promoted decomposition of sodium dithionite in aqueous HCl; purpose is to generate sulfur dioxide gas and neutralize the dithionite; key transformation: Na2S2O4 + 2 HCl → 2 NaCl + H2O + 2 SO2 (overall stoichiometry may vary with oxidation state); typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; solvent is water; the reaction proceeds readily upon addition of dilute to concentrated HCl.

Aerobic oxidation; converts 4‑hydroxybenzaldehyde to 4‑hydroxybenzoic acid by oxidation of the aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using molecular oxygen, typically catalyzed by a transition‑metal (e.g., Cu, Co) or base in a polar solvent such as water/acetone under mild heating.

Acid dissolution of cerium(III) sulfide with hydrofluoric acid; converts the sulfide into cerium(III) fluoride while evolving hydrogen sulfide; Ce2S3 is treated with aqueous HF, often in PTFE‑lined equipment, at 50–80 °C; yields CeF3 precipitate and H2S gas; HF acts both as solvent and fluorinating reagent; no additional catalyst is used.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification of tetrahydrofurfuryl acetate with n‑propanol; affords tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol and propyl acetate. Conducted by refluxing the acetate in excess n‑propanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or using a base such as n‑propoxide; excess alcohol drives the reaction forward.

Dess‑Martin oxidation; secondary alcohol in the nitrosamine‑pyridyl substrate is oxidized to the corresponding ketone while Dess‑Martin periodinane is reduced to iodobenzoic acid and water. Performed at 0 °C to rt in dichloromethane, under anhydrous conditions.

Halogen exchange (chlorination) of a metal oxide; thionyl chloride reacts with tantalum(V) oxide to replace O²⁻ by Cl⁻, yielding tantalum pentachloride and sulfur dioxide gas. Conducted under reflux in an inert atmosphere, no solvent needed or in a dry non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., CS₂).

Acid‑base neutralization of magnesium carbonate with hydroiodic acid; carbonate is protonated releasing CO₂ and H₂O while forming soluble magnesium iodide; proceeds at ambient temperature in aqueous HI solution; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation); HCl adds to 2,3‑dimethyl‑1‑butene in a Markovnikov fashion to give 2‑chloro‑2,3‑dimethylbutane. Typically carried out at 0 °C to rt in an inert solvent such as chloroform or without solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) of salts; copper(II) nitrate reacts with lithium formate in aqueous solution to exchange anions, forming copper(II) formate precipitate (or soluble) and lithium nitrate. Stirred at ambient temperature, water as solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a C–Br bond; 3‑bromo‑3‑ethylpentane is reduced over palladium on carbon under H₂ pressure (1‑5 atm) to remove the bromine and give 3‑ethylpentane; solvent commonly ethanol or THF; room temperature to 50 °C.

Redox displacement; bromine oxidizes potassium hydride, producing hydrogen gas and potassium bromide. Performed under dry, inert conditions (e.g., THF) at 0 °C to rt, with careful exclusion of moisture.

Type: O‑methylation (nucleophilic substitution). Purpose: Convert a phenolic hydroxyl to a methoxy group. Key transformation: The oxygen of 8‑hydroxypsoralen attacks the methyl group of diazomethane, displacing N₂ and forming 8‑methoxypsoralen; nitrogen gas is released as by‑product. Typical conditions: Reaction performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dry diethyl ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; excess diazomethane is often used. No additional catalyst is required.

Type: Epoxide ring‑opening alkylation of an amine. Purpose: Introduce a 2‑hydroxyethyl substituent onto piperidine. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack of the lone pair on piperidine nitrogen at the less‑substituted carbon of ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to give N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)piperidine. Typical conditions: Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or acetonitrile, often at 0 °C to reflux; the reaction may be base‑catalyzed (e.g., triethylamine) to neutralize the generated proton. No metal catalyst is required.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ester. Purpose: Saturate the carbon–carbon double bond of methyl acrylate to afford methyl propionate. Key transformation: Addition of H₂ across the C=C bond of methyl acrylate, leaving the ester functionality intact. Catalyst Palladium on barium sulfate (Pearlman’s catalyst). Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature ranging from 25 °C to 50 °C; reaction time varies from 1 to several hours depending on scale.

Type: Acid‑base salt hydrolysis. Purpose: Convert calcium thioglycolate to the free acid, thioglycolic acid. Key transformation: Protonation of the thioglycolate anion by hydrochloric acid, releasing thioglycolic acid and forming calcium chloride. Typical conditions: Aqueous 2 M HCl, stirring at ambient temperature or gentle heating; the reaction proceeds quantitatively without need for additional reagents.

Type: Hydrolysis of a metal telluride (salt‑water reaction). Purpose: Generate hydrogen telluride (H₂Te) gas from disodium telluride. Key transformation: Water protonates the telluride ion to produce H₂Te, while the sodium ions form sodium hydroxide. Typical conditions: Aqueous medium at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature; the reaction is often performed in a sealed apparatus because H₂Te is volatile and toxic. No catalyst is required.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation of an allylic alcohol. Purpose: Reduce the C=C double bond of 2‑methyl‑3‑buten‑2‑ol to give the saturated secondary alcohol 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol. Key transformation: Syn‑addition of H₂ across the carbon–carbon double bond while the hydroxyl group remains unchanged. Catalyst: Palladium on carbon (Pd/C). Typical conditions: H₂ pressure of 1–3 atm, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25 °C to 40 °C; reaction usually completes within 30 minutes to a few hours.

Intramolecular dehydration via triflic anhydride activation; the secondary alcohol of (-)-ecgonine methyl ester is converted into a triflate by Tf2O in the presence of the hindered base 2,6‑lutidine, followed by spontaneous intramolecular SN2 displacement to give (-)-anhydroecgonine methyl ester. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous dichloromethane under nitrogen; no metal catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 1‑butanol to 1‑butene (E1 elimination). Concentrated sulfuric acid (≈95 %) acts as the dehydrating agent; the reaction is performed by heating the alcohol‑acid mixture to 160–180 °C, often in a sealed chamber or using a short‑path distillation setup to collect the liberated alkene. No additional solvent is required; the acid itself serves as medium.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of 1‑bromopropane to propane with concomitant formation of HBr. Performed with H₂ (1–5 atm) over a metal hydrogenation catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in a protic solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at ambient temperature or mild heating.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of zinc chromite (ZnCr₂O₄). Stoichiometric ZnO and Cr₂O₃ are intimately mixed, calcined in air at 1000–1300 °C for several hours to promote diffusion and formation of the spinel phase; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (alkylation of carboxylate) – Williamson‑type ester synthesis; sodium 2‑methylbutanoate reacts with ethyl bromide to give ethyl 2‑methylbutanoate and NaBr; performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO, usually with reflux and possibly a phase‑transfer catalyst.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification of benzoic acid with tert‑butanol using dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC). DCC activates the carboxyl group to an O‑acylurea intermediate that reacts with tert‑butanol to afford tert‑butyl benzoate; dicyclohexylurea precipitates as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or THF, 0°C to rt, under nitrogen atmosphere.

Hydrolysis of chromyl chloride to regenerate chromium(VI) oxide and hydrochloric acid; this is a reversible hydrolysis reaction; key transformation is addition of water across the Cr=O/Cr–Cl bonds producing CrO3 and HCl; occurs readily in aqueous solution at room temperature, often observed as dissolution of red fumes.

Selective catalytic hydrogenation of the α,β‑unsaturated carbonyl p‑hydroxybenzalacetone to the saturated ketone 4‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)‑2‑butanone. Reaction uses H₂ (1–3 atm) with 5–10 % Pd/C in ethanol or ethyl acetate at 25–50 °C; the C=C bond is reduced while the carbonyl remains untouched.

Oxidative demethylation; purpose: convert 1‑methylxanthine to xanthine; key transformation: cleavage of the N‑CH₃ bond releasing formaldehyde; typical conditions: aqueous medium with molecular oxygen (or H₂O₂) and a transition‑metal catalyst such as Fe²⁺/Cu²⁺ or an enzymatic monooxygenase; solvent: water or water‑compatible organic co‑solvent.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction; beryllium oxide, a basic oxide, is dissolved by aqueous hydrochloric acid, typically at room temperature or mild heating, yielding soluble beryllium chloride and water; aqueous medium, no catalyst.

Conversion of 4‑methylbenzyl alcohol to 4‑methylbenzyl chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); the reaction proceeds at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or pyridine, releasing gaseous SO₂ and HCl.

Acid–base neutralization / precipitation reaction; purpose is to convert diphosphoric acid into an insoluble zinc pyrophosphate salt. Key transformation: the basic oxide ZnO reacts with the di‑acid, releasing two molecules of H2O and forming Zn2P2O7. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, gentle heating to dissolve ZnO and drive off water, followed by cooling to precipitate the product. No catalyst required; common solvent is water.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis): calcium iodide in aqueous solution reacts with silver nitrate to precipitate insoluble silver iodide while forming soluble calcium nitrate. Conducted at room temperature in water; the formation of the yellow‑white AgI precipitate is used as a qualitative test for iodide ions.

Base‑alcohol (acid‑base) reaction; potassium carbonate reacts with methanol to afford potassium methoxide, CO₂, and H₂O; similar proton transfer and decomposition of the carbonate; conducted by refluxing methanol with K₂CO₃, often under a nitrogen atmosphere; methanol is the solvent; no additional catalyst.

Acid–base dissolution of thallium(I) sulfide in hydrochloric acid; the sulfide is protonated to release hydrogen sulfide gas, while thallium ions form soluble thallium chloride. Conducted in aqueous HCl solution, often with gentle heating to promote H2S evolution; no additional catalyst required.

Direct synthesis (combination reaction). Produces samarium(III) iodide for uses in electronics or catalysis. Solid samarium reacts with iodine vapors or solid iodine. Conducted under heat or inert atmosphere to facilitate reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl chloride by ammonia; purpose is to install an amino group on the pyridine ring. Key transformation: 4‑CH2Cl‑C5H4N + NH3 → 4‑CH2NH2‑C5H4N + HCl. Conducted in excess aqueous or gaseous NH3, often in ethanol or isopropanol as solvent, with heating (reflux) for several hours. The generated HCl is typically neutralized in situ by an additional base (e.g., Na2CO3) or removed by azeotropic distillation.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – Williamson‑type alkylation of a carboxylate. Purpose: synthesize methyl butanoate (methyl ester) from the lithium carboxylate. Key transformation: methyl iodide transfers a CH₃ group to the oxygen of the butanoate anion, forming the ester and LiI. Conditions: aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or THF, inert atmosphere, temperature 0‑25 °C, addition of MeI dropwise; reaction typically complete within a few hours. No additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; purpose is to cleave the amide bond of formanilide to obtain aniline and formic acid. Key transformation: HCl protonates the carbonyl, water attacks, leading to breakdown of the C–N bond and formation of formic acid and aniline (as its protonated form, which is neutralized upon work‑up). Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous 1–6 M HCl for 1–3 h, often using excess acid and water as solvent. No additional catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of glycerol β‑chlorohydrin back to glycerol in water, releasing hydrochloric acid. Purpose is the reversible cleavage of the C–Cl bond. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water displaces chloride, regenerating the diol. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (25‑60 °C); can be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed, but often proceeds under neutral conditions; no catalyst required.

Acidic nitrile hydrolysis; purpose is to convert cyclopropanecarbonitrile to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Key transformation: protonated nitrile undergoes nucleophilic attack by water, eventually yielding cyclopropanecarboxylic acid and releasing ammonia, which captured as NH4Cl. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous hydrochloric acid (1–6 M) for several hours; aqueous medium serves as both solvent and acid source. No extra catalyst required.

High‑temperature synthesis of carbon monosulfide by direct combination of carbon and sulfur; purpose: prepare CS gas; key transformation: C + S → CS; typical conditions: temperatures >1200 °C under inert atmosphere (argon) to prevent oxidation; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization forming a metal‑organic acetate; purpose is to prepare triphenyltin acetate from the hydroxide precursor. Key transformation: the hydroxide ligand of triphenyltin hydroxide is protonated by acetic acid, producing water and the acetate‑bound organotin complex. Typical conditions: mix equimolar amounts in a non‑protic solvent such as toluene, THF, or dichloromethane at room temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously without catalyst. Removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification; purpose is to hydrolyze pentadecyl acetate to the corresponding primary alcohol. Key transformation: hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of the ester, generating a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to give pentadecanol and acetate, which pairs with Na⁺ to form sodium acetate. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) heated under reflux (60–100 °C) for 1–4 h, often in a water–methanol or water–ethanol mixture. No additional catalyst needed.

Conversion of a primary alcohol to an alkyl chloride using thionyl chloride; purpose is to replace the hydroxyl group with chlorine. Key transformation: the alcohol oxygen attacks SOCl₂, forming an alkoxysulfonium intermediate that collapses, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases and generating hexyl chloride (SN2 displacement). Typical conditions: add thionyl chloride dropwise to a solution of hexan‑1‑ol in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is often performed under nitrogen. No catalyst; pyridine can act as a base to scavenge HCl.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis) used to liberate the free base from its HCl salt; aqueous sodium carbonate deprotonates N,N‑dimethylaminoethyl chloride hydrochloride, forming carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂/H₂O), sodium chloride, and the free 2‑chloro‑N,N‑dimethylethanamine; typically performed in water at ambient to mild heating with stirring, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed (or base‑catalyzed) ester hydrolysis of an aromatic acetate; water attacks the carbonyl of 2,6‑dimethyl phenyl acetate, giving acetic acid and 2,6‑dimethyl phenol; commonly carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) or aqueous NaOH, refluxing for several hours; solvent is water or a water/organic mixture; purpose is cleavage of the acetate protecting group.

Selective carbonyl reduction of isatin with sodium borohydride to afford oxindole (2‑oxindole); NaBH₄ delivers hydride to the C‑3 carbonyl of the indole‑2,3‑dione, reducing it to a hydroxyl which tautomerizes to the keto form of oxindole; typically run in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; purpose is preparation of the oxindole scaffold for heterocyclic synthesis.

Redox comproportionation reaction forming indium(I) iodide (InI) from indium(III) iodide and elemental indium; In³⁺ is reduced while In⁰ is oxidized to the same +1 state, yielding InI; usually performed in a sealed tube or under inert gas at 200–300 °C, often in the absence of solvent or in dry, high‑boiling inert solvents (e.g., THF, toluene); purpose is synthesis of the low‑valent indium halide.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) – NaOH attacks the carbonyl of 2-(pyridin-2-yl)ethyl acetate, producing 2-(pyridin-2-yl)ethanol and sodium acetate; employed for deprotection of acetate groups. Reaction is performed in aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) at room temperature or under reflux; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is needed.

Electrophilic addition (acid‑catalyzed hydration) of water to 2‑methyl‑2‑butene to give 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol (Markovnikov addition); the alkene is protonated to form a tertiary carbocation, which is attacked by water, followed by deprotonation; carried out in aqueous acid such as 5–10 % H₂SO₄ or HCl, refluxing for 1–2 h; solvent may be a mixture of water and an organic co‑solvent (e.g., acetone); purpose is conversion of an alkene to the corresponding tertiary alcohol.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of decahydronaphthalene (decalin) to naphthalene with evolution of hydrogen gas; the saturated bicyclic hydrocarbon loses five equivalents of H₂ to form the aromatic naphthalene system; typically requires a metal catalyst (e.g., Pt, Pd, Ni, or Pt‑Sn alloy) at elevated temperatures (400–600 °C) under inert atmosphere; purpose is generation of aromatic compounds and H₂, used in industrial aromatization processes.

Hydrolysis of aluminium acetylacetonate; a ligand‑exchange reaction that converts the metal‑chelate Al(acac)3 into free acetylacetone and precipitates aluminium hydroxide. Typically carried out in aqueous media, often with gentle heating or reflux; no catalyst required. Water acts as the reactant and solvent; the reaction may be performed in a water/ethanol mixture to improve solubility of the starting complex.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid with lithium aluminium hydride; a strong hydride reduction that transforms decanoic acid into decyl alcohol (primary aliphatic alcohol). Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ether solvents such as THF or diethyl ether, usually at 0 °C to start and then warmed to reflux. LiAlH4 is used in stoichiometric excess; the reaction is quenched with aqueous acid (e.g., dilute HCl) after completion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzylic bromides by cyanide; the bis‑bromomethyl benzene undergoes double displacement with potassium cyanide to afford 1,2‑bis(cyanomethyl)benzene and potassium bromide as byproduct. Typical conditions employ a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at 50–100 °C, often under nitrogen to avoid moisture. No additional catalyst is required; excess KCN drives the reaction to completion.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between barium nitrate and potassium phosphate. In aqueous solution the ions exchange to form soluble potassium nitrate and insoluble barium phosphate, which precipitates out. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; filtration isolates the Ba₃(PO₄)₂ solid. No special reagents or catalysts are needed.

Multistep formation of an isothiuronium bromide salt. Cysteamine reacts with carbon disulfide under basic (often NaOH) aqueous conditions to generate the dithiocarbamate anion, which is then alkylated with allyl bromide to give an allyl‑substituted thiourea intermediate. Subsequent treatment with hydrobromic acid protonates the nitrogen and furnishes S‑(2‑aminoethyl)isothiuronium bromide hydrobromide. Typical procedure uses water or aqueous ethanol as solvent, maintains the reaction at 0–25 °C for the alkylation step, and finishes with acidification at room temperature. No metal catalyst is employed.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride to vinyl ethyl ether (hydrohalogenation of an alkene). HCl adds across the C=C bond in a Markovnikov fashion, yielding 1‑chloro‑1‑ethoxyethane. The reaction is usually performed in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, with gaseous or aqueous HCl introduced. No catalyst is required, though the reaction may be accelerated by a slight excess of HCl.

Acid‑carbonate reaction (neutralization and gas evolution). Potassium carbonate reacts with hydroiodic acid to yield carbon dioxide gas, water, and soluble potassium iodide. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with excess HI; no catalyst required. Purpose is to convert a carbonate to its iodide salt while releasing CO₂.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a carboxylate salt. 3‑Mercaptopropionic acid is deprotonated by sodium hydroxide to give sodium 3‑mercaptopropionate and water. Conducted in water or aqueous alcohol, often at room temperature; stirring ensures complete neutralization. No catalyst needed. Used to prepare the soluble thiolate salt for further reactions.

Acylation (N‑acetylation) of the amino group of L‑cysteine using acetyl chloride; serves to protect the amine as N‑acetyl‑L‑cysteine. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature; a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃) scavenges the generated HCl.

Strong acid–strong base neutralization (salt formation). Sulfuric acid reacts with magnesium hydroxide to produce magnesium sulfate and water. Carried out in aqueous medium, usually at room temperature or with mild heating to ensure dissolution of the solid base. No catalyst required. Common method for preparing MgSO₄ solutions.

Base-catalyzed ester saponification: diethyl maleate is hydrolyzed with aqueous sodium hydroxide, cleaving the ethoxy groups to form sodium maleate and ethanol. Typical conditions: 1 M NaOH in water/ethanol, reflux 1–2 h, no additional catalyst required.

Direct fluorination / oxidation of iodine. Elemental iodine is oxidized by fluorine gas to give iodine pentafluoride (IF₅). Conducted in anhydrous, inert fluorinating media such as liquid HF or fluorocarbon solvents at low temperature (often –78 °C to 0 °C) and under controlled pressure. No additional catalyst; the reaction is highly exothermic and must be handled with specialized equipment. Provides the high‑valent iodine halide.

Chlorination of boron carbide: reaction of solid B4C with chlorine gas yielding boron trichloride (BCl3) and carbon tetrachloride (CCl4). Purpose is to generate volatile chlorides for purification or analytical use. Key transformation replaces B–C bonds with B–Cl and C–Cl bonds, producing BCl3 and CCl4 gases. Typical conditions: excess Cl2 gas passed over powdered B4C at elevated temperature (150–500 °C) in a corrosion‑resistant reactor; reaction is vigorous and exothermic, often performed under inert carrier gas (e.g., Ar) to control rate. No solvent; products are collected by condensation or gas‑scrubbing.

Ester hydrolysis (neutral or acid‑catalyzed). Pentyl formate reacts with water to afford formic acid and pentanol. In practice the reaction is accelerated by adding a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., HCl) or base (saponification) and heating reflux in a suitable solvent such as aqueous methanol or toluene. The transformation converts the ester linkage back to the parent carboxylic acid and alcohol.

Type: SN2 nucleophilic substitution (amine displacement). Purpose: synthesize an α‑amino ester. Key transformation: ammonia attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displaces Cl⁻ to give methyl 2‑aminopropanoate and HCl (often neutralized by a base). Typical conditions: excess NH₃ (aqueous or gaseous) in ethanol or methanol, reflux or ambient temperature, sometimes with Na₂CO₃ to scavenge HCl. No catalyst required.

Reduction; chemical reduction of anthraquinone to its hydroquinone form (anthrahydroquinone) using sodium dithionite; key transformation: anthraquinone + Na₂S₂O₄ → anthrahydroquinone + Na₂SO₃ (by‑products); typical conditions: aqueous alkaline solution, temperature 0‑25 °C, excess dithionite, stirring under inert atmosphere optional.

Ammonolysis (aminolysis) of methyl nicotinate to form nicotinamide and methanol. Ammonia acts as nucleophile, replacing the methoxy group and generating the amide. Typical procedure uses excess gaseous or aqueous NH3, heated to 100–150 °C in a sealed tube or autoclave, sometimes with a catalytic amount of base (e.g., NaOH) to promote reaction; solvent can be water or ethanol.

Metathesis (anion exchange) reaction. Silver nitrate and hexafluorophosphoric acid exchange anions to give silver hexafluorophosphate and nitric acid. Performed in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C, protected from light to prevent silver reduction. No additional catalyst; the precipitation or solubility shift drives the reaction. Used to prepare AgPF₆, a common non‑coordinating silver salt for organometallic synthesis.

Esterification (acetylation) of 2‑propoxyethanol with acetic anhydride; nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the anhydride carbonyl forms 2‑propoxyethyl acetate and releases acetic acid; typically performed at 0 °C to reflux in anhydrous dichloromethane or neat, often with a catalytic amount of pyridine or DMAP to scavenge the acid.

Condensation of 1,3‑cyclohexanedione with ammonia to form 3‑aminocyclohex‑2‑en‑1‑one; purpose is to introduce an amino group at the central carbon of a 1,3‑diketone, yielding an enaminone. Ammonia attacks one carbonyl, followed by dehydration to give the C=C‑NH‑C=O system. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic ammonia (≈ 5 % NH₃) heated under reflux (80–100 °C) for 3–6 h, often with a Dean‑Stark trap or molecular sieves to remove water.

Type: electrophilic halogenation of an aryl lithium (metal‑halogen exchange). Purpose: generate a synthetically versatile aryl iodide for coupling reactions. Key transformation: 4‑(trifluoromethyl)phenyllithium attacks I2, forming 4‑(trifluoromethyl)iodobenzene and LiI. Typical conditions: low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere, dry ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether); no additional catalyst required.

Type: ozonolysis of an alkene. Purpose: cleave the C=C bond of vinyl fluoride to afford carbonyl fragments. Key transformation: O3 adds across the double bond to give a primary ozonide that, on reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide), furnishes formaldehyde (CH2O) and fluoroacetaldehyde (F‑CHO). Typical conditions: O3 gas bubbled through a solution of the alkene in dichloromethane or acetonitrile at ‑78 °C, followed by a mild reducing work‑up; solvent is inert, no metal catalyst needed.

Base‑base neutralization; deprotonation of hydrosulfide by hydroxide to generate sulfide ion and water. Transformation: HS⁻ + OH⁻ → S²⁻ + H₂O; Na⁺ balances to give Na₂S. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst.

Type: acidic reductive conversion of a nitro compound to an amine (Zn/HBr reduction). Purpose: reduce nitromethane to methylammonium ion. Key transformation: nitromethane is protonated by HBr and reduced by metallic zinc, producing methylammonium bromide (CH3NH3⁺ Br⁻) while Zn is oxidized to ZnBr2; water is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux of nitromethane with excess aqueous HBr and zinc powder; aqueous medium; no external catalyst beyond zinc.

Nitrite exchange (alcoholysis of alkyl nitrite); purpose: swap the alkoxy groups between ethanol and n‑propyl nitrite; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of ethanol on n‑propyl nitrite forming n‑propyl alcohol and ethyl nitrite; typical conditions: ambient temperature, inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) or neat; no catalyst required.

Type: Electrophilic addition of halogen (bromination). Purpose: Install four bromine atoms across the two double bonds, yielding a vicinal tetrabromo product useful for further substitution or elimination chemistry. Key transformation: Two successive anti‑addition steps of Br₂ across each C=C, converting CH2=CH‑CH2‑CH2‑CH=CH2 to BrCH2‑CHBr‑CH2‑CH2‑CHBr‑CH2Br. Typical conditions: Add a solution of bromine (1.0–1.2 equiv) dropwise to a solution of hexa‑1,5‑diene in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, with stirring in the dark to avoid photolysis. The reaction is fast; the mixture is quenched with aqueous sodium thiosulfate and product extracted.

Type: acid–base neutralization followed by chelation (formation of a lanthanum oxalate complex). Purpose: synthesize the dinuclear lanthanum(III) oxalate complex [La₂(C₂O₄)₃]. Key transformation: oxalic acid protonates lanthanum carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O; the liberated La³⁺ ions coordinate three oxalate dianions to give the tri‑oxalato‑dilanthanum species. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, heating to evolve CO₂, pH maintained around 4–5; water as solvent; no special catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of boron tribromide. BBr3 acts as a Lewis acid and is attacked by water, replacing the three bromide ligands with hydroxyl groups to give boric acid while releasing three equivalents of hydrogen bromide. The reaction is highly exothermic and is usually carried out at 0 °C to ambient temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or diethyl ether, followed by aqueous work‑up. No additional catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis of a halogen fluoride. Bromine monofluoride reacts with water to produce hydrofluoric acid and hypobromous acid. Performed in aqueous solution, usually at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

General type: C‑alkylation of an enolate (SN2 alkylation). Purpose: Extend the carbon skeleton of diethyl malonate to introduce an ethoxycarbonyl substituent. Key transformation: Sodium hydride deprotonates diethyl malonate to its enolate, which attacks ethyl bromoacetate, displacing bromide to give diethyl 2-(ethoxycarbonyl)malonate; NaBr is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: Anhydrous aprotic solvent (THF, DMF, or DMSO) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; NaH added slowly, then alkyl halide added dropwise. Common reagents/catalysts: NaH (base); dry inert atmosphere.

General type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) forming a diamine. Purpose: Synthesize ethylenediamine from a mono‑chloroamine. Key transformation: Ammonia attacks the carbon bearing chlorine in 2‑chloroethylamine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming ethylenediamine; HCl is released. Typical conditions: Excess aqueous or gaseous NH₃, reflux (≈80‑100 °C) in a sealed vessel or pressure reactor; removal of generated HCl by excess NH₃ or by trapping in a base. Common reagents/catalysts: None; high concentration of NH₃ drives the reaction.

General type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: Exchange of counter‑ions to isolate insoluble silver dichromate. Key transformation: Two Ag⁺ ions pair with the dichromate anion to give Ag₂Cr₂O₇ precipitate; Na⁺ pairs with nitrate to remain in solution as NaNO₃. Typical conditions: Aqueous solutions of AgNO₃ and Na₂Cr₂O₇ mixed at room temperature, often under stirring; the silver dichromate precipitates immediately. Common reagents/catalysts None; reaction proceeds spontaneously in water.

Acid- or base‑catalyzed transesterification of methyl phenyl carbonate with methanol; converts the phenyl carbonate into dimethyl carbonate and phenol. Common conditions employ a catalytic amount of sodium methoxide or p‑toluenesulfonic acid in methanol/toluene solvent at 60–80 °C, with removal of phenol or methanol to shift the reaction.

General type: Electrophilic aromatic substitution – Friedel‑Crafts alkylation. Purpose: Introduce three tert‑butyl groups onto phenol to afford the sterically hindered 2,4,6‑tri‑tert‑butylphenol. Key transformation: tert‑Butyl cation (generated from tert‑butyl chloride by AlCl₃) attacks the activated phenolic ring at the ortho positions; repeated alkylation yields the tri‑tert‑butyl product; AlCl₄⁻ and HCl are by‑products. Typical conditions: Anhydrous environment, dry solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, dichloromethane, or chloroform; AlCl₃ (1.5–3 equiv) added to phenol at 0‑25 °C, then tert‑butyl chloride introduced slowly; reaction stirred 1‑3 h. Common reagents/catalysts: Aluminum chloride (Lewis acid catalyst); excess AlCl₃ often required to maintain acidity.

General type: Direct combination (metal halogen synthesis) – redox reaction. Purpose: Prepare samarium(III) chloride from elemental samarium and chlorine gas. Key transformation: Samarium metal is oxidized from 0 to +3 oxidation state, while Cl₂ is reduced to chloride, yielding SmCl₃; stoichiometry 2 Sm + 3 Cl₂ → 2 SmCl₃. Typical conditions: Dry chlorine gas passed over heated samarium (≈400‑600 °C) under an inert atmosphere; reaction vessel is often a tube furnace or sealed quartz tube; reaction conducted in the absence of moisture to avoid hydrolysis. Common reagents/catalysts: None; pure Cl₂ gas serves as oxidant.

nucleophilic substitution fluorination; replaces hydroxyl oxygen in methanol with fluorine; yields methyl fluoride, sulfur dioxide, hydrogen fluoride; reaction occurs under similar conditions to reaction 2; thionyl fluoride acts as fluorinating agent.

Type: Dehydrative condensation (anion activation). Purpose: generation of trifluoroacetic anhydride, a potent acylating agent, and removal of DCC byproduct. Key transformation: two molecules of a carboxylic acid (trifluoroacetic acid) are coupled through removal of water, with dicyclohexylcarbodiimide acting as the dehydrating agent, yielding one molecule of trifluoroacetic anhydride and dicyclohexylurea. Typical conditions: performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to ambient temperature, under nitrogen; DCC is added portionwise to a solution of the acid, and the reaction mixture is stirred until gas evolution ceases. No additional catalyst required; the by‑product (DCU) precipitates and is filtered off.

Metal reduction; preparation of samarium(II) chloride from samarium(III) chloride using lithium metal as a reductant; typically performed in dry THF under inert atmosphere at ambient temperature, often with stirring; the by‑product lithium chloride remains in solution and is removed by filtration.

Dehydration (elimination) of β‑nitro alcohol; purpose: generate the nitroalkene nitroethene; key transformation: removal of water from 2‑nitroethanol to form nitroethene; typical conditions: phosphorus pentoxide (P₂O₅) as a strong dehydrating agent, heating at 100–150 °C under nitrogen; solvent: none or dry non‑polar solvent such as toluene.

Esterification (acetylation) of a primary alcohol; acetylation of cis‑3,7‑dimethyl‑2,6‑octadien‑1‑ol with acetic anhydride to give the acetate and acetic acid; commonly run at 0 °C to rt in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a catalytic amount of pyridine or DMAP to accelerate the reaction.

Type: Coordination complex formation (chelation). Purpose: synthesize gallium maltolate, a metal‑based pharmaceutical precursor with improved bioavailability. Key transformation: three deprotonated maltol ligands replace the nitrate anions around a Ga³⁺ center, producing the neutral gallium maltolate chelate and liberating three equivalents of nitric acid. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic solution (water, methanol, or ethanol) heated to reflux; the pH is adjusted (often with a base such as NaOH) to deprotonate maltol, facilitating ligand coordination. No external catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon mixing the reagents.

Precipitation/metal acetylide formation reaction in which silver nitrate reacts with acetylene in aqueous ammonia to give silver acetylide precipitate and ammonium nitrate in solution. The basic ammonia deprotonates acetylene, allowing Ag⁺ to bind as Ag₂C₂. Conducted at low temperature (0–5 °C) in dilute aqueous NH₃; no additional catalyst.

Type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: exchange of counter‑ions to precipitate silver cyanide, a photosensitive material, while forming soluble mercury(II) nitrate. Key transformation: cyanide ions from mercuric cyanide replace nitrate ions of silver nitrate, yielding insoluble AgCN (precipitate) and soluble Hg(NO₃)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring in the dark or subdued light to prevent photodecomposition of AgCN; the mixture is filtered to collect the silver cyanide solid. No catalyst or special solvent is required beyond water.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduction of an N‑hydroxy amidine to the corresponding amidine (benzamidine). Hydrogen gas is applied in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni or Pt‑O₂ under mild pressure (1–5 atm) in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol, or THF). The reaction removes the N‑O bond, delivering the primary amidine functional group.

Partial fluorination of a hydride (halogenation/oxidation). Germane (GeH4) reacts with elemental fluorine to replace two hydrogen atoms with fluorine, producing difluorogermane (GeH2F2) and hydrogen fluoride as a by‑product. Carried out in a controlled gas‑phase setup at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) to avoid over‑fluorination, often in a fluorinated solvent or using a flow of dry F2 diluted in inert gas (e.g., N2). No catalyst; stoichiometric F2 is required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis). The ammonium salt of (E)-2‑butenedioic acid (fumaric acid) is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide, resulting in exchange of cations to give sodium fumarate in solution and ammonium hydroxide (NH4OH) formed in the aqueous phase. Typically performed at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Swern oxidation (oxalyl chloride/DMSO variant); converts the secondary allylic alcohol but‑3‑en‑2‑ol to the α,β‑unsaturated ketone but‑3‑en‑2‑one. Key steps: low‑temperature activation of DMSO with oxalyl chloride to form a chlorodimethylsulfonium intermediate, nucleophilic attack by the alcohol, then deprotonation by triethylamine to afford the ketone while releasing CO, CO₂, and dimethyl sulfide. Typical conditions: –78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere, anhydrous dichloromethane (or CHCl₃) as solvent; TEA added after alcohol addition; work‑up with aqueous NaOH or NH₄Cl.

Type: Reductive amination (hydrogenation). Purpose: convert the ketone 1‑phenyl‑2‑propanone to the secondary amine lefetamine, a psychoactive compound, by installing an ethylamine moiety. Key transformation: the carbonyl group of the ketone reacts with ethylamine to form an imine (or iminium ion), which is subsequently reduced by molecular hydrogen to yield the N‑ethyl‑1‑phenyl‑2‑propanamine product; two molecules of hydrogen are consumed per ketone reduced, generating water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: the ketone is mixed with excess ethylamine in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol), the mixture is placed in a pressurized reactor, and hydrogen gas is introduced (1–5 atm) in the presence of a palladium‑on‑carbon (Pd/C) or Raney nickel catalyst at 25–50 °C. Reaction time varies from 1–12 h scale; the reaction mixture is filtered to remove the catalyst and the product is purified by distillation or chromatography.

Grignard addition to aldehyde; phenylmagnesium bromide acts as nucleophile adding to the carbonyl carbon of propynal, forming a propargylic alkoxide that after aqueous work‑up gives 2‑phenyl‑3‑butyn‑2‑ol. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions in dry diethyl ether or THF, at 0 °C to room temperature, with inert atmosphere; quench with dilute acid.

Redox oxidation (hypochlorite oxidation). Sodium hypochlorite in alkaline aqueous medium oxidizes potassium manganate to potassium permanganate, generating NaCl and NaOH as by‑products. Reaction proceeds at ambient to modest temperatures with stirring; water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis; aqueous HCl cleaves the 1,3‑dioxolane protecting group of 2‑(2‑bromoethyl)‑1,3‑dioxolane to give ethylene glycol and 2‑bromoacetaldehyde; typically reflux in aqueous HCl or at ambient temperature; solvent is water or aqueous HCl solution.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (deoxygenation) of a primary alcohol; H₂ with a metal catalyst (Raney Ni, Pd/C, Pt) converts 3‑methyl‑1‑heptanol to 3‑methylheptane with water as by‑product; conditions: high‑pressure H₂ (50–100 atm), elevated temperature (120–150 °C), solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol.

Redox reaction between iodic acid and hydroiodic acid; HIO₃ oxidizes I⁻ from HI to elemental I₂ while itself being reduced, yielding iodine and water; carried out in aqueous solution, often heated; no special catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification via acyl chloride); converts prop‑2‑ynoyl chloride to phenyl propiolate by attack of sodium phenoxide, yielding NaCl as by‑product; typically performed in dry aprotic solvents such as THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Type: strong hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Purpose: convert pent‑4‑ynoic acid into pent‑4‑yn‑1‑ol while preserving the alkyne. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ reduces the –COOH group to –CH₂OH, producing aluminum hydroxide as by‑product. Typical conditions: dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, addition of LiAlH₄ at 0 °C followed by reflux for 1–3 h. No additional catalyst; inert atmosphere is essential.

Type: Acid–base displacement (generation of hydrogen chloride gas). Purpose: Produce gaseous HCl and sodium bisulfate from inexpensive reagents. Key transformation: H2SO4 + NaCl → NaHSO4 + HCl↑; the strong acid protonates chloride, displacing it as volatile HCl while forming the acid salt of sulfuric acid. Typical conditions: Concentrated (≈98 %) sulfuric acid added to solid NaCl in a dry flask, gentle heating (100–150 °C) to evolve HCl gas, which is collected or passed into a downstream absorber. No solvent other than the acid; the reaction is self‑sustaining, no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of acetyl cyanide with ethoxide; sodium ethoxide attacks the carbonyl of CH₃COCN, displacing cyanide to give ethyl acetate and NaCN; performed in anhydrous ethanol under reflux; purpose is ester synthesis.

Buchwald‑Hartwig N‑arylation; couples an aryl iodide with pyrrole to form N‑phenylpyrrole; key transformation is C–N bond formation with NaI by‑product and regeneration of Pd(0); typically performed under inert atmosphere at 80‑120 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene, dioxane or THF, using Pd(OAc)₂, a bulky phosphine ligand (tri‑tert‑butylphosphine) and sodium tert‑butoxide as base.

Fischer esterification; acetic acid reacts with cyclodecanol in the presence of an acid catalyst (conc. H₂SO₄ or HCl) under reflux to give cyclodecyl acetate and water; common solvent is excess acetic acid or toluene with azeotropic water removal.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation); methanesulfonic acid reacts with methanol to give methyl methanesulfonate and water; catalyzed by concentrated sulfuric acid, refluxing methanol (60‑80 °C) with removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark) to drive the equilibrium.

This is a hydrolysis reaction. The methyl ester of N-methylcarbamic acid is cleaved by water, yielding methanol and N-methylcarbamic acid. The reaction typically occurs under aqueous conditions, possibly under acidic or basic catalysis, where water attacks the ester bond.

Lithiation‑carboxylation. n‑BuLi effects metal‑halogen exchange on the aryl iodide at −78 °C in dry THF, giving an aryl‑Li species which captures CO₂ to form the carboxylate; acidic work‑up affords 4‑methoxybenzoic acid. Conditions: 2–3 equiv n‑BuLi, THF, −78 °C → 0 °C, CO₂ (dry ice or balloon), then 1 M HCl quench.

Electrophilic addition of HBr to an alkene (Markovnikov addition); converts the C=C of 1‑methylcyclohexene into a C–Br bond yielding 1‑bromo‑1‑methylcyclohexane. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or ether; no catalyst is required.

Electrophilic addition (halogenation); Br2 adds across the C=C double bond of styrene to give the vicinal dibromide 1,2-dibromo-1-phenylethane. The reaction proceeds via a bromonium ion intermediate and gives anti addition. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); proton transfer from acetic acid to hydroxylamine generates the ionic pair hydroxylammonium acetate. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at 0 °C to rt; no additional reagents or catalysts are needed.

Double displacement precipitation; purpose is to generate insoluble copper(II) sulfide and soluble ammonium perchlorate; key transformation: Cu(ClO4)2 + (NH4)2S → CuS(s) + 2 NH4ClO4; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Thermal cracking (pyrolysis) of an internal alkene; 2,3,4-Trimethylpent-2-ene undergoes C–C bond scission at high temperature (≈400–600 °C) to yield the smaller olefin 2,3-dimethyl-1-butene and ethylene. Conducted in the gas phase under inert atmosphere (e.g., N2); no catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an allylic chloride with acetate ion to form an ester (cinnamyl acetate). Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, or DMSO) with NaOAc, often under reflux; a phase‑transfer catalyst may be employed to enhance the reaction rate.

Conversion of a primary alcohol to a chloride using thionyl chloride; thionyl chloride reacts with 1,2‑propane diol to replace one hydroxyl group by chlorine, producing 1‑chloro‑2‑propanol together with gaseous HCl and SO₂. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to rt, with an added base (pyridine or triethylamine) to absorb HCl.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid–base reaction between iron(II) acetate and nitric acid; the acetate ligands are protonated to give acetic acid while nitrate ions coordinate to Fe(II) forming ferrous nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst is required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); NaOH hydrolyzes ethyl pyrrole‑2‑carboxylate to the corresponding carboxylic acid (pyrrole‑2‑carboxylic acid) and ethanol. Conducted in aqueous NaOH, usually under reflux; after completion the mixture is acidified to isolate the acid.

Acid‑solubilisation/anion exchange of terbium(III) phosphate with hydrochloric acid. Used to convert the insoluble phosphate into soluble terbium(III) chloride while regenerating phosphoric acid. TbPO₄ + 3 HCl → TbCl₃ + H₃PO₄. Typically carried out by refluxing the solid phosphate in concentrated HCl (4‑6 M) at 80‑100 °C until dissolution is complete. Water acts as solvent; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation). Dimethylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetyl fluoride, displacing fluoride to give N,N‑dimethylacetamide and HF. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; the generated HF may be scavenged with a weak base (e.g., pyridine).

Reductive dehalogenation (metal‑mediated halogen exchange). Activated zinc metal reduces 1,1,1,2,3,3‑hexachloropropane removing two equivalents of chloride as ZnCl₂ and forming the alkene 1,1,2,3‑tetrachloropropene. Commonly carried out in dry ether or THF under reflux with zinc dust.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution. The sulfhydryl anion (HS⁻) from sodium hydrosulfide attacks methyl chloride, displacing chloride to afford methanethiol and NaCl. Reaction proceeds in polar protic or aprotic solvents (e.g., aqueous ethanol) at ambient temperature; excess NaSH drives the reaction to completion.

Selective reduction of aldehyde to primary alcohol. Sodium borohydride delivers hydride to the carbonyl of cyclohexanal, yielding cyclohexanol after work‑up. Conducted in methanol, ethanol, or THF at 0 °C to rt; the reaction is quenched with dilute acid or water.

Peroxide oxidation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes As2Se3, converting As(III) to arsenic acid (H3AsO4) and Se(IV) to selenous acid (H2SeO3); usually carried out by stirring the solid in dilute (30 %) H2O2 at room temperature or mild heating (25–60 °C); aqueous solution, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base protonation of an alkoxide; generates hexan‑1‑ol from its sodium alkoxide; sodium hexan‑1‑olate receives a proton from HCl to give hexan‑1‑ol and NaCl; typically carried out in aprotic solvents such as THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to rt; no catalyst needed.

Reductive dehalogenation (zinc‑mediated coupling). o‑Bis(bromomethyl)benzene is reduced by zinc dust in glacial acetic acid; the benzylic bromides are replaced by hydrogens, producing ortho‑xylene while ZnBr₂ forms as a by‑product. Reaction performed by refluxing the mixture; acetic acid serves both solvent and proton source.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of HBr to an alkyne. Hydrogen bromide adds across acetylene in a Markovnikov fashion, giving vinyl bromide (bromoethene). Typically carried out at low temperature (0–25 °C) in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride; no catalyst is required.

Type: acid–base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: generate calcium levulinate for use as a biodegradable detergent or fertilizer additive. Key transformation: two equivalents of levulinic acid deprotonate calcium carbonate, forming calcium levulinate, releasing CO₂ and water. Typical conditions: stir aqueous suspension of levulinic acid and solid CaCO₃ at ambient temperature until gas evolution ceases. No organic solvent required; the reaction proceeds in water.

Sulfonylation (activation of alcohol); methanesulfonyl chloride reacts with cyclohex‑2‑en‑1‑ol to form the corresponding mesylate ester, a good leaving group for subsequent substitution reactions. Triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl, giving triethylammonium chloride. Commonly carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine, 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere.

Hydrolysis (de‑acetylation) of N‑acetylbenzotriazole; water cleaves the N‑acetyl bond to regenerate 1H‑benzotriazole and release acetic acid. Typically performed in aqueous medium, often heated (50‑100 °C) without additional catalyst.

Metathesis (acid–salt exchange) between nitric acid and barium formate; the acid protonates the formate anion, yielding formic acid and barium nitrate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; excess HNO₃ may be used to drive the reaction to completion.

Acid chloride alcoholysis; nucleophilic acyl substitution of a carbamoyl chloride with methanol to give a methyl carbamate; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to rt, using a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize the released HCl.

Redox reaction of cesium metal with dilute nitric acid; cesium is oxidized to Cs⁺ forming cesium nitrate, while nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen monoxide (NO) and water is generated. Carried out in aqueous, dilute HNO₃ (≈1 M) at low temperature (0‑25 °C) under an inert atmosphere to control vigor of the metal dissolution.

Oxidation reaction; chlorine oxidizes thiocyanate anion to thiocyanogen while being reduced to chloride. Key transformation: 2 SCN⁻ → (SCN)₂; Cl₂ → 2 Cl⁻. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at 0–5 °C with chlorine gas bubbled through a sodium thiocyanate solution; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic sulfonation followed by condensation to form the sulfonamide sulfaquinoxaline; chlorosulfonic acid sulfonates quinoxaline (or forms a sulfonyl chloride intermediate) which then reacts with p‑phenylenediamine to give the sulfonamide product, liberating HCl. Performed in a strong‑acid medium (often chlorosulfonic acid or anhydrous SO₂Cl₂) at 0‑50 °C, typically using inert solvents such as dichloromethane or chloroform.

Ester acetylation (acylation of an alcohol): converts the primary hydroxy group of methyl 5‑hydroxyhexanoate into an acetate ester, yielding methyl 5‑acetoxyhexanoate and acetic acid. Typical conditions involve stirring the substrate with excess acetic anhydride (1–2 equiv) in an aprotic solvent such as pyridine, dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to reflux; pyridine or DMAP is used as a base to trap the generated HCl/AcOH and drive the reaction to completion.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne bearing nitrile groups: acetylenedicarbonitrile (NC‑C≡C‑CN) is hydrogenated with H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO₂) to reduce the triple bond, affording butanedinitrile (NC‑CH₂‑CH₂‑CN). Conditions: 1–3 atm H₂, ethanol or methanol solvent, 25–80 °C, 2–6 h.

Oxidative C‑H hydroxylation of ellipticine using dimethyldioxirane (DMDO); DMDO transfers an oxygen atom to the 9‑position of ellipticine to afford 9‑hydroxyellipticine. Reaction is carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, with DMDO generated in situ from acetone and oxone or used as a solution in acetone.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) between strontium chloride and sodium carbonate; forms insoluble strontium carbonate; SrCl2(aq) + Na2CO3(aq) → SrCO3(s) + 2 NaCl(aq); performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); conversion of propan-1‑amine to its hydrochloride salt. The amine accepts a proton from HCl, giving the ionic propan‑1‑amine·HCl solid. Usually carried out in aqueous HCl at 05 °C to control exotherm and minimize volatilization of the amine.

Double nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1,2‑diiodoethane by ammonia; each carbon undergoes displacement of iodide by NH₃, producing ethylenediamine and hydrogen iodide. Conducted in excess aqueous or alcoholic ammonia, often under reflux (60‑80 °C); the HI formed can be neutralized with a base if desired.

Oxidative cleavage/oxidation using potassium permanganate; the alkene of indene is oxidized to the carbonyl compound 1‑indanone while KMnO4 is reduced to MnO2 precipitate and water is formed; typical conditions are aqueous alkaline medium (NaOH or KOH), gentle heating (reflux) or controlled temperature, with KMnO4 added portionwise; MnO2 precipitates out, and water is the solvent.

Transesterification; purpose: exchange the methyl ester for an ethyl ester; key transformation: methyl 6‑aminohexanoate + EtOH → ethyl 6‑aminohexanoate + MeOH; typical conditions: excess ethanol, catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOEt), reflux to drive off methanol; common solvent: ethanol itself (used in large excess); often a Dean‑Stark trap is used to remove methanol.

Transfer hydrogenation (catalytic hydrogenation) using formic acid as the hydrogen donor; purpose is to reduce anthracene to 9,10‑dihydroanthracene while oxidizing formic acid to CO2. Key transformation: addition of two hydrogen atoms across the central aromatic ring of anthracene. Typical conditions: PdCl2 (or Pd on carbon) catalyst, aqueous or alcoholic solvent, 80–120 °C, inert atmosphere; excess formic acid serves both hydrogen source and solvent.

Double‑displacement precipitation: Silver propionate reacts with ammonium chloride, yielding a white precipitate of silver chloride and ammonium propionate in solution. Carried out in water at room temperature; AgCl is removed by filtration.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of 1H‑benzotriazole; purpose is to introduce a nitro group at the 5‑position. Key transformation: substitution of a hydrogen atom on the benzotriazole ring by a nitro (‑NO2) group, producing water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: concentrated HNO3 (often with conc. H2SO4 as a catalyst) at 0–5 °C to control regioselectivity, performed in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as glacial acetic acid or neat acid mixture.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange anions to isolate barium iodate. Key transformation: replacement of chloride ions from BaCl2 with iodate ions from HIO3, forming insoluble Ba(IO3)2 and liberating HCl into solution. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; the precipitated barium iodate is filtered and washed, while the HCl remains in the filtrate.

Hydrolysis of phosphorus trifluoro dichloride (PCl2F3); purpose is to decompose the halogenated phosphorus compound to yield phosphoric acid and hydrogen halides. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on PCl2F3, replacing the two Cl and three F atoms with OH groups, generating HCl, HF, and H3PO4. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, controlled addition of water to the phosphorus halide at 0–25 °C to moderate the exothermic reaction; the mixture is often diluted with water after completion.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt hydrolysis). Potassium hydroxide acts as a base to liberate cyclohexylamine from its hydrochloride salt, producing cyclohexylamine, KCl and water. Conducted in water, usually at room temperature; no additional reagents needed.

Reductive dechlorination (hydrogenolysis) of zirconium tetrachloride; purpose is to lower the oxidation state of zirconium from +4 to +2 while producing hydrogen chloride gas. Key transformation: cleavage of two Zr‑Cl bonds by H2, forming ZrCl2 and HCl. Typical conditions: high‑temperature furnace (400–600 °C) under a flow of dry H2 gas, often in a tubular reactor; no solvent is used, and the reaction is conducted under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction in aqueous medium; calcium hydroxide neutralizes sodium dihydrogen phosphate, generating soluble sodium hydroxide and insoluble calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate as a precipitate. Conducted at ambient temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst required; often performed in a beaker or reactor with filtration of the solid product.

Thermal cracking of a straight‑chain alkane; high‑temperature (400‑800 °C) pyrolysis, often over silica‑alumina or zeolite catalyst, breaks C–C bonds to give a smaller alkane (ethane) and an alkene (propene).

Selective reduction of the ketone carbonyl of xanthone to the secondary alcohol xanthydrol using sodium borohydride. Typical conditions: NaBH4 (1–1.5 equiv) added to a solution of xanthone in methanol, ethanol or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, reaction complete within 1–3 h. No additional catalyst; work‑up involves aqueous quench and extraction.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of thiophene to give mainly 2‑nitrothiophene. Mixed acid system (concentrated HNO3/H2SO4) generates the nitronium ion (NO2⁺). Reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C initially, then allowed to warm to ≤25 °C to limit polymerization. Solvent is the sulfuric acid medium; no external catalyst. Product isolated by quench with ice water and extraction.

Reaction type: Transesterification. Purpose: Exchanges the butyl group in an ester with a phenolic group. Key: Phenol acts as a nucleophile to displace butanol from the ester. Conditions: Heat; catalyzed by acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOH); solvent like toluene or alcohol.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification of methyl benzoate with isopropanol to afford isopropyl benzoate and methanol. Uses a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H2SO4, p‑TsOH) and excess isopropanol as both reactant and solvent. Reaction refluxes (≈80–120 °C) for several hours; removal of methanol (e.g., by azeotropicillation drives the equilibrium to completion. No additional catalyst needed.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification); purpose is to form an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates butanoic acid to an O‑acylurea, which is attacked by benzyl alcohol to give benzyl butanoate and dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Performed at 0 °C to rt in dry dichloromethane; catalytic DMAP often added to accelerate; reaction is run under inert atmosphere.

Condensation/cyclocondensation of glyoxal with cyanamide to form 2‑aminooxazole, releasing water. Typically performed by heating equimolar amounts of glyoxal and cyanamide in a polar protic solvent (water, ethanol) or under solvent‑free conditions at 80‑120 °C for 1–3 h. Neutral or mildly acidic conditions favor ring closure; no metal catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous scandium sulfate reacts with sodium phosphate to precipitate scandium phosphate while sodium sulfate stays dissolved; typical conditions are room‑temperature aqueous stirring; no catalyst, water is the solvent.

Halogen exchange reaction converting 2,2‑difluoroacetyl chloride to 2,2‑difluoroacetyl fluoride using hydrogen fluoride. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often in a dry solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0‑25 °C, with HF (or pyridinium HF) as reagent. Hydrogen chloride gas is evolved; the acid fluoride product is isolated after removal of solvent and neutralization of HCl. No external catalyst is necessary.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of phenol with chlorine gas; purpose is synthesis of 2,3,5,6‑tetrachlorophenol; key transformation: successive chlorine electrophile attacks on the activated phenol ring produce tetrachlorophenol and hydrogen chloride; typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH solution) to dissolve phenol, excess Cl₂ gas passed at 0‑30 °C with stirring; water solvent; no additional catalyst.
Acid‑base neutralization; sulfuric acid protonates the ammonium fumarate salt yielding freeic acid and ammonium sulfate; performed in water at room temperature, no special reagents required.

Nucleophilic substitution (alkylation of a nucleobase); 3‑chloro‑1,2‑propanediol reacts with guanine in basic aqueous NaOH (or NaHCO₃) to replace the chloride by a guanine substituent, forming penciclovir after deprotonation and work‑up. Commonly carried out in polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) at elevated temperature (50‑80 °C) with excess base to promote SN2 displacement; product isolated by precipitation or chromatography.

Acylation (acyl substitution) of a diamine – ethylenediamine reacts with two equivalents of acetic anhydride to give N,N‑diacetyl‑ethylenediamine, releasing two equivalents of acetic acid; usually performed under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as pyridine, dichloromethane or acetonitrile, which also acts as acid scavenger.

Strong reduction of an aliphatic methyl ester to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; reaction performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, delivering the corresponding 4‑methylpentanol and methanol (from the methoxy group) after aqueous work‑up.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; aqueous KOH reacts with mercuric chloride exchanging anions to form soluble potassium chloride and insoluble mercury(II) oxide, water is produced; typically carried out in water at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde – tribromoethanol is oxidized by Dess‑Martin periodinane to give tribromoacetaldehyde; carried out in a dry, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; the by‑product is iodobenzene‑derived acetate.

Direct chlorination of thorium dioxide to thorium tetrachloride; a high‑temperature gas‑phase halogenation where ThO₂ reacts with Cl₂ to produce volatile ThCl₄ and O₂; usually carried out at 800‑1000 °C under a chlorine flow, sometimes with a carbon reductant; no solvent; product collected by condensation.

Acidic oxidative conversion of a side‑chain alkyl group to a ketone – ethylbenzene is oxidized by sodium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid to acetophenone, with chromium(VI) reduced to chromium(III) sulfate and water formed; reaction is run at reflux (≈100 °C) in aqueous acidic medium, often with stirring to ensure contact between organic substrate and the aqueous oxidant.

Redox (carbothermic reduction); carbon reduces selenium dioxide to elemental selenium with evolution of CO2; employed to prepare pure selenium; conducted at high temperature (600–1000 °C) in a furnace under inert or reducing atmosphere; solid reactants mixed intimately; no additional catalyst required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl phenyl carbonate with sodium hydroxide yielding sodium phenoxide, methanol and carbon dioxide; carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (80–100 °C) without additional catalyst; provides phenoxide salt for further transformations.

Oxidative desulfurization of a thiourea – tetramethylthiourea reacts with hydrogen peroxide, oxidizing the thio‑carbonyl to a carbonyl and releasing elemental sulfur, affording tetramethylurea and water; typically performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent at ambient temperature, sometimes buffered mildly acidic to neutral pH to control peroxide decomposition.

Metal reduction: Sodium amalgam reduces samarium(III) chloride to samarium(II) chloride, generating a low‑valent Sm(II) reagent; performed in dry THF under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to rt, with NaCl as by‑product.

Reductive amination: Piperazine condenses with 3‑chloro‑4‑fluorobenzaldehyde to form an imine that is reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride, yielding 3‑chloro‑4‑fluorophenylpiperazine; carried out in methanol or ethanol (often with a catalytic amount of AcOH) at 0–25 °C.

Acid‑base deprotonation: tert‑butylammonium iodide is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide, which abstracts the proton from the ammonium ion, yielding free tert‑butylamine, sodium iodide and water; carried out in water or water/ethanol at room temperature, no catalyst.

Thioester formation (acylation of a thiol): Acetyl chloride reacts with benzyl mercaptan to give benzyl thioacetate and HCl; typically run in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt with a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to trap the acid.

Epoxide ring‑opening azidolysis: Sodium azide attacks ethylene oxide, opening the ring to produce 2‑azidoethanol; performed in polar aprotic solvents (DMF or DMSO) at 0 °C to rt, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal (dioxolane) formation: Ethylene glycol condenses with formaldehyde generated from paraformaldehyde in the presence of Montmorillonite K‑10, yielding 1,3‑dioxolane and water; heated (≈110 °C) often solvent‑free or in toluene, with water removed by azeotropic distillation.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; swaps nitrate for formate to isolate copper(II) formate, which often precipitates from aqueous solution. Typically performed by dissolving Cu(NO₃)₂ and NaHCOO in water, stirring at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, then filtering off the solid Cu(HCOO)₂. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification (Fischer esterification) of ethanol with in‑situ generated trifluoroacetic acid from sodium trifluoroacetate and H₂SO₄, yielding ethyl trifluoroacetate. Conducted by mixing ethanol, NaCF₃CO₂ and a catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄, then refluxing to drive water removal. Excess ethanol serves as solvent; removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) improves yield.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of 4‑hydroxybenzonitrile, installing bromine atoms at the 3‑ and 5‑positions to give 3,5‑dibromo‑4‑hydroxybenzonitrile with HBr as by‑product. Usually carried out by adding Br₂ dropwise to a solution of the substrate in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or glacial acetic acid) at 0 °C to room temperature. A Lewis acid catalyst such as FeBr₃ can be used but is often unnecessary because the phenolic OH activates the ring.

Hydrolysis/decomposition of tin(II) acetate in water, producing tin(II) oxide precipitate and acetic acid. The reaction is performed by heating an aqueous suspension of Sn(CH₃COO)₂, often under reflux, allowing the oxide to form and settle. No additional catalyst is required; water acts as both reactant and solvent.

Copper(II) chloride‑catalyzed oxidative coupling of 2‑chlorophenol and 2,4‑dichlorophenol in the presence of molecular oxygen to form 2,3,7,8‑tetrachlorodibenzofuran, with water as the only small‑molecule by‑product. Typical conditions involve stirring the phenols in an organic solvent such as acetonitrile or toluene, adding a catalytic amount of CuCl₂, and bubbling O₂ (or using air) at temperatures of 80–120 °C. The reaction proceeds via radical or Cu‑mediated oxidation leading to C–O bond formation and cyclization.

Halogenolysis/oxidative cleavage; dimethylmercury reacts with chlorine to break the Hg‑C bond, producing methyl chloride and methylmercury chloride; typically carried out in a dry inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride at low temperature under inert atmosphere, no catalyst required.

Halogen exchange fluorination; thiophosphoryl chloride is fluorinated by elemental fluorine, replacing three chlorine atoms with fluorine to give phosphorothioic trifluoride and chlorine monofluoride gas; performed in the gas phase or in a dilute fluorine stream at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in a quartz reactor, no solvent or additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative aromatic hydroxylation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes 2,4‑dichlorobenzene to 2,4‑dichlorophenol, generating water as the by‑product; usually catalyzed by transition‑metal ions (e.g., Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺) or solid acid catalysts in aqueous acidic medium, temperatures 25‑80 °C, water as solvent.

Hydride reduction of acid chloride; lithium aluminium hydride reduces butyryl chloride to n‑butanol by delivering hydride to the carbonyl carbon; conducted in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C then warmed to reflux; stoichiometric LiAlH₄ is used, no additional catalyst.

Dehydration (E1/E2 elimination): 2‑fluoroethanol loses water to give fluoroethylene. Usually performed with a strong acid (e.g., concentrated H2SO4) at high temperature (150–180 °C). Reaction may be carried out neat or in the acid as solvent; no external catalyst beyond the acid.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation); arsenic pentachloride decomposes upon heating to release chlorine gas and form arsenic trichloride; carried out in a sealed tube or under inert atmosphere at 150‑200 °C, no solvent or catalyst required.

Esterification (condensation) to triglyceride; three molecules of caprylic (octanoic) acid react with glycerol, eliminating three waters to give tricaprylin; acid‑catalyzed (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) or enzymatic (lipase) under reflux with removal of water, often in toluene or using excess acid, temperatures 180‑200 °C.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) with an acid chloride; furnishes N‑butyl‑3‑nitrobenzamide. n‑Butylamine is reacted with 3‑nitrobenzoyl chloride in a dry, non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or CHCl3) at 0 °C to 20 °C, in the presence of a base such as triethylamine, pyridine, or N‑methylmorpholine to capture the generated HCl.
