The reaction mixture is stirred under nitrogen; after completion, the organic layer is washed to remove the amine‑hydrogen chloride salt. No metal catalyst is required.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of 4‑tert‑butylphenol using N‑bromosuccinimide; the reaction selectively brominates the ortho positions to give 2,6‑dibromo‑4‑tert‑butylphenol and succinimide as the by‑product; typically performed in CHCl3 or CCl4 at ambient temperature, often with light or a catalytic amount of acid to promote bromine generation.

Acid dissolution of antimony oxychloride: SbOCl reacts with concentrated hydrochloric acid to regenerate antimony trichloride and water. Typically carried out in aqueous HCl solution, sometimes gently heated to accelerate. No catalyst; used to convert the oxychloride back to the halide form.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration (Markovnikov addition) of prop‑1‑en‑2‑ylbenzene to give 2‑phenyl‑2‑propanol. Sulfuric acid (typically 5–10 % H2SO4) protonates the double bond, forming a benzylic carbocation that is attacked by water. The reaction is carried out in aqueous medium under reflux (≈80–100 °C). The net transformation converts the alkene into a tertiary benzylic alcohol.

Grignard carboxylation; tert‑butylmagnesium chloride reacts with carbon dioxide in anhydrous ether (or THF) at ‑78 °C to 0 °C, forming the tert‑butyl carboxylate which on acidic work‑up (aqueous HCl) gives pivalic (trimethylacetic) acid; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) forming an alkyl nitrite; tert‑butyl chloride is treated with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO₂ + HCl) in a cold aqueous or biphasic medium, yielding tert‑butyl nitrite and HCl; typically performed at 0–25 °C, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed redox decomposition of a nitrate; concentrated H₂SO₄ heated (≈150–200 °C) with aluminum nitrate causes nitrate reduction to NO₂ gas while sulfate replaces nitrate to give Al₂(SO₄)₃ and water; the reaction is carried out neat, no solvent, and the NO₂ is evolved.

Halogenolysis/oxidation; elemental bromine oxidizes bismuth(III) selenide to bismuth tribromide and elemental selenium. The mixture is heated, often in carbon tetrachloride or CS₂ under reflux, to promote complete conversion; no external catalyst.

LiAlH₄ reduction of octan‑3‑yl acetate. Purpose: fully reduce the ester to two alcohols. Key transformation: R‑OCOCH₃ + 4 [H] → R‑OH (3‑octanol) + CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol). Typical conditions: dry ether or THF, addition of LiAlH₄ under N₂ at 0 °C followed by reflux; quench with water then dilute acid. No additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition of ammonia to an isothiocyanate; phenyl isothiocyanate is reacted with aqueous ammonium acetate (or ammonia) at reflux (water or water/ethanol) to give 1‑amino‑3‑phenylthiourea; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Double‑displacement acid‑base (metathesis); solid beryllium bromide is mixed with concentrated H₂SO₄ and gently heated, producing hydrogen bromide gas and solid beryllium sulfate; the reaction is typically performed in a closed tube or under a gas‑scrubbing setup, no solvent needed.

Double replacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to prepare insoluble lead(II) cyanide from soluble salts. Aqueous solution of potassium cyanide reacts with lead(II) sulfate, exchanging anions to give soluble potassium sulfate and precipitated lead(II) cyanide. Typically carried out in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Transmetallation/alkylation of an organomercury compound; key transformation is replacement of the chloride on ethylmercury chloride by an ethyl group from ethyl‑lithium, producing diethylmercury and lithium chloride. Conducted at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere (argon), in an aprotic ether solvent such as THF or diethyl ether; no additional catalyst.

Ring-opening hydrolysis of malonic anhydride with ammonia. General type: hydrolysis. Purpose: formation of malonic acid and its ammonium salt. Key transformations: ammonia reacts with the cyclic anhydride to yield one molecule of malonic acid and one equivalent of ammonium malonate. Conditions: room temperature. Solvents: aqueous or alcoholic ammonia.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride by cyanide; synthesis of 3‑chloropropionitrile. 1,3‑Dichloropropane is treated with potassium cyanide in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often with a phase‑transfer catalyst, at 50–80 °C. One chloride is displaced giving KCl and the mononitrile product.

High‑temperature gas‑phase redox (disproportionation) reaction; reduction of carbon dioxide by silicon monoxide. CO₂ reacts with SiO at >1000 °C (often in a furnace flow of inert gas) to produce carbon monoxide and solid silica (SiO₂). No solvent; the reaction proceeds under dry, high‑temperature conditions.

Redox reduction of iodine by thiosulfate; sodium thiosulfate reduces iodine to iodide while being oxidized to tetrathionate; overall: I₂ + 2 Na₂S₂O₃ → Na₂S₄O₆ + 2 NaI; fundamental reaction in iodometric titrations and starch indicator decolorization; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often near neutral pH; no catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation); conversion of 4‑ethoxybenzoic acid to its ethyl ester. The acid is refluxed with excess ethanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid, typically 60–80 °C. Water formed is removed by azeotropic distillation or a Dean–Stark trap. Ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using a chromium(VI) pyridine complex (trioxobis(pyridine)chromium). Cyclohexanol is oxidized in dichloromethane (or another aprotic solvent) at room temperature, yielding cyclohexanone, pyridine (released from the complex), and chromium(III) oxide as a solid by‑product. The reagent acts as a stoichiometric oxidant; no external catalyst is needed.

Metal‑mediated reduction of a quinoline N‑oxide to quinoline; deoxygenation using zinc in acetic acid. 1‑Oxidoquinolin‑1‑ium (quinoline N‑oxide) is combined with zinc powder in glacial acetic acid, refluxed to give quinoline and zinc acetate. The acetic acid acts as solvent and proton source; zinc serves as the reducing agent.

Oxidative acid digestion (acid‑base plus redox); used to dissolve copper arsenate and convert arsenic to soluble arsenic acid while forming copper nitrate. Key transformation: Cu3(AsO4)2 + HNO3 → 3 Cu(NO3)2 + 2 H3AsO4. Performed with concentrated nitric acid, heating to 80‑120 °C in aqueous solution; no catalyst required.

Redox oxidation of iron(II) to iron(III) by persulfate; purpose is to generate ferric sulfate and reduce persulfate to sulfate. Key transformation: 2 FeSO4 + K2S2O8 → Fe2(SO4)3 + K2SO4. Conducted in aqueous solution, usually at ambient or mildly elevated temperature, pH neutral to slightly acidic; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement/precipitation metathesis; prepares mercury(II) telluride and exchanges iodide for telluride. Key transformation: HgI2 + Na2Te → HgTe(s) + 2 NaI. Carried out in aqueous medium with stirring at room temperature, often under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; no catalyst required.

Condensation/dehydration synthesis of nitramide from hydroxylamine and nitrous acid; purpose is nitramide preparation. Key transformation: HO‑NH2 + HNO2 → H2N‑NO2 + H2O. Performed in dilute acidic aqueous solution at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to limit side reactions; no catalyst involved.

Halogen‑exchange (fluorination) of disulfur dichloride; replaces chlorine atoms with fluorine, releasing chlorine gas. Key transformation: S2Cl2 + F2 → S2F2 + Cl2. Conducted in the gas phase, dry conditions, typically at low temperature (‑78 to 0 °C) in a fluorination apparatus; no solvent or catalyst required.

Kornblum‑type oxidation of benzyl bromide by dimethyl sulfoxide; converts a benzylic halide to benzaldehyde while reducing DMSO to dimethyl sulfide and generating HBr. Key transformation: C6H5CH2Br + (CH3)2SO → C6H5CHO + (CH3)2S + HBr. Performed in polar aprotic solvent (often DMSO itself) at room temperature to gentle reflux, sometimes with a base (e.g., triethylamine) to trap HBr; no metal catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to exchange metal cations and isolate insoluble copper(II) carbonate. Ferrous carbonate reacts with copper(II) sulfate in aqueous solution, forming a precipitate of CuCO₃ while FeSO₄ remains dissolved. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at room temperature, stirring; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to convert soluble yttrium sulfate into insoluble yttrium oxalate. Oxalic acid reacts with Y₂(SO₄)₃ in water, producing Y₂(C₂O₄)₃ solid and liberating H₂SO₄. Conditions solution, often heated to improve solubility; no catalyst; water as solvent.

Hydroboration‑oxidation of an alkene; provides anti‑Markovnikov addition of water to 2‑heptene to give 2‑heptanol. First, diborane (or BH₃·THF) adds across the C=C bond in anhydrous ether to form the alkyl‑borane intermediate; then aqueous H₂O₂/NaOH oxidizes the borane to the alcohol. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere, ether (or THF) for hydroboration, followed by aqueous 30 % H₂O₂ with NaOH at 0‑25 °C; no additional catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of selenophene; purpose is to introduce a chlorine substituent at the most activated 2‑position. Key transformation: Cl₂ adds across the aromatic π‑system, generating 2‑chloroselenophene and HCl as by‑product. Typical conditions: dilute Cl₂ gas passed into a solution of selenophene at 0 °C to rt in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as chloroform, carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; sometimes a Lewis acid (e.g., FeCl₃) is employed to promote the reaction.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification (Fischer esterification) of adipic anhydride with methanol to afford dimethyl adipate. p‑Toluenesulfonic acid protonates the anhydride, facilitating nucleophilic attack by methanol; the intermediate collapses, releasing water and forming the di‑ester. Conditions: reflux in excess methanol or toluene (Dean‑Stark apparatus) at 60‑80 °C, catalytic amount of PTSA; water is removed to drive equilibrium.

Double displacement (metathesis) complexation; aims to generate soluble bismuth citrate by reacting bismuth sulfate with citric acid. Citric acid ligates Bi³⁺, forming bismuth citrate while sulfuric acid is released into solution. Conducted in water at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; no catalyst required; aqueous medium is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (protecting group installation); the aldehyde functionality of 4‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde is converted to a 1,3‑dioxolane ring by condensation with ethylene glycol in the presence of p‑toluenesulfonic acid as a Brønsted acid catalyst. Typical procedure uses dry dichloromethane or toluene with molecular sieves or a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water; reaction is performed at room temperature to reflux, giving the protected pyridine derivative.

Acidic nitrosation (nitrosamine synthesis); guanidine is treated with aqueous sodium nitrite in the presence of hydrochloric acid, generating nitrous acid in situ which nitrosates the guanidine nitrogen to afford N‑nitrosoguanidine. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to 5 °C to control nitrosating species, in water, and the by‑products are water and sodium chloride.

Halogenation‑oxidation (metal halide synthesis); chlorine gas oxidizes titanium(II) chloride to titanium(III) chloride, effecting a redox conversion from Ti(II) to Ti(III) while incorporating an additional chloride ligand. The reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions, usually in a dry inert atmosphere, with chlorine bubbled through a suspension of TiCl₂ in a non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or toluene at low to moderate temperature.

Methyl ester formation with diazomethane; diazomethane methylates the carboxylic acid to give methyl 2‑chlorobutyrate, with evolution of N₂ gas; reaction run at –5 to 0 °C in diethyl ether or THF under inert gas; diazomethane generated in situ.

Metal–water reaction (hydrolysis of a lanthanide metal); dysprosium metal reacts with liquid water, being oxidized to dysprosium(III) hydroxide while liberating hydrogen gas. The reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature or with mild heating; excess water ensures complete conversion and the evolution of H₂ is typically observed as bubbling.
double displacement reaction; purpose: form copper(II) oxalate; transformation: replacement of acetate with oxalate in cupric acetate; aqueous medium at room temperature; no catalyst

Reaction type: phosphorylation (esterification) of a primary alcohol. Purpose: formation of sn‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate, a key intermediate in lipid metabolism. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the terminal primary hydroxyl of glycerol on phosphoric acid, forming a mono‑phosphate ester and releasing water. Typical conditions: heating glycerol with excess phosphoric acid (often 85 % aqueous) at 120‑150 °C, sometimes under reduced pressure to remove water; the reaction can be conducted in the melt (no external solvent) or in a water‑rich medium. No external catalyst is required, though the acidity of phosphoric acid drives the reaction.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅). Butyric acid reacts with PCl₅ to afford butyryl chloride, while producing phosphoryl chloride (POCl₃) and hydrogen chloride gas. The reaction is carried out in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; the exothermic mixture is typically cooled initially before gradual addition of PCl₅.

Base‑catalyzed crossed aldol condensation (Claisen‑Schmidt type) leading to a conjugated diketone; two equivalents of benzaldehyde undergo sequential aldol addition to acetone in the presence of aqueous sodium hydroxide in ethanol, followed by dehydration to give dibenzylideneacetone and water as the only by‑product. The mixture is kept cold during base addition to avoid side reactions, then warmed to promote condensation and full dehydration.

Mild oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane; the benzylic primary alcohol of 4‑hydroxyphenethyl alcohol is oxidized to 4‑hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde under neutral conditions. Typical conditions employ 1.1–1.5 equivalents of DMP in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, with the reaction conducted under nitrogen and quenched with aqueous sodium bicarbonate.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of benzene with acetyl chloride using diethylaluminum chloride as Lewis acid; purpose to install an acetyl group onto the aromatic ring forming acetophenone; key electrophilic aromatic substitution; by‑product ethyl chloride generated from the aluminum ethyl groups; typical conditions: anhydrous, inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, carbon tetrachloride or nitrobenzene.

Acid‑base salt metathesis between silver cyanate and perchloric acid; proton transfer from HClO₄ to the cyanate ion yields cyanic acid (HOCN) and silver perchlorate; generally performed in aqueous or mixed solvent at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Carbonation (gas‑liquid) reaction: aqueous barium acetate is treated with carbon dioxide (dissolved as carbonic acid) leading to precipitation of barium carbonate and formation of acetic acid; carried out by bubbling CO₂ through the solution at ambient temperature; used for in‑situ generation of barium carbonate.

Selective reduction of a nitrile to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H); converts 2‑phenoxyacetonitrile to 2‑phenoxyacetaldehyde with release of ammonia; key transformation is C≡N → CHO; typical conditions: 1 equiv DIBAL‑H, −78 °C to 0 °C, in dry THF or toluene under nitrogen; quench with aqueous acid.

Double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; exchanges K⁺ from potassium ferrocyanide with Ca²⁺ from calcium chloride to precipitate calcium ferrocyanide while forming soluble potassium chloride; carried out at room temperature in water with stirring, no catalyst required.

High‑temperature oxidation/hydrolysis of tungsten diselenide (WSe₂) by steam; produces volatile hydrogen selenide (H₂Se) and solid tungsten(VI) oxide (WO₃); carried out in a furnace at ≥600 °C with a flow of water vapor; no solvent or catalyst required.

This is a hydrogenolysis reaction, removing the chlorine atom from 1-chloro-1-methylcyclopropane using molecular hydrogen. Palladium on carbon catalyzes the cleavage of the carbon-chlorine bond, producing 1-methylcyclopropane and hydrochloric acid. The reaction requires hydrogen gas under atmospheric or elevated pressure, with common solvents including ethanol or ethyl acetate. This reaction is often used to deprotect or modify cyclopropane derivatives containing good leaving groups like chloride.

Metathesis/acid‑base precipitation; replaces iodide with sulfide to give gallium(III) sulfide and hydroiodic acid, key formation of Ga₂S₃ precipitate and release of HI gas; usually carried out by bubbling H₂S gas through an aqueous solution of GaI₃ at 0–50 °C; water as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation; aqueous samarium nitrate reacts with ammonium hydroxide to precipitate samarium hydroxide (Sm(OH)3) while forming soluble ammonium nitrate; carried out at near‑room temperature with gentle stirring; the hydroxide precipitate is filtered, washed and dried; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic addition of ethylmagnesium bromide (Grignard reagent) to the carbonyl of N,N‑dimethylformamide followed by acidic work‑up; serves as a formylation to give propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO); key step is attack of Et⁻ on the formyl carbon, then elimination of dimethylamine; performed anhydrously in ether or THF at 0 °C to rt, then quenched with dilute acid.

Copper(I) iodide‑catalyzed Ullmann‑type amination of 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde with aqueous ammonia; replaces the aryl chloride with an amino group to afford 2‑aminobenzaldehyde; key C–Cl → C–NH₂ substitution; typical conditions: CuI (≈10 mol %), optional ligand (e.g., 1,10‑phenanthroline), aqueous NH₃, heating at 100‑120 °C in DMSO or water; inert atmosphere often employed.

Cyanate addition (urea formation) with sodium cyanate; analogous to reaction 3, tert‑butylamine reacts with NaOCN to afford tert‑butylurea and sodium hydroxide. Conducted in water or ethanol, warmed to 50–80 °C; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; KMnO4 in aqueous alkaline medium (often dilute solution, pH ~ 8‑10) at room temperature to gentle heating oxidizes the 2‑chloro‑2‑methylpropanal carbonyl to the corresponding 2‑chloro‑2‑methylpropanoic acid; work‑up typically involves acidification and extraction, no additional catalyst required.

Redox (halogen oxidation of a metal oxide); chlorine gas oxidizes arsenic(III) oxide, releasing O2 and forming arsenic trichloride; core change is oxidation of oxide to elemental oxygen and chlorination of arsenic; conducted by passing dry Cl2 over heated solid As2O3 in an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Base‑promoted deprotonation (salt hydrolysis) of benzylammonium chloride; aqueous NaOH neutralizes the ammonium ion, liberating free benzylamine, while forming NaCl and water; performed at ambient temperature in water or aqueous ethanol; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of 2‑methylindole with Br₂, an EAS reaction that installs bromine at the C‑3 position of the indole ring, producing 2‑methyl‑3‑bromoindole and hydrogen bromide; typically carried out in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, with slow addition of bromine to control over‑bromination.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a benzylic chloride to the corresponding benzylic alcohol; NaOH (often aqueous or ethanolic) attacks the diphenylmethyl chloride, displacing chloride and yielding diphenylmethanol after acid work‑up; reflux conditions (80‑100 °C) are common; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of an ester; under H₂ pressure (typically 30‑50 atm) and a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂, octyl acetate is reduced to the two corresponding primary alcohols, ethanol from the acetyl fragment and octanol from the octyl fragment; reactions are conducted in a suitable solvent (e.g., ethanol, THF) at 80‑150 °C.

Nitration/esterification; converts both hydroxyl groups of isosorbide into nitrate esters to give isosorbide dinitrate, a high‑energy explosive/vasodilator; key transformation is –OH → –ONO2 with loss of water; typically performed by refluxing isosorbide with fuming (concentrated) nitric acid, often in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid as a dehydration catalyst, at 0 °C to 40 °C under inert atmosphere; common solvent is excess nitric acid itself (no additional solvent needed).

Redox oxidation of a metal halide: MoBr3 is oxidized by O2 to MoO6 (as MoO3) while Br− is liberated as Br2. The reaction is a solid‑state oxidation (high‑temperature) where oxygen acts as the oxidant. Usually performed by heating a mixture of the bromide and air or pure O2 at 300–500 °C in a furnace; no additional catalyst is required.

Doubledis precipitationmetathesis) in aqueous solution: MnSO4 reacts with (NH4)2CO3, exchanging anions to give insoluble MnCO3 precipitate and soluble (NH4)2SO4. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed. No catalyst needed.

Reverse of reaction 1, a metathesis in concentrated sulfuric acid; dissolves terbium(III) phosphate back to the sulfate form by displacing phosphate with excess sulfate, producing Tb₂(SO₄)₃ and regenerating H₃PO₄; carried out in aqueous H₂SO₄ under heating and stirring; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic addition (halogenation) of a conjugated diene: 1,3‑Butadiene undergoes addition of two equivalents of Br2 across both C=C bonds, yielding the fully saturated 1,2,3,4‑tetrabromobutane. Typical conditions are solution of the diene in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as CCl4 or CHCl3, at 0 °C to room temperature, often under dark or dim light to control the rate. No catalyst is required.

Neutral/aqueous amide hydrolysis; hydrolysis of (2S)‑2‑amino‑3‑methylbutanamide in water to afford L‑valine and ammonia; can be carried out by heating the aqueous solution (often 100 °C) possibly with slight acid or base catalysis; no additional reagents required.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization). HBF₄ protonates the phosphate of (NH₄)₃PO₄, yielding phosphoric acid and ammonium tetrafluoroborate (NH₄BF₄). Reaction proceeds in water, usually at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Enzymatic decarboxylation (non‑oxidative) of cysteine sulfinic acid: The α‑carboxyl group of cysteine sulfinic acid is removed as CO2, converting the amino‑acid side chain into hypotaurine (2‑aminoethanesulfinic acid). In vivo the reaction is catalyzed by cysteine‑sulfinic‑acid decarboxylase, a pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate (PLP) dependent enzyme, operating in aqueous buffer at neutral pH (≈7.0) and physiological temperature (≈37 °C).

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) – sodium hydroxide attacks hexan‑2‑yl acetate to give sodium acetate and hexan‑2‑ol; the reaction is carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux, often in water or aqueous ethanol.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification (Fischer‑type) to form oxybuprocaine hydrochloride: p‑Aminobenzoic acid reacts with 2‑diethylaminoethanol in the presence of HCl, giving the ester linkage and the HCl salt of the product (oxy­buprocaine·HCl) with loss of water. The reaction is performed in an aprotic, non‑aqueous solvent such as toluene or benzene, under reflux with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water, or alternatively in dry dichloromethane with catalytic HCl. No metal catalyst is required.

O‑Methylation (nucleophilic substitution) of phenolic hydroxyls with dimethyl sulfate. Key transformation: conversion of both phenolic OH groups in bis(4‑hydroxyphenyl)methane to methoxy groups, yielding bis(4‑methoxyphenyl)methane and methyl hydrogen sulfate. Typical conditions: base (NaOH, K₂CO₃, or pyridine) in aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or dichloromethane, 0 °C to ambient temperature, under inert atmosphere. Dimethyl sulfate is used in slight excess; reaction is usually quenched with water after completion.

Type: Electrophilic quench of a Grignard reagent; purpose: convert cyclohexylmagnesium chloride to the corresponding alkyl iodide. Key transformation: nucleophilic carbon of the Grignard attacks I2, forming cyclohexyl‑I and MgICl. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, temperature 0 °C to rt. No additional catalyst required.

Type: SN2 halogen exchange (Finkelstein reaction); purpose: replace chlorine with iodine in chloroacetonitrile. Key transformation: I⁻ displaces Cl⁻ on the nitrile carbon, yielding iodoacetonitrile and NaCl precipitate. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone, reflux (or reflux‑compatible temperature), often with excess NaI to drive equilibrium. Reaction performed under inert atmosphere.

Type: Electrophilic aromatic nitrosation; purpose: introduce a nitroso group ortho to the hydroxyl of 2‑naphthol. Key transformation: NO⁺ (generated from nitrosyl chloride) attacks the activated aromatic ring, forming 1‑nitroso‑2‑naphthol and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: low temperature (0–5 °C) in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or dichloromethane) with careful control of acid buildup. Reaction often conducted under dry, inert conditions.

Type: Acyl transfer (amide formation) from an acid anhydride; purpose: acetylate piperidine to give N‑acetylpiperidine. Key transformation: the lone pair on the piperidine nitrogen attacks one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, displacing acetate and forming the amide; the liberated acetate protonates to give acetic acid. Typical conditions: neat or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane, at rt; often no external base is needed because the generated acetic acid can be removed. Mild heating can be applied if needed.

Type: Chalcogenide metathesis/redox exchange; purpose: swap tellurium for selenium, generating sodium selenide. Key transformation: Na₂Te reacts with elemental Se; selenium oxidizes the telluride to elemental tellurium while being reduced to selenide, producing Na₂Se. Typical conditions: high temperature (150–200 °C) in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., liquid ammonia, THF) under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

Transesterification between a bulk ester (butyl acetate) and a primary alcohol (ethanol) giving a new ester (ethyl acetate) and a new alcohol (1‑butanol); acid (e.g., H2SO4, p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOEt) catalyst is typical; reaction is run under reflux in an inert solvent such as toluene or without solvent, with removal of the more volatile product to drive equilibrium.

Type: Oxidation of a phosphorothioate to a phosphate; purpose: convert the P=S functionality to P=O to obtain the corresponding phosphate ester. Key transformation: peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the phosphorus, oxidizing the thio‑phosphate to the phosphate and generating acetic acid as a by‑product. Typical conditions: low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetone; stoichiometric amount of peracetic acid, often generated in situ from acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide. No metal catalyst is required.

Silylation reaction; converts benzoic acid into trimethylsilyl benzoate by replacing the hydroxyl group with a trimethylsilyl group; trimethylsilyl acetate acts as the silylation agent, generating acetic acid as a byproduct; commonly proceeds under mild conditions in a solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane; no catalyst typically required.

Hydrogenation reduction; transforms nitro groups in 2,4-dinitrotoluene into amino groups to yield 2,4-diaminotoluene; uses palladium on carbon as a catalyst and hydrogen gas as the reducing agent; conducted under hydrogen atmosphere in a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate at ambient or elevated temperature.

Acid-base protonation; hydrolyzes potassium thioacetate to thioacetic acid using hydroiodic acid as a strong acid proton source, producing potassium iodide as a byproduct; typically carried out in aqueous or polar protic solvents (e.g., water, acetic acid) without a catalyst.

DDQ (2,3-dichloro-5,6-dicyano-1,4-benzoquinone)-mediated oxidation; converts tetrahydrocarbazole into aromatic carbazole via dehydrogenation; DDQ acts as an oxidizing agent; reaction often occurs in a solvent like dichloromethane or acetonitrile, sometimes with acid catalysis (e.g., trifluoroacetic acid), at room temperature or heating.

General type: Hydrolysis. Purpose: Production of hydrazoic acid. Key transformation: Azide ion (N3-) acts as a weak base, protonated by water to form hydrazoic acid (HN3). Conditions: Room temperature, aqueous solution. Solvent: Water. No catalyst required.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann homocoupling of 2‑bromopyridine to give 2,2′‑bipyridine. Potassium carbonate deprotonates the pyridyl bromide and neutralizes generated HBr; CuI mediates C–C bond formation. Typical conditions: dry DMF or DMSO, 100–150 °C, inert atmosphere, 12–24 h. By‑product potassium bromide and copper(I) bromide are formed.

Double displacement precipitation reaction; phosphate anion from sodium phosphate reacts with copper(II) to form insoluble copper(II) phosphate precipitate while sodium acetate remains in solution; performed in water with stirring, sometimes at slightly elevated temperature; no catalyst needed.

Carboxylic acid alkylation; methylates acrylic acid using diazomethane to form methyl acrylate and nitrogen gas; proceeds via electrophilic methylation; commonly conducted in aprotic solvents (e.g., diethyl ether, THF) at low temperatures to prevent diazomethane decomposition.

Thermal oxidation (combustion) of a metal dichalcogenide. MoTe₂ is heated in an oxygen‑rich atmosphere (air or pure O₂) at 400–600 °C. The sulfide is oxidized, yielding molybdenum trioxide (MoO₃, volatile at the reaction temperature) and tellurium dioxide (TeO₂, solid). No catalyst; the reaction proceeds in the gas phase.

Condensation (intramolecular cyclodehydration); oxalic acid reacts with urea to form the heterocyclic 2,4‑oxazolidinedione, releasing one molecule of water; key step is formation of two C‑N bonds and loss of water to close the five‑membered ring; carried out by heating a mixture of the reagents (150‑200 °C) in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or xylene, often under reduced pressure to remove water; acid or base catalysts can accelerate the cyclization but are not always necessary.

Oxidation of tetrachlorophenol to tetrachloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone using potassium permanganate; typically performed in aqueous alkaline medium at room temperature to reflux, producing water and precipitating manganese dioxide as a by‑product.

Acyl transfer (esterification) of glycidol with acetic anhydride; usually catalyzed by a base or nucleophilic catalyst such as pyridine or DMAP in dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, yielding glycidyl acetate and one equivalent of acetic acid.

Dehydrogenative coupling of dimethylsilane (two equivalents) to give hexamethyldisilane and hydrogen gas; typically mediated by a transition‑metal catalyst such as Pt, Rh, or Ir under mild heating, often in an inert solvent like toluene or xylene.

Fischer esterification of 2‑ethylhexanol with 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoic acid to give 2‑ethylhexyl 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoate; carried out under reflux in toluene or a Dean‑Stark apparatus with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) to remove water and drive the equilibrium.

Oxidative cyclization of o‑phenylenediamine with sulfuryl chloride (SO₂Cl₂) to afford 1,2,4‑benzothiadiazine‑1,1‑dioxide; typically performed in a chlorinated solvent (CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to room temperature, where SO₂Cl₂ acts as a chlorinating and oxidizing agent to close the heterocyclic ring.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction used to exchange anions between salts; converts potassium hexafluorophosphate and 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium bromide into the ionic liquid 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium hexafluorophosphate and potassium bromide. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or methanol at ambient temperature; the insoluble potassium bromide is removed by filtration or extraction.

Transfer hydrogenation (reductive hydrogenation) of pyridine to piperidine using ammonium formate as the hydrogen source; the formate decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O while delivering hydrogen to the aromatic heterocycle, usually performed in a sealed tube at 80‑120 °C with a catalytic amount of a hydrogenation metal (e.g., Pd/C, Pt/C) in a polar solvent such as MeOH or EtOAc.

Acid–base neutralization and salt metathesis that converts mepivacaine hydrochloride to its free‑base form. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates the protonated amine, generating mepivacaine, water, and sodium chloride. Conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic media (e.g., water/ethanol) at room temperature with stirring; the free base is usually extracted into an organic solvent such as dichloromethane.

Free‑radical chlorination producing 2‑chloro‑2‑methylpropane (tert‑butyl chloride) and HCl. Same radical mechanism as above but abstracts a tertiary hydrogen, which is markedly more reactive; therefore this product is the major one. Conducted under UV or thermal initiation, Cl2 gas, in non‑reactive solvent (e.g., CCl4).

Double‑replacement precipitation reaction between calcium carbonate and thallium(I sulfate. The exchange of anions yields thallium(I) carbonate (which remains largely soluble) and calcium sulfate, which precipitates as gypsum. Performed in water at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; the solid calcium sulfate is isolated by filtration and the aqueous thallium carbonate solution may be further processed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde to 3‑pyridinemethanol. Molecular hydrogen is added across the carbonyl bond in the presence of a metal catalyst such as palladium on carbon, Raney nickel, or platinum oxide. The reaction is carried out in a solvent like ethanol or methanol, at 1–5 atm H₂ pressure and temperatures ranging from 0 °C to 50 °C, yielding the corresponding primary alcohol.

Oxime formation; nucleophilic addition‑elimination of hydroxylamine to a ketone carbonyl to give the corresponding oxime and water; purpose is functional‑group interconversion or protection of the carbonyl; typically carried out in ethanol or methanol at 0–25 °C, often with a weak base (pyridine) to neutralize the generated H⁺; no metal catalyst required.

Jones oxidation (secondary alcohol oxidation); chromic acid oxidizes 3‑chloro‑2‑butanol to the ketone 3‑chlorobutan‑2‑one while reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III) oxide and producing water; used to convert secondary alcohols to ketones; commonly performed in aqueous H₂SO₄/acetone mixture at 0–25 °C; solid CrO₃ is dissolved to generate the oxidant; no additional catalyst.

Halogenation of an alcohol (Appel‑type conversion of an aliphatic primary alcohol to a chloride); phosphorus trichloride reacts with chlorine to generate PCl₅ in situ, which converts 1‑hexanol to 1‑chlorohexane, releasing HCl and forming POCl₃; purpose is preparation of alkyl chlorides; usually carried out in anhydrous carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; no metal catalyst.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid using a strong chromic acid oxidant. The ethanol carbon bearing the OH is converted to a carbonyl then further to a carboxyl group, yielding acetic acid. Chromium(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) forming chromium(III) sulfate. Typically performed in aqueous sulfuric acid with potassium dichromate, refluxed at 60–80 °C; the medium is strongly acidic and aqueous, co‑solvent.

Double displacement precipitation where AgNO3 reacts with GaBr3 to precipitate AgBr and generate soluble Ga(NO3)3; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature, AgBr is filtered off, water or dilute acid serves as solvent.

Acid–base neutralization: potassium hydride deprotonates benzoic acid to afford potassium benzoate and hydrogen gas. The key step is proton transfer from the carboxylic acid to the hydride ion. Typically performed in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as THF or diethyl ether under an inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of a triazine hydrochloride salt; NaOH deprotonates 1,3,5‑triazine·HCl to give free 1,3,5‑triazine, water, and NaCl; purpose is liberation of the free heterocycle; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; straightforward stoichiometric neutralization, no catalyst.

S‑alkylation of 2‑aminoethanethiol with iodoacetic acid yielding S‑carboxymethylcysteamine and HI; thiolate attack on the iodoacetyl carbon forms the thioether; carried out in aqueous or mixed solvent with a base (Na₂CO₃, NaHCO₃) to deprotonate the thiol and suppress amine reaction, typically at 0–25 °C.

Gas‑phase condensation/dehydration; CO2 reacts with H2S to give carbonyl sulfide (COS) and water. Purpose: synthesis of COS, a useful intermediate. Key transformation: O=C=O + H‑S‑H → O=C=S + H₂O. Typical conditions: elevated temperature (300–600 °C) and often a solid metal‑oxide catalyst (e.g., Al₂O₃, ZnO, TiO₂). Reaction carried out in the gas phase, no solvent.

Combustion (oxidation) reaction; ethane reacts with excess oxygen, ignited by heat or flame, to fully oxidize to carbon dioxide and water; highly exothermic, conducted at high temperature with sufficient O₂, no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of a thioester; purpose is to cleave the thioester into a carboxylate and a thiol; key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of S‑propyl ethanethioate, breaking the C–S bond to give acetate ion and propyl thiolate, which is protonated on workup to afford propane‑1‑thiol; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–2 h; solvent: water (may be mixed with a miscible organic co‑solvent); after reaction the mixture is acidified (pH≈2) to liberate the thiol.

Direct combination (oxidation) synthesis; forms dysprosium(III) chloride by reacting elemental dysprosium with chlorine gas. Key transformation: 2 Dy + 3 Cl2 → 2 DyCl3. Performed at elevated temperature (300–600 °C) in a dry chlorine stream, often in a quartz tube or furnace under inert carrier gas. No solvent or catalyst; high‑temperature gas‑phase conditions are essential.

Acid‑base conversion of a selenate salt to selenic acid; sodium selenate reacts with hydrochloric acid to give aqueous selenic acid (H₂SeO₄) and sodium chloride; purpose is preparation of the strong acid from its salt; performed in water at room temperature; simple stoichiometric neutralization, no catalyst.

Redox oxidation‑precipitation reaction. Chromium(II) chloride is oxidized by molecular oxygen in aqueous solution to chromium(III) hydroxide, which precipitates as a green solid. Chloride ions combine with protons from water to give hydrochloric acid. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, ambient temperature, exposure to air or O₂ gas; no added catalyst required.

Type: hydrolysis. Purpose: generate nitrous acid and hydrochloric acid from nitrosyl chloride. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on NOCl cleaves the N–Cl bond, producing HNO₂ and HCl. Conditions: aqueous solution, often kept cool (0‑25 °C) and protected from light due to instability of NOCl; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; generates terbium carbonate for material preparation or purification; Tb³⁺ exchanges nitrate for CO₃²⁻ yielding solid Tb₂(CO₃)₃ and soluble NaNO₃; performed in aqueous medium, typically at room temperature with vigorous stirring; water solvent, no catalyst.

Esterification (methylation) of a carboxylic acid using diazomethane. Diazomethane reacts with the carboxyl group of caffeic acid to form the methyl ester (methyl caffeate) while liberating nitrogen gas. Reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an ether or THF solvent under inert atmosphere; no catalyst is needed.

Condensation/cyclization reaction forming hexamethylenetetramine (urotropine). Ammonia reacts with the formaldehyde equivalents released from trioxane (the cyclic trimer of formaldehyde) to give water and the tetrahedral heterocycle hexamethylenetetramine. Conducted in aqueous ammonia solution, usually heated to reflux (≈100 °C); no additional catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition/precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction. Sodium carbonate reacts with rhodium(III) nitrate in aqueous solution; upon heating the carbonate decomposes, releasing CO₂ gas and converting rhodium(III) to insoluble rhodium(III) oxide, while sodium nitrate remains in solution. Conditions: aqueous mixing followed by drying and calcination at 400–600 °C; no catalyst needed.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation of a ketone. Peracetic acid oxidizes 1‑phenyl‑1‑pentanone to the corresponding ester (phenyl pentanoate) with concomitant formation of acetic acid. The reaction is typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0–25 °C, with slow addition of the peracid; no additional catalyst is required, though a catalytic amount of acid can accelerate the process.

E2 β‑elimination (dehydrohalogenation) of a tertiary alkyl bromide using a bulky strong base; yields the alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑butene and potassium bromide. Conducted with potassium tert‑butoxide in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMSO or THF, usually under reflux; no catalyst needed.

Reductive amination. 3‑Methylphenylacetone reacts with methylamine to form an imine intermediate, which is subsequently reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to afford 3‑methylamphetamine (a secondary amine) and water. Conducted in methanol or a methanol/dichloromethane mixture at pH 5–6, usually at 0 °C to room temperature; NaBH₃CN serves as the reducing agent.

Reduction; the triphenylmethane dye malachite green is chemically reduced to its colorless leuco form using zinc metal as the electron donor in an acidic aqueous medium (typically dilute HCl). The reaction proceeds at ambient or gentle reflux temperature, with zinc dust providing electrons that convert the central carbonyl-like group to a hydroquinone-like center, yielding leucomalachite green. No additional solvent beyond water is required; the purpose is decolorization or preparation of the reduced dye for analytical or synthetic steps.

Double‑displacement (acid–base) metathesis; malic acid reacts with calcium acetate in aqueous solution to exchange the cations, forming calcium malate (the calcium salt of malic acid) and liberating acetic acid. The mixture is usually heated under reflux to drive off the produced acetic acid and shift equilibrium toward salt formation. Water serves as the reaction medium; the goal is preparation of calcium malate as a dietary supplement or analytical reagent.

SN2 hydrolysis of 1‑bromo‑2‑propanol with aqueous sodium hydroxide to regenerate propane‑1,2‑diol; purpose is removal of the bromide to restore the diol. Key transformation: Br replaced by OH, forming NaBr. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH, heating (often 50‑80 °C); water is the solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Eschweiler‑Clarke methylation of 2‑heptanamine: formaldehyde reacts with the primary amine to form an iminium intermediate, which is reduced by formic acid, installing a methyl group to give N‑methyl‑2‑heptanamine; by‑products are CO₂ and H₂O. The reaction is typically carried out at 80‑100 °C in a sealed vessel using excess formic acid and formaldehyde (often as a 37 % aqueous solution) in a solvent such as MeCN or MeOH.

Fischer esterification (condensation); benzoic acid and 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol condense to form (4‑methoxyphenyl)methyl benzoate with loss of water. The reaction is acid‑catalyzed, commonly using a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, and performed under reflux in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or benzene. Water is removed continuously (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation. The purpose is synthesis of the benzyl benzoate ester for fragrance or polymer applications.

Salt formation (acid‑base neutralization); free‑base DL‑methamphetamine is protonated by hydrochloric acid to give DL‑methamphetamine hydrochloride, a crystalline salt. The reaction is typically carried out in anhydrous ether, ethanol, or dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, with gaseous or aqueous HCl added dropwise. The resulting hydrochloride salt is less volatile, more water‑soluble, and is the pharmaceutical form used for dosing.

Acid‑base neutralization; gamma‑hydroxybutyric acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate in aqueous solution, yielding sodium gamma‑hydroxybutyrate (the sodium salt of GHB) along with carbonic acid, which rapidly decomposes to carbon dioxide and water. The reaction proceeds readily at room temperature with gentle stirring; evolution of CO₂ indicates completion. The purpose is to generate the more water‑soluble sodium salt for analytical standards or formulation studies.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution; acylation of hydrogen cyanide by acetic anhydride to give the acyl cyanide (acetyl cyanide) and acetic acid. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions at 0 °C to rt in aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a mild base (e.g., pyridine) to scavenge the generated acid.

Acid‑base salt formation; theophylline (a weak base) reacts with ethylenediamine dihydrochloride to afford theophylline ethylenediamine salt (aminophylline). Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic medium, usually at ambient temperature with stirring; pH adjustment may be used to ensure complete neutralization. No catalyst required.

Halogen displacement/redox exchange; elemental chlorine oxidizes bromide in BeBr₂ to molecular bromine while chlorine is incorporated into the metal halide, yielding BeCl₂ and Br₂; conducted in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dry CCl₄) or in the gas phase, often with gentle heating to promote the exchange.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (ammonolysis); bromide of 3‑bromopropan‑1‑ol is displaced by the amide ion from sodium amide, yielding 3‑amino‑1‑propanol. Carried out in liquid ammonia (or dry THF) at –33 °C to0 °C under inert atmosphere; sodium amide serves as both base and nucleophile.

Sulfonyl‑fluoride exchange (SuFEx) condensation; the amine of 2,4‑diaminopyrimidine attacks the sulfonyl fluoride group of 4‑aminobenzenesulfonyl fluoride, forming the sulfonamide bond of sulfadoxine and releasing HF. Usually performed in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO) with a tertiary amine base (triethylamine, N‑methyl‑imidazole) at rt to mild heating (40–80 °C).

nucleophilic substitution (sn2), purpose ether synthesis (williamson ether), transformation alkoxy group installation via alkoxide attack on methyl electrophile. common solvent is polar aprotic such as dmso or acetone.

Hydride reduction / transmetallation; lithium triethylborohydride (LiHBEt₃) reduces triisopropylsilyl chloride, transferring ethyl groups to boron to give triethylborane while the silicon center is protonated to triisopropylsilane, and LiCl precipitates. Conducted under argon in dry THF at 0 °C to rt; no additional catalyst required.

Direct solid‑state synthesis (high‑temperature combination); elemental indium reacts with selenium in a 2:3 stoichiometry to afford indium(III) selenide (In₂Se₃). Performed in a sealed evacuated quartz tube or under flowing inert gas at 700–900 °C for several hours, then cooled slowly; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; exchanges cations between KOH and cadmium selenite to give insoluble cadmium hydroxide precipitate and soluble potassium selenite. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Base‑induced deprotonation to generate a phosphorus ylide (Wittig reagent); methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide is deprotonated by n‑butyllithium to afford methylenetriphenylphosphorane and LiBr. Conducted under inert atmosphere in dry THF (or Et₂O) at –78 °C to 0 °C; no additional catalyst needed. Used as the key intermediate for Wittig olefination of aldehydes or ketones.

Condensation/cyclization to form a benzimidazole heterocycle; o‑phenylenediamine reacts with ethyl isothiocyanate in the presence of NaOH, undergoing nucleophilic addition and intramolecular cyclization to give 2‑(ethylthio)benzimidazole. Usually performed in refluxing ethanol or aqueous ethanol; NaOH acts as both base and catalyst. The reaction installs an ethylthio substituent on the benzimidazole core.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of 1‑methoxy‑3‑methylbenzene catalyzed by iron(III) bromide. The methoxy group directs substitution to the para position, yielding 4‑bromo‑1‑methoxy‑3‑methylbenzene and hydrogen bromide. Typical conditions: Br₂ (1 equiv) and FeBr₃ (≈10 mol %) in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt.

Electrophilic addition of halogen to an alkene; purpose is to install two vicinal chlorine atoms on the ring. Chlorine adds across the C=C of cycloundecene via a cyclic halonium ion intermediate, yielding 1,2‑dichlorocycloundecane. The reaction is usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature, with no catalyst, in an inert non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane. Light should be avoided to prevent radical side reactions.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; 3‑iodoindolizine reacts with phenylboronic acid using Pd(OAc)₂ and Na₂CO₃ as base to give 3‑phenylindolizine, NaI and Pd⁰; typical conditions employ DMF/H₂O or dioxane/H₂O, heated 80‑110 °C under nitrogen.

O‑methylation (alkylation) of an indol‑5‑ol using dimethyl sulfate; the phenolic hydroxyl is methylated to afford 5‑methoxyindole. Carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetone with a mild base (e.g., NaH, K₂CO₃) at 0 °C to room temperature. Dimethyl sulfate acts as the methylating agent; no additional catalyst is needed, though a base is required to deprotonate the phenol.

Acid‑catalyzed ketal formation (acetalization); cyclohexanone reacts with ethylene glycol in the presence of catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid to give the ethylene acetal (cyclohexanone ethylene acetal). Typical conditions involve reflux in toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water; p‑TsOH provides the Brønsted acid catalyst. The reaction protects the carbonyl group as a stable cyclic acetal.

Type: base‑catalyzed etherification (glycidylation) of a polyol to form a triglycidyl ether. Purpose: synthesize an epoxy resin monomer. Key transformation: each hydroxyl of trimethylolpropane attacks epichlorohydrin, forming an oxirane (glycidyl) group and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: 50–80 °C, excess epichlorohydrin, NaOH or KOH (10–20 % w/w) as catalyst, often in diphenyl ether or toluene as solvent; HCl is removed as gas or neutralized with a base.

Type: oxidative chlorination / halogen‑sulfide exchange. Purpose: convert palladium(II) sulfide into palladium(II) chloride while liberating elemental sulfur. Key transformation: Cl₂ oxidizes S²⁻ to S⁰ and substitutes Cl⁻ for S²⁻ in the metal lattice, yielding PdCl₂ and S. Typical conditions: dry Cl₂ gas passed over solid PdS at 200–300 °C in a sealed quartz tube or furnace under inert atmosphere; no solvent required.

Type: transesterification (alcohol–ester exchange). Purpose: prepare 2‑phenylethyl benzoate from ethyl benzoate. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the phenylethanol oxygen on the carbonyl carbon of ethyl benzoate, displacing ethanol and forming the new ester. Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous toluene or benzene with catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, 1–5 %) or base (e.g., NaOMe); removal of ethanol by azeotropic distillation drives equilibrium to completion.

Type: high‑temperature solid‑state redox (reduction of Nb₂O₅ by Si). Purpose: produce niobium(IV) oxide and silicon dioxide. Key transformation: Si is oxidized from 0 to +4, while Nb⁵⁺ in Nb₂O₅ is reduced to Nb⁴⁺, yielding SiO₂ and NbO₂. Typical conditions: intimate powder mixture heated to 1300–1600 °C in a furnace under inert (Ar) or slightly reducing atmosphere; no solvent, reaction proceeds in the solid state.

Type: metal oxidation by concentrated nitric acid (oxidizing acid). Purpose: dissolve manganese metal and generate manganese(II) nitrate while reducing nitrate to nitrogen dioxide. Key transformation: Mn⁰ is oxidized to Mn²⁺; nitrate ion is reduced to NO₂ gas; water is formed. Typical conditions: cold (0–20 °C) to moderate (25–50 °C) concentration of HNO₃ (≈68 %), slow addition of Mn to control vigorous evolution of brown NO₂; reaction often conducted in a fume hood with cooling bath.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; Fe³⁺ exchanges anions with Na⁺ to form insoluble iron(III) arsenate which precipitates and soluble sodium nitrate remains in solution; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst.

Type: crossed Claisen condensation (base‑catalyzed acylation of a ketone). Purpose: synthesize ethyl 3‑phenyl‑3‑oxopropanoate (ethyl benzoylacetate). Key transformation: enolate of acetophenone, generated by NaOEt, attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethyl acetate; after elimination of ethoxide, the β‑keto‑ester product is formed. Typical conditions: anhydrous ethanol as solvent, NaOEt (1.1 equiv) added at 0 °C then warmed to reflux (≈78 °C); reaction mixture quenched with dilute acid and product isolated by extraction.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation). N‑methyl‑aniline reacts with benzoyl chloride to give N‑methyl‑benzamide and HCl. Same general conditions as the acetylation: dry solvent (CH₂Cl₂ or THF), 0 °C to rt, and a stoichiometric base (pyridine, TEA) to neutralize HCl. Reaction proceeds in 1‑2 h; the amide is isolated after aqueous work‑up and column chromatography if needed.

Acid‑base neutralization / salt formation; concentrated sulfuric acid dissolves antimony(III) oxide, converting the basic oxide into antimony(III) sulfate while releasing water. Usually carried out by heating antimony trioxide in 95‑100 % H₂SO₄ at 150–200 °C under reflux; the acid acts as both reactant and solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative dimerization (disulfide formation); hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the thiol group of 2‑mercaptopyridine N‑oxide, coupling two molecules to give the disulfide dipyrithione and water. Performed in aqueous or mixed organic‑aqueous medium at 0–40 °C, often under neutral to slightly basic pH; H₂O₂ is the sole oxidant, no metal catalyst is essential though trace transition‑metal catalysts can accelerate the reaction.

Nucleophilic addition of cyanide to a carbonyl (cyanohydrin formation); acetaldehyde reacts with HCN (or NaCN/HCl) to give 2‑hydroxyacetonitrile (glycolonitrile); usually performed in water or methanol at 0–25 °C; base may be added to generate CN⁻; purpose is to introduce a nitrile and a hydroxyl group.

Kolbe‑Schmitt carboxylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution); sodium hydroxide deprotonates 4‑aminophenol to the phenoxide, which reacts with CO₂ under pressure to install a carboxyl group ortho to the phenoxide, affording 4‑aminosalicylic acid after acid work‑up. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH1–2 M), CO₂ at 5–10 atm, temperature 120–150 °C, followed by acidification with dilute HCl; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl sulfonate; sodium benzenethiolate attacks the methyl carbon of methyl p‑toluenesulfonate, displacing p‑toluenesulfonate anion and forming methyl phenyl sulfide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at 0 °C to reflux (25–80 °C); stoichiometric base (Na⁺) is already present, no extra catalyst required.

Salt metathesis / in‑situ generation of a nitronium salt; copper(II) nitrate reacts with anhydrous HF and BF₃, converting nitrate anions into nitronium tetrafluoroborate (NO₂⁺ BF₄⁻) while producing CuF₂ and water. Performed in a dry HF/BF₃ mixture at –30 to 0 °C under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); the BF₄⁻ counter‑ion stabilizes the nitronium ion, and no additional catalyst is employed.

Hydrolysis of a metal nitride; neodymium nitride reacts with water, cleaving the N³⁻ ion to release ammonia gas and forming neodymium hydroxide. Usually carried out by suspending NdN in excess water or steam and heating to 200–300 °C; the reaction proceeds spontaneously without catalyst, producing NH₃ gas that can be collected and Nd(OH)₃ as a solid precipitate.

. Nucleophilic substitution at silicon (silylation). Hydrogen cyanide donates the cyanide anion to chlorotrimethylsilane, displacing chloride to give trimethylsilyl cyanide while generating hydrogen chloride. Generally performed under anhydrous conditions in a dry non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often at 0 °C to room temperature, with an inert atmosphere; no catalyst is required.

Free radical halogenation (substitution). Purpose: synthesis of a primary alkyl bromide. Key transformation: a bromine radical abstracts a hydrogen from hexadecane, forming 1‑bromohexadecane and hydrogen bromide. Typical conditions: UV light or thermal initiation, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or benzene, often performed at reflux temperature.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation). Silver nitrate exchanges anions with europium tribromide in aqueous solution, precipitating insoluble silver bromide while forming soluble europium nitrate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon mixing, and the solid AgBr is filtered off. No additional reagents are needed.

Direct halogenation/formation of metal iodides. Iodine oxidatively reacts with magnesium antimonide, converting antimony to antimony triiodide and magnesium to magnesium iodide. The reaction is carried out by heating the solid mixture or suspending it in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., dry toluene or molten iodine) under an inert atmosphere to avoid moisture; stoichiometric amounts ensure complete conversion.

Oxidation–reduction (redox) in acidic medium. Sodium dichromate (Cr(VI)) oxidizes iodide ions from potassium iodide to elemental iodine while being reduced to chromium(III) sulfate; sulfuric acid provides the necessary acidity and forms potassium sulfate as a by‑product. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution, typically heated gently (≈60–80 °C) to accelerate the oxidation; the liberated iodine precipitates or dissolves in the acid, and the mixture is cooled before isolation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with hydroxide to form an alcohol. Key transformation: CH₃Br + NaOH → CH₃OH + NaBr. Usually carried out in aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) with heating (reflux or 80–100 °C) to increase rate; water is both solvent and reactant.

Acyl chloride esterification (acylation of phenol). Acetyl chloride reacts with 3,5‑dichlorophenol to form 3,5‑dichlorophenyl acetate; pyridine acts as a base to capture the generated hydrogen chloride, driving the reaction forward. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; the reaction mixture is stirred under nitrogen, and the crude product is isolated after aqueous work‑up and purification.

Type: conversion of a primary alcohol to a chloride using thionyl chloride (nucleophilic substitution). Purpose: install a chloro substituent on N‑methyl‑2‑hydroxyacetamide to give N‑methyl‑2‑chloroacetamide. Key transformation: OH → Cl with loss of SO2 and HCl. Conditions: anhydrous environment, reflux in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine (pyridine acts as HCl scavenger). No additional catalyst required.

Type: reduction of an amide to a primary amine (hydride reduction). Purpose: convert propionamide into propylamine. Key transformation: carbonyl of the amide is reduced, oxygen is removed as water and the nitrogen becomes an NH2 group. Conditions: LiAlH4 (1–2 equiv) in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, typically reflux or gentle heating; aqueous acid work‑up to protonate the amine. No extra catalyst.

Type: oxidative conversion of a benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid (KMnO4 oxidation). Purpose: oxidize toluene to benzoic acid. Key transformation: –CH3 → –COOH, Mn(VII) reduced to MnO2. Conditions: excess KMnO4 in aqueous alkaline medium (KOH or NaOH), heated to 80–100 °C until reaction completion, MnO2 precipitates; acidic work‑up isolates benzoic acid. No organic solvent or catalyst required.

Type: thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of a metal lactate (decarboxylation). Purpose: generate acetaldehyde from magnesium lactate. Key transformation: β‑hydroxy acid fragments to give acetaldehyde and carbon dioxide, leaving magnesium oxide as solid residue. Conditions: solid magnesium lactate heated at high temperature (≈300–400 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst employed.

Type: SN2 alkylation of phenoxide (nucleophilic substitution). Purpose: synthesize phenoxyacetic acid. Key transformation: phenoxide O− attacks the CH2Br carbon of bromoacetic acid, displacing Br− to form PhOCH2COOH. Conditions: sodium phenoxide in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or acetone) at 0 °C to reflux; stoichiometric NaBr is formed; no additional catalyst needed.
Direct oxidation of elemental selenium by oxygen to give selenium dioxide (SeO₂). Performed by heating selenium in a flow of O₂ or air at 200‑300 °C; no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Type: esterification of a diol with methacrylic anhydride (acylation/condensation). Purpose: prepare triethylene glycol dimethacrylate (a cross‑linkable monomer) and generate methacrylic acid as by‑product. Key transformation: each hydroxyl of triethylene glycol reacts with one equivalent of methacrylic anhydride, forming ester linkages and releasing methacrylic acid. Conditions: triethylene glycol mixed with 2 equiv methacrylic anhydride in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with catalytic DMAP or pyridine, mild heating (20–60 °C) under nitrogen; the acid by‑product is removed by washing.

Oxidation of thiirane (a three‑membered sulfide) to thiirane‑oxide (the sulfoxide) using potassium peroxymonosulfate (Oxone). The reaction transfers an oxygen atom to sulfur, generating water as a by‑product and leaving potassium bisulfate in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous or water‑acetone medium, ambient to mild heating, no additional catalyst required.

O‑methylation (alkylation) of a sulfonic acid using dimethyl sulfate; forms the methyl sulfonate ester and methyl hydrogen sulfate; key step is nucleophilic attack of the sulfonate oxygen on a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate; usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as pyridine or aqueous Na2CO3 at 0–25 °C to control exotherm; pyridine or a similar base scavenges the generated H2SO4.

Acid–base reaction of mercuric oxide with acetic acid; forms mercuric acetate and water; usually conducted by stirring HgO in glacial acetic acid or dilute acetic acid solution with gentle heating; solvent is acetic acid (or aqueous); no catalyst.

Strong oxidative conversion of 2‑chloro‑3‑methylphenol to 2‑chloro‑3‑methylbenzoic acid using potassium permanganate. The methyl group is oxidized to a carboxyl group while the phenolic oxygen is retained; MnO₂ precipitates and water is formed. Performed in alkaline aqueous solution, heated (reflux) with excess KMnO₄.

Acid‑base neutralization between sulfuric acid and sodium 3‑nitropropionate. Proton transfer converts the sodium salt to free 3‑nitropropionic acid and generates sodium hydrogen sulfate. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Grignard addition to an ester (nucleophilic acyl substitution); methylmagnesium bromide attacks the carbonyl of butyl propionate, the butoxy group departs as n‑butanol and two methyl groups add to give the tertiary alcohol 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol; typically performed in dry ether or THF under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, using excess Grignard reagent.

Acid–base metathesis/decomposition of ammonium phosphate; magnesium ammonium phosphate hexahydrate reacts with aqueous NaOH, the ammonium ion is liberated as NH₃ gas, magnesium precipitates as Mg(OH)₂, and sodium hydrogen phosphate remains in solution; performed in aqueous medium at ambient to mildly elevated temperature with vigorous stirring to evolve ammonia.

Thermal dehydration (condensation) of metasilicic acid; H₂SiO₃ loses water upon heating to give solid SiO₂ (silica) and H₂O; typically heated to 200–400 °C in a furnace or oven, no catalyst is required.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of a saturated cycloalkane; cycloheptane is converted to cycloheptene with the release of H₂, usually over a metal catalyst such as Pt, Pd, or Ni at 500–600 °C under an inert atmosphere; the reaction is driven by the high temperature and removal of hydrogen.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis). NaOH deprotonates the hydrochloride salt of N,N,N',N'-tetramethyl‑p‑phenylenediamine, liberating the free diamine and forming NaCl and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of ammonia. Ammonia attacks 1‑bromobutane three times, successively forming mono‑, di‑, and finally tributylamine with concomitant release of three equivalents of HBr. Conducted under reflux in anhydrous solvent (e.g., ethanol or diethyl ether) with excess 1‑bromobutane to drive the reaction to the tertiary amine; the reaction is moisture‑free and does not need a catalyst.

Solid‑state high‑temperature synthesis (carbonate decomposition and double‑replacement). Manganese carbonate decomposes to MnO and CO₂, which then reacts with MoO₃ to form manganese molybdate (MnMoO₄). Performed by grinding the powders together and calcining at 600–800 °C in a furnace under air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification. p‑Toluenesulfonic acid catalyzes the exchange of the ethoxy groups of diethyl phthalate with 2‑methoxyethanol, yielding dimethoxyethyl phthalate and ethanol as a by‑product. The reaction is run under reflux in excess 2‑methoxyethanol (which acts as solvent) and the volatile ethanol is removed (e.g., by distillation) to drive the equilibrium forward.

Fischer esterification (condensation) to give phenyl salicylate (salol). Salicylic acid reacts with phenol in the presence of a strong acid catalyst (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), forming phenyl salicylate and water. The reaction is performed under reflux in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or xylene, often with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to continuously remove water and shift the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (acidic hydrolysis). Purpose: convert N,N‑diethylbenzamide back to benzoic acid and regenerate diethylamine. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl carbon under strong acid, leading to cleavage of the C‑N bond and formation of benzoic acid plus the free amine; sulfuric acid provides the catalytic proton and also supplies the aqueous medium. Typical conditions: reflux the amide in excess concentrated H₂SO₄ with water (often 1 : 1 to 1 : 3 ratio) at 120–150 °C; after cooling, the mixture is neutralized and the products are extracted.

Fischer esterification of 3‑phenylpropanoic acid with methanol to give methyl 3‑phenylpropionate. Purpose is to protect the carboxyl group or prepare the ester for further reactions. Key transformation: carboxylic acid + MeOH ↔ methyl ester + H2O. Typical conditions: excess dry methanol, catalytic amount of concentrated H2SO4 (≈1–5 % v/v), reflux (≈65 °C) for 4‑12 h; removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark) drives equilibrium to the ester. Reaction performed in methanol as both reactant and solvent.

Oxidative dissolution (redox) of silver by hot concentrated nitric acid; metallic Ag reacts with conc. HNO₃ (~68 %) under reflux to form AgNO₃, nitrogen dioxide gas and water; performed in nitric‑acid/water mixture, no additional catalyst.

Catalytic oxidation of ethanol using tert‑butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP). In the presence of a metal or radical catalyst (commonly Fe(II), Cu(II), or Mn salts) the hydroperoxide oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde while being reduced to tert‑butanol, with water formed as a side product. Typically carried out in an organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) at room temperature to 80 °C; the catalyst is required to initiate the radical chain process.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration (acylation–condensation) of 2‑aminoethanol with acetic anhydride to afford a 2‑oxazoline and one equivalent of acetic acid. The anhydride first acetylates the amine, then the hydroxyl attacks the carbonyl, closing the five‑membered oxazoline ring and eliminating acetic acid. Conducted under reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, often in the presence of a base catalyst (e.g., pyridine) to scavenge the liberated acid.

Redox (metal displacement) reaction between elemental zinc and silver(I) oxide. Zinc is oxidised to ZnO while silver(I) oxide is reduced to metallic silver (2 Ag⁰). Usually carried out by mixing the solid reagents and heating gently (150‑250 °C) in a sealed tube or under an inert atmosphere; no additional solvent or catalyst is required.

Base‑promoted cleavage (saponification) of methyl dimethyldithiocarbamate with NaOH; hydroxide attacks the methyl thio‑group, liberating methanol and converting the species to its sodium salt, sodium dimethyldithiocarbamate. Conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous–organic solvent (e.g., water/ethanol) at ambient temperature; stoichiometric NaOH is used, no additional catalyst.

Type: nucleophilic addition of organolithium to a nitrile followed by hydrolysis (nitrile‑to‑ketone conversion). Purpose: synthesis of 4‑methylacetophenone. Key transformation: MeLi attacks the carbon of the nitrile forming a lithium‑imidate intermediate, which on aqueous work‑up is protonated and hydrolyzed to give the aryl methyl ketone and LiOH. Typical conditions: 1–2 equiv MeLi in dry THF or diethyl ether at –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere, then quench with cold water or dilute acid. No catalyst needed; dry etheric solvent is essential.

Reduction; LiAlH4 reduces the acetate ester (pentan-3‑yl acetate) to the corresponding secondary alcohol (pentan‑3‑ol) while the acetyl group is reduced to ethanol; performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous acid work‑up.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl bromide with trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN). The cyanide transferred from TMSCN attacks the primary carbon, displacing bromide as trimethylsilyl bromide and forming propionitrile (CH₃CH₂CN). The reaction is usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; a catalytic amount of a Lewis acid (e.g., ZnCl₂) can be added to enhance the rate.

Metal‑acid reaction (acid‑base redox); purpose is to generate hydrogen gas and the strontium salt; strontium metal is oxidized to Sr²⁺ while formic acid is deprotonated to formate and H⁺ is reduced to H₂; typically performed at ambient temperature under inert atmosphere in anhydrous ether or THF, using excess formic acid; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of aldehyde); purpose is to convert 4‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde to 4‑pyridylmethanol; the carbonyl C=O is reduced to a primary alcohol (CH₂OH); common conditions are H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 wt %), ethanol or methanol as solvent, 25–50 °C, reaction time 1–6 h; no additional reagents needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis of alkyl chloride); purpose is to replace the chloride with a hydroxyl group to give 3‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol; water (or OH⁻) attacks the primary carbon in an SN2 process, releasing HCl; typical conditions are reflux in aqueous NaOH or water at 80–100 °C2–4 h, followed by acid work‑up to isolate the alcohol; no catalyst required.

hydrolysis (reverse alkoxide formation); calcium methoxide reacts with water to regenerate calcium hydroxide and methanol; equilibrium shifts toward products with excess water; carried out at ambient temperature in aqueous medium; water is the solvent, no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution of alkyl bromide with ammonia (SN1/ SN2 depending on substrate); purpose is to synthesize 1‑adamantylamine; ammonia attacks the electrophilic carbon of 1‑adamantyl bromide, displacing Br⁻ and forming the amine, with HBr generated; usually carried out with excess liquid NH₃ or aqueous NH₃ under reflux (≈65 °C for liquid NH₃ or sealed tube at ≈100 °C), inert atmosphere; no metal catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; purpose is to deprotect the acetate and obtain furan‑2‑ylmethanol; aqueous HCl protonates the carbonyl, water attacks, and acetic acid is released, yielding the free alcohol; typical conditions are 1–2 M HCl, reflux at 60–100 °C for 2–6 h, followed by neutralization and extraction; HCl itself serves as the catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution – Gattermann‑Koch formylation; purpose is to introduce a formyl group para to the methoxy substituent of anisole, giving para‑anisaldehyde; CO and HCl in the presence of AlCl₃ (often with CuCl) generate a formyl cation that attacks the aromatic ring; reaction is performed under dry, inert conditions with CO gas (1–5 atm), dry HCl, Al₃ (1–2 equiv) in a non‑protic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or nitrobenzene, at 0 °C to room temperature for 2–8 h work‑up yields the aldehyde.

Redox/metal‑sulfur synthesis: Sulfur dichloride reacts with aluminum metal to form aluminum sulfide and liberate chlorine gas. This high‑temperature solid‑state reaction is performed without solvent, often in a sealed tube under an inert atmosphere. No catalyst is required; the driving force is the formation of strong Al–S bonds and release of Cl₂.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; purpose: isolate insoluble zinc oxalate while generating nitric acid in solution; key transformation: Zn(NO3)2 + H2C2O4 → ZnC2O4↓ + 2 HNO3; typical conditions: aqueous medium, usually at ambient or slightly cooled temperature to promote precipitation; solvent: water; no catalyst.

General type: acid‑halogenation (oxide dissolution in acid). Purpose: prepares soluble vanadium(II) chloride and generates water; useful for subsequent coordination or reduction chemistry. Key transformation: V²⁺O + 2 HCl → VCl₂ + H₂O. Typical conditions: V O is suspended in concentrated aqueous HCl and the mixture is heated gently (50–80 °C) with stirring until dissolution is complete; the solution may be filtered to remove insoluble residues. Common solvents/catalysts: concentrated hydrochloric acid; mild heating assists the reaction.

Fischer esterification of benzyl alcohol with acetic acid; purpose is to produce benzyl acetate; the reaction is acid‑catalyzed (e.g., catalytic H2SO4 or p‑TsOH) and proceeds via protonated acetic acid; water is formed as by‑product; typical conditions involve refluxing the alcohol in excess acetic acid with a few drops of strong acid, often with a Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water to drive equilibrium.

Hydrolysis of acetylhydrazide: Heating acetylhydrazide with water cleaves the N‑acetyl bond, yielding acetic acid and hydrazine. The reaction is a simple aqueous hydrolysis, typically carried out under reflux in water; an acid or base catalyst (e.g., dilute HCl or NaOH) can accelerate the process. No special solvent beyond water is needed.

Acidic conversion to soluble salt; sulfuric acid protonates sulfide in CdS producing H₂S gas and forming cadmium sulfate in solution. Performed by adding solid or aqueous CdS to dilute H₂SO₄ (≈1 M) at ambient temperature, often with stirring; water is the medium, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl sulfonate: Potassium thiocyanate displaces the p‑toluenesulfonate group of ethyl p‑toluenesulfonate, producing ethyl thiocyanate and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate. The reaction is performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at reflux; no catalyst is required.

N‑Methylation (Menshutkin reaction) of 2‑chloro‑phenethylamine: Methyl iodide alkylates the amine nitrogen to give 2‑chloroamphetamine. The reaction proceeds via an SN2 pathway in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, DMF) in the presence of a mild base such as K₂CO₃ or NaH to deprotonate the amine. Temperature is kept moderate (0–50 °C) to avoid side reactions; no additional catalyst is needed.

Reaction type: hydrolysis of a chloroformate (acid chloride) ester. Purpose: cleave the tert‑butyl chloroformate to give the corresponding alcohol, CO2 and HCl. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon, releasing CO2 and HCl while forming tert‑butanol. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, mild heating (30–60 °C) or ambient temperature; reaction may be performed under reflux. Solvent: water or a water/acetone mixture. The HCl generated can be neutralized with a base if desired.

Selective reduction of a nitro group with sodium dithionite: In aqueous solution, sodium dithionite reduces the nitro group of 3‑nitrobenzamide to an amine, affording 3‑aminobenzamide. The reaction is typically carried out at ambient temperature or mild heating (20–50 °C) under slightly alkaline conditions (pH ≈ 8–9). No organic solvent is required; the dithionite serves as the reductant.

Swern oxidation of 1‑propanol: Dimethyl sulfoxide is activated by oxalyl chloride at –78 °C in a dry aprotic solvent (commonly CH₂Cl₂). Triethylamine is added to deprotonate the intermediate, converting the primary alcohol to propionaldehyde. By‑products are dimethyl sulfide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and triethylammonium chloride. The reaction requires anhydrous conditions, low temperature, and the reagents listed; no metal catalyst is used.

Condensation (aminal formation) between ammonia and formaldehyde; purpose is to synthesize methanediamine (CH2(NH2)2) with water as by‑product. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of NH3 on the carbonyl carbon of HCHO followed by loss of H2O to give the bis‑amine. Typically carried out in aqueous solution or dilute ammonia, at ambient to moderate temperature (0–50 °C); excess ammonia drives the equilibrium. No catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type SN2) converting a bromoacetate to iodoacetate; purpose is to prepare 2‑iodoacetic acid; key transformation is substitution of bromide by iodide using NaI; ordinarily carried out in dry acetone where NaBr precipitates, driving the reaction forward; reflux of 2‑bromoacetic acid with excess NaI in acetone (or a acetone/ethanol mixture) for several hours gives 2‑iodoacetic acid after filtration and acidification; the reaction benefits from the poor solubility of NaBr in acetone.

Salt metathesis/precipitation double‑displacement reaction; used to exchange halide for acetate and to prepare platinum(II) acetate while precipitating silver bromide. Key transformation: Ag+ swaps its acetate for Br− from PtBr2, forming insoluble AgBr and soluble Pt(OAc)2.
